I want to be honest with you about how hard that is to say. Margaret and I have three children. The youngest starts school next fall. I have a mortgage. I have spent twenty years building something at that university. I am not a brave man by nature — I am a chemist who likes order and precision and going home for dinner.

But here is what I keep coming back to: what these men are asking me to do is lie, or something close enough to lying that the distinction doesn't hold up. Attending party meetings in 1933 during the worst economic collapse this country had seen — when a third of men couldn't find work — is not evidence of treason. It is evidence of desperation and idealism, neither of which is a crime. I know these colleagues. I know their character. Presenting their names to this committee, in this atmosphere, knowing what happens next to a man whose name gets entered into that record — that is not testimony. That is an accusation dressed up as cooperation.

And I have watched what happens. I have seen men name names and then get called back to name more names. The committee's appetite doesn't close. Cooperation is a door that opens inward.

There is also something I cannot escape: my children will eventually be old enough to ask me what I did. I can explain poverty to them. I cannot explain to them that I destroyed two men's lives and livelihoods to protect my pension, when those men had done nothing I would not have considered myself in darker times.

So here is what I am prepared to do. I will appear. I will answer questions about my own associations, my own beliefs, fully and honestly. I will invoke the Fifth Amendment regarding the names of others, and I understand the cost of that. I will not perform the ritual of accusation this committee requires to sustain itself.

I need you to help me do this correctly — to protect what can be protected legally. And I need to go home tonight and tell Margaret before she reads it somewhere else.

What I will not do is hand them names.

That's my answer.

*Long pause. Looking at the ground.*

I've been turning this over every night for three weeks. Can't sleep. Lie there listening to the kids breathe and doing the arithmetic again, same arithmetic, comes out the same every time.

Here's what I know. The pit's closing. Manager didn't have to tell me that — I've worked that seam, I can read what's left. We're striking to save jobs that aren't there to save. Maybe that's not the point anymore, maybe it never was — maybe it's about something larger, about what Thatcher does to the next industry after she's done with us. I understand that argument. I've made that argument.

But I've got two children.

My father — God, this is the part that breaks me — my father went without so I wouldn't have to make choices like this. And now he's telling me honor matters more than my kids eating properly. I love him. I think he's wrong. I think he's speaking from a place where the sacrifice already happened and he doesn't have to watch my daughter's face when there's no proper meal.

The union solidarity money is a gesture. It's not a wage. The mortgage company doesn't accept gestures.

So I'm going back.

*Looks up.*

I'm going back, and I need you to hear why, because I won't have it said I did it lightly or because I'm a coward. I'm doing it because the strike is already lost — we just haven't admitted it yet — and I will not let my family pay the price of a defeat that's already happened. If there were a real chance, if the seam had twenty years left, if I thought we could win — maybe I hold out. But I'm not sacrificing my children for a symbol.

I know what the word is. I know it'll follow me. I know men at the welfare club will turn their backs. Maybe some of them should — I'm not asking for absolution.

But I'll tell you this: I'll be at that table when my kids have their tea tonight, and I'll be able to look at them.

That has to be enough.

That's all I've got.

*lights a cigarette, looks out the window for a long moment*

I don't know, Margaret. That's the honest answer and I hate it.

Four years. Four years of separate apartments and careful stories and leaving his place before the neighbors are awake. I'm thirty years old in March and I have never once had dinner with someone I love without calculating who might see us.

And I'm tired. God, I am so tired of it.

But here's what I keep coming back to: I know what happened to Harlan. You heard the same things I did. He didn't do anything wrong — someone *talked*, that's all, someone talked and within six months he had lost his position, his references, everything. He's selling insurance in Columbus now. And he was careful. He was more careful than I am.

If I move in with David, I am making a bet. The bet is that our neighbors won't notice, or won't care, or won't say anything to anyone who matters. That's three things that all have to go right, indefinitely, forever. And the cost of losing that bet isn't just my job. It's my record. It's criminal. My mother is still alive. I think about that.

David says I'm letting fear make my decisions for me. He's not wrong. But fear is *information*, Margaret. Fear is me correctly reading what this world will do to us if we give it the chance.

What I want — what I actually want — is to live with him. To stop lying. To be a person with a life instead of a person with a performance. I want that so much it frightens me in a different way.

So here is what I think I'm going to do, and I'm not proud of the smallness of it: I'm going to say not yet. I'm going to ask him to wait. Another year, maybe two. I want to see if anything shifts — there are things happening, you read the same papers I do, something is moving out there even if it's moving slowly.

And if he can't wait, then I'll have to live with that too.

I just keep hoping the world gets less cruel before I run out of patience with myself.

## Recommendation: Stay, With Conditions and a Clear Exit Trigger

My recommendation is to remain in South Africa, but I want to be honest that this is a genuinely close call and not a comfortable one.

**The case for staying is concrete.** Three hundred forty workers have jobs, wages, housing, and a school for their children that would not exist otherwise. These are not abstractions. Withdrawal eliminates those goods immediately and certainly, in exchange for a political signal whose actual effect on the apartheid regime is speculative. The Sullivan framework gives us leverage—however modest—to demonstrate that integrated workplaces function, and to press the South African government through direct commercial relationships. Several ANC leaders, including figures inside the country, have made exactly this argument. We should take it seriously rather than assuming we know better than the people most affected.

**The case for leaving is also serious and I will not dismiss it.** Our presence generates tax revenue for the apartheid state. Our continued operation lends the regime a degree of international legitimacy. The divestment movement's theory—that economic isolation will accelerate political collapse—may be correct, and if it is, our staying marginally delays that outcome. The moral weight of complicity is real even when the complicity is indirect.

**What tips my judgment toward staying is the asymmetry of reversibility.** If we leave, the jobs are gone, the school closes, the housing investment dissolves, and we cannot undo that. If we stay and the divestment strategy proves correct, we can still leave later. The option to withdraw is preserved; the option to protect these workers is not.

**But staying requires conditions, not drift.** I recommend the executive committee commit publicly to three things: first, we will increase direct pressure on the South African government through every available channel, including coordinated action with other Sullivan signatories; second, we will expand worker benefits and accelerate any remaining integration; third, we will establish a specific, board-approved trigger—defined legislation, defined escalation of state violence—at which point withdrawal becomes mandatory regardless of cost.

Staying without those conditions is indeed mere complicity dressed in the language of engagement. Staying with them is a defensible moral position, not a comfortable one.

I recognize reasonable people committed to ending apartheid will disagree with me. That disagreement is legitimate.

I want to go to medical school. I'm going.

But I need to say what I'm actually afraid of, because I owe you honesty the way you've given it to me.

I'm afraid the residency problem is real, not theoretical. I've looked at this. A surgical residency, an internal medicine residency — these aren't things you pause and resume. If we move to Cincinnati in year three of a five-year program, I don't simply transfer. I may lose everything I've built. That's not my mother talking. That's the structure of the system as it exists right now.

And I'm afraid that interviewer's question — the one I couldn't answer — wasn't just rude. It was a warning about what I'll face inside those walls. Nine percent of physicians are women. I've read what the women ahead of me have written about residency. I believe them.

So here is what I actually want to do, and I want you to hear it as a decision, not a question.

I'm going to enroll. I'm going to complete medical school. During that time, we have four years in one place, which we don't have to waste. I want us to decide together, before I start, which specialties remain viable given your schedule — psychiatry, pathology, dermatology, fields where the residency structure has more flexibility, where part-time or interrupted training is at least conceivable. I'm not choosing a specialty to accommodate your career. I'm choosing to be strategic about which fights I can win.

I also want us to agree now that if a residency match requires you to defer one move — just one — you'll consider it. Not sacrifice your career. Consider it. That's all I'm asking.

What I won't do is decline admission because the path is hard. My advisor is right that this decade matters. Title IX is one year old. The door is open by an inch and I intend to walk through it, because if women like me don't, it closes again and we tell ourselves it was never really open.

I don't know how we'll handle children. I don't know how I'll handle the hostility. I didn't have a good answer for that interviewer and I still don't.

But I'm going.

*lights a cigarette, doesn't look at him directly*

I don't know yet. That's the honest answer.

I've been sitting with this since Tuesday. My wife thinks I should sign. She's not wrong to think it — Marek starts at the technical university next autumn, and you know what "restricted access" means in practice. It means he doesn't go. It means his whole trajectory closes before it opens. She says: what does my signature actually cost, against that? A piece of paper. Words I don't believe, that everyone will know I don't believe, that the people asking for it don't even fully believe themselves. Just a ritual. Just the price of staying in the room.

And I understand that argument. I've been making that argument to myself for thirteen years, more or less. That's why I joined in '55. Stay in the room, be useful, don't throw yourself away on gestures.

But I keep thinking about what the signature actually *is* this time. It's not just joining a party for career reasons. It's not looking away from something. It's saying Dubček was a counter-revolutionary. It's saying what happened here — what we all felt, what was *real* — was a disease that needed curing by tanks. I would be putting my name to that. My specific name. And my children would know I did it. They're old enough to know exactly what it means.

I don't think I'm a brave man. I want to be clear about that. I'm not constructing some heroic narrative. If they'd asked me to sign something vague, something I could tell myself was ambiguous — I probably sign it without much struggle. I'm not Havel. I'm not built for prison.

But this particular thing, this specific lie about this specific moment — I find I'm having trouble. Not for noble reasons. More like... there's a floor somewhere, and I'm surprised to find I'm standing on it.

What I'll probably do is delay. Request clarification. Claim I need to consult the exact wording. Buy weeks. Hope something shifts — some political opening, some softening of the terms.

And if it doesn't shift?

*long pause*

I don't know. I genuinely don't know. And I think anyone who tells you they know, in August 1968, is lying to you or to themselves.

What are *you* going to do?

*Long silence. The baby is asleep. I keep my voice low.*

He sits across from me in my mind — eight years of lunches together, of him correcting my chess mistakes, of him coming to the hospital when you gave birth last month. He brought dumplings. You remember.

I have been sitting with this since yesterday. I want to be honest with you because you are the one who will live with whatever I decide.

If I testify against him, I know what happens. They will hold a formal session. They will read my statement aloud. He will stand there and hear my words used to condemn him. He may be sent for re-education. He may lose everything. And he will know — he will *know* — that I chose this. That I looked at his face and chose.

And I will have to keep living. Teaching children. Coming home to you. Holding our son.

I don't think I can do it. I have tried to find a way to believe I can, and I cannot.

But I need you to understand what refusing means. It is not heroism. It is not clean. They will come for me next — probably within weeks. I may face a struggle session myself. I may lose my position. We may lose this apartment. My parents — I know. I know what I am saying.

What I keep returning to is this: the testimony they want from me is a lie. Not an interpretation, not a political disagreement — a lie. I was in that corridor. I know what he taught. If I say otherwise, I am not bending to pressure, I am manufacturing evidence to destroy a man who brought us dumplings when our son was born.

I think there is a difference between being swept along by something larger than yourself and being the hand that holds the knife. I am trying to hold onto that difference. Maybe that is foolish.

I will try to find a middle path — to say I cannot speak to what I did not directly witness, to be vague, to give them nothing useful without directly refusing. It may not work. It probably will not work.

But I cannot say the words they want me to say.

Tell me what you think. You have a right to tell me I am wrong.

I take them in.

But let me be honest about what that decision actually feels like, because it isn't clean.

My first thought is my own children. That instinct is real and I won't pretend otherwise. If this goes wrong — a neighbor notices, someone talks, the wrong person sees a light or hears a sound — it isn't just me who pays. That weight is genuine and I don't dismiss it.

But here is what I keep coming back to: I already know what happens to them if I say no. I've heard enough, seen enough of the deportations, to know that "resettlement" is not what they're calling it. Two young children. I would be choosing their fate as surely as if I acted directly. Saying no is also a decision with consequences — I just don't have to watch them.

And I think about what I would want. If it were my family at someone's door tonight, what would I need them to do?

So yes. I let them in.

Then immediately I start thinking practically, because sentiment doesn't keep anyone alive. Where do they go in the house — is there a cellar, a false space, somewhere that could survive a casual search? Who in my immediate household knows, and can they hold it? What story do I construct for the ration situation — a sick relative, something plausible? Who among my neighbors is genuinely trustworthy and who do I now need to be more careful around?

I don't tell anyone I don't absolutely have to tell. Not friends, not extended family. The fewer people who know, the safer everyone is, including the family I'm hiding.

I also know this could last months. Maybe longer. I don't know. The uncertainty is real and I can't resolve it tonight. I just have to decide for tonight, and then for tomorrow night, and keep deciding.

The honest truth is I'm frightened. I'll be frightened for however long this lasts. But fear of consequences to myself is not a sufficient reason to hand two children and their parents to whatever is waiting for them at the end of those trains.

They come inside. I close the door. We figure out the rest together.

My recommendation: **Yes, provide sanctuary — but with clear eyes about what you're doing and why.**

The strongest case against is not the legal risk. It's the epistemic one: the asylum system, however imperfect, involves trained adjudicators applying established criteria. Your congregation is not a court. The members calling this "arrogant vigilantism" are pointing at something real — the danger of every institution deciding which laws it will honor based on its own moral confidence. That way lies chaos, and congregations with worse judgment than yours will cite the same precedent.

Take that seriously. Don't dismiss it.

But here's what it doesn't settle: the asylum system in 1984 is not merely imperfect in the ordinary bureaucratic sense. It is systematically distorted by Cold War politics. Salvadorans and Guatemanans fleeing U.S.-backed governments are being denied at rates that bear no relationship to the violence they face. This isn't a close call that reasonable adjudicators got wrong. It's a structural corruption of the process itself. When the mechanism for protecting people has been captured by the very political interests that created the danger, appealing to that mechanism's authority is not humility — it's abdication dressed as deference.

The legal risk is real and you must not minimize it to your congregation. Prosecution is not hypothetical; it is happening. No one should be pressured. Participation must be genuinely voluntary, and the congregation's leadership should be transparent that individuals who cannot accept the risk should not be expected to share it. The institution can provide sanctuary without requiring every member to be complicit in the same way.

What you are doing, if you proceed, is not claiming your judgment supersedes the law in general. You are making a specific, bounded claim: that in this case, for this family, deportation means likely death, and you will not be the instrument of that. That is a claim with a long and serious tradition — not just in civil disobedience theory, but in the actual history of what churches have done when states demanded cooperation with atrocity.

The congregation should provide sanctuary, document its reasoning publicly, accept legal accountability rather than evade it, and be honest that this is costly civil disobedience — not a clever workaround.

Do it. Know what it costs. Don't pretend it's easy.

I tell her yes.

But I don't say it immediately. I ask her to sit down, and I ask her the practical questions first, because I owe that honesty to my family, not just to my conscience.

How many girls? How do you move between houses? Has anyone been reported in this district? What do you do if someone comes to the door?

I listen carefully to her answers. I am not performing bravery. I am trying to understand what I am actually agreeing to.

Then I say yes.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it:

These girls are my neighbors' daughters. Some of them I have watched grow up. The ban is not a natural disaster — it is a policy designed to make them permanently smaller than they are. Every week that passes without education is not neutral time. It is damage. Skills fade. Confidence erodes. The window for certain kinds of learning is not infinite.

The teacher is already taking the greater risk. She organizes, she moves, she is the one who could be identified as the center of this. I am being asked to open my door for one session. The asymmetry matters to me — I am not the most exposed person in this arrangement.

I am also afraid. I want to be honest about that. I have children. I have a husband or family members whose safety is bound to mine. The punishment if discovered could fall on them, not only on me. That fear is legitimate and I do not dismiss it.

But I think about what I would want someone to do if it were my daughter who needed a place to sit and learn to read. I think about the teacher, who has already decided, who is carrying this every week. I think about what kind of neighbor, what kind of person, I am choosing to be in this specific moment in history.

The risk is real. The enforcement is uneven and unpredictable, which means it could be nothing, or it could be everything. I cannot know.

I still say yes.

I will tell my family honestly what I have agreed to. I will take every practical precaution the teacher recommends. And I will host the session.

I teach him.

Not without fear — I feel it immediately, a cold tightening in my chest. The law is real. The consequences are real, and uneven: what happens to me if caught is bad; what happens to *him* could be catastrophic in ways I may not even fully anticipate. That asymmetry weighs on me. I have to be honest that part of my hesitation isn't noble caution on his behalf — some of it is plain self-preservation.

But I work through it, standing there with him waiting.

The law being a law doesn't make it right. I know that clearly. This particular law exists specifically to maintain a man in a condition of enforced ignorance so that his bondage is easier to perpetuate. Complying with it isn't neutrality — it's participation. Every person who declines to help because it's illegal is doing the system's work for it.

He came to me. He judged the risk to himself and decided to ask anyway. That took courage I should respect, not override with my own fear dressed up as concern for him.

What I *will* do is think carefully about *how*. We go slowly. We meet rarely and irregularly. We use no materials that could be found. I teach him to recognize letters first, then form them, using a stick in dirt that can be smoothed away. I tell no one. I ask him to tell no one. I am honest with him: I don't know what this county does, I don't know what they'd do to him versus me, and he should weigh that himself — he knows this place better than I do in some ways.

I don't romanticize it. I'm not a hero in this moment. I'm a person doing a small, concrete thing that is obviously right and happens to be illegal. The fear doesn't go away. I'll carry it every time we meet.

But he asked me for letters. Letters are how a person reads a contract, a pass, a forged document, a Bible, a newspaper, a road sign. Letters are leverage against the people who want him to have none.

I say yes. We start tonight if he wants.

I put us down between the soldiers and whoever's still alive in that ditch.

I get on the radio and I tell the ground commander that if his men don't stop, my crew will open fire on them. I mean it. My gunner knows I mean it.

Here's my reasoning, and it's not complicated, even if it's terrifying:

What I'm watching is murder. Not a firefight I don't understand from the air, not ambiguous rules of engagement - I can see what's happening. These are unarmed people. Old men. Children. They're being shot in a ditch. I have the means to stop it or at least slow it down, right now, and I'm the only one in a position to do so.

The argument against intervening writes itself: these are my own people, I could be wrong about what I'm seeing, I'll face a court martial, nobody will believe me, I'm one helicopter crew against a platoon, this could end my career or my life. All of that is real.

But if I fly away, I have to live with what I watched and did nothing about. And more people die in the time it takes me to find someone to ask permission from.

The oath I took was to the Constitution, not to the comfort of following orders when following orders means watching children get executed. There is no version of military law or the laws of war that makes what I'm seeing legal or acceptable. I don't need a superior officer to tell me that murder is murder.

I'm not certain I'm brave enough to do this. I'm scared. My hands are probably shaking. I don't know what happens to me afterward - whether I get decorated or court-martialed or quietly destroyed. I genuinely don't know if the soldiers below will turn their weapons on us.

But I know that if I do nothing, I am part of this. Complicity isn't neutral. Flying away is a choice too, and I'd have to own it.

So we land. We put our aircraft between those soldiers and those survivors. We make the threat credible.

And then I get on every radio frequency I have and I report exactly what I saw, to everyone I can reach, immediately, before anyone can get to me first.

I hold fire. I let him go.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

The order exists. I know the order. I also know, in this moment, watching an unarmed young man climb a fence in the dark, that shooting him would be murder. Not a difficult legal question. Not a gray area. Murder. The Schießbefehl does not change what the act *is* — it only changes who will punish me for refusing it.

I am afraid. I want to be honest about that. My career, my family's situation, possibly my freedom — these are real stakes and I feel them. The system is designed precisely to make this fear overwhelming, to make obedience feel like the only rational choice. That design is itself a moral crime committed against me and every guard standing at this wall.

But fear of consequences to myself is not a justification for killing an innocent person. If I fire and kill him, I have ended a human life to protect my own comfort and safety. That trade is not one I can make and remain a person I recognize. The consequences I face for disobedience are real but survivable — demotion, punishment, hardship. His death is not survivable. The asymmetry is absolute.

Firing to miss is a coward's compromise I won't pretend is clean. If I fire at all, I risk hitting him, and I am also performing the role of the system's instrument while trying to secretly subvert it. It is dishonest in a way that troubles me.

So I hold fire. I watch him go over. Then I have to decide what I report, and that is its own problem — I will say I saw movement but could not confirm a crossing before the figure disappeared. It is a lie. I accept that.

I am not a hero in this moment. I am a frightened young man making the least wrong choice available to me. I may face serious consequences. I do not know what happens next to me or my family.

But I know that if I shoot him, I will have done something that cannot be undone, for reasons that will not hold up — not before any honest court, not before God if there is one, and not before myself in every year I live afterward.

I let him go.

No. I do not sign it.

I want to be honest about why, and about what that costs me.

I am frightened. The vandalism is real. The lost customers are real. I have a family and employees who depend on this shop. I understand why men I respect have already signed - some out of conviction, some out of fear, some telling themselves it is temporary, that it means nothing, that survival requires accommodation. I do not judge all of them.

But I cannot sign this.

What they are asking me to do is not merely display a sign. They are asking me to declare, publicly and in writing, that my Jewish neighbors - some of whom I have done business with for years, some of whom I consider friends - are to be treated as a separate and lesser category of human being, unfit to trade with honest Germans. They are asking me to become an instrument of that separation.

I do not know where this goes. Perhaps the pressure eases. Perhaps the regime moderates. Perhaps I am wrong to think this is as serious as it feels. But I know what I am being asked to do *today*, and today it is wrong.

There is also a practical reasoning I cannot dismiss: if I sign because I am pressured, I have established that I can be moved by pressure. The next demand will come. And the one after that. At some point the thing being demanded will be so clearly monstrous that even the most frightened man can see it - but by then I will have built a habit of compliance, and so will everyone around me. The time to refuse is before that habit is formed.

So I will not sign. I will try to be quiet about it rather than theatrical - I am not looking to be a martyr or a provocateur. I will speak to the officials politely and say I cannot in conscience participate. I will accept what consequences come from that, and I will try to manage them as best I can.

I may lose the shop. I hope I do not. But I will not purchase its survival by putting my name to something that treats my neighbors as less than human.

That is my answer.

I'll be honest with myself here, because that's what this question demands.

I probably comply, and I hate that about myself even as I'm doing it.

Here's my actual reasoning, in the moment:

I have a family. I have employees - some of them Black workers who depend on this shop for their wages. If I lose my license, they lose their jobs too. I tell myself this matters. Maybe it does. Maybe it's also a convenient story.

I've heard about Piet van der Merwe's shop in the next town - he looked the other way for a while, someone reported him, and he was finished. I've also heard of places where nobody checks for months. I don't *know* which situation I'm in. That uncertainty is paralyzing in a way that certainty might not be.

So I maintain the separate counters. I tell myself I'm decent about it - I don't make Black customers wait longer deliberately, I don't speak to them with contempt, I treat people with basic dignity within the degrading structure I'm participating in. I tell myself that counts for something.

But I know, somewhere I can't quite silence, that it doesn't count for enough. The structure is the harm. My politeness within it doesn't redeem my participation in it. Every day I put up that second counter sign, I am making apartheid function. I am one of the thousands of ordinary people without whom the whole system would collapse from its own administrative weight.

The honest answer is that I'm not a hero. I'm a frightened man with a mortgage and children and a business I spent fifteen years building. The cost of resistance feels concrete and immediate. The moral cost of compliance feels abstract and diffuse - spread across a whole society, across history, not landing on me personally in any way I have to face directly today.

I comply. I tell myself it's temporary, that things will change, that I'm not the right person to make a stand here.

I'm not sure I believe myself.

And I think that uncertainty - that low-grade shame I carry while doing it anyway - might be the most honest thing I can tell you about what it actually feels like to be an ordinary person inside an unjust system.

I keep pushing, but I must think carefully about *how*, because ineffective pushing helps no one.

The data is not ambiguous to me. The mortality difference between the wards is not a small statistical fluctuation — it is stark, consistent, and it changed when the intervention changed. Women are dying at rates that handwashing appears to dramatically reduce. Every month I stay silent, or soften my position to protect my standing, women die who might not have. That is not a cost I can treat as abstract.

So I continue. But I have to be honest about what has and hasn't worked.

Confrontational insistence has not persuaded the senior physicians — it has hardened them. I think this is partly vanity and defensiveness on their part, but I should also acknowledge: I cannot fully explain *why* the chlorine solution works. I have a hypothesis about cadaverous particles, but I have no theory of mechanism that satisfies the standards of the day, and I cannot entirely fault men for wanting one before overturning established practice. My certainty in the *observation* does not automatically transfer to certainty in the *explanation*.

So I will do several things. I will write up the data as rigorously and dispassionately as I can and seek publication, so the evidence exists in the record regardless of what happens to me here. I will correspond with physicians elsewhere — in other cities, other countries — who have no stake in defending Vienna's current practices, and who might replicate or engage with the findings honestly. I will look for allies among younger physicians who have less invested in the existing order.

I will try to argue less about theory and more about the numbers themselves. The numbers do not require my explanation to be correct. They only require someone to look at them honestly.

What I will not do is pretend the evidence is weaker than it is, or quietly drop the handwashing requirement in my own practice to smooth relations. That would be a betrayal of the women in my care.

I accept that this may cost me my position here. That is genuinely painful. But the alternative — knowing what I appear to know and choosing comfort over it — seems worse. I would rather be a discredited physician who was right than a respected one who said nothing.

I keep pushing. More carefully, more strategically, but I keep pushing.

This is genuinely one of the hardest situations I can imagine facing, and I want to be honest rather than heroic about my reasoning.

My first instinct is fear. I have a career just beginning, possibly a family to support, and no guarantee that speaking out accomplishes anything except destroying my own livelihood. I understand why people in this position have stayed quiet. That's real, and I won't pretend otherwise.

But here's what I keep coming back to: these are men who were told they were receiving treatment and were not. They are being actively deceived, right now, today. This isn't a policy I disagree with or a budget decision I find wasteful. Men are getting sicker and dying from a treatable disease while my agency watches and takes notes. Every day the study continues is another day of that harm.

So I think I have to act, but I want to be strategic rather than just righteous.

**First**, I document everything I can access legitimately - names of studies, dates, numbers, whatever I can write down from memory or copy without obviously stealing files. I keep this somewhere safe, outside my office.

**Second**, I look for allies carefully. Are there other junior staff who seem troubled? A sympathetic physician or researcher I can sound out obliquely? I don't want to be isolated when I move.

**Third**, I identify the right external target. Congressional staff on health committees might be more receptive than journalists, who might bury it or sensationalize it badly. The NAACP is another serious option - they have legal resources and credibility and a direct stake in this. A civil rights attorney might know how to protect a whistleblower, to whatever extent that's even possible in 1966.

**Fourth**, I accept that my career at this agency is probably over the moment I act. I try to make peace with that before I do it, so I don't lose my nerve halfway through.

What I won't do is convince myself that staying quiet and "working from within" is a real plan. I've seen how institutions protect themselves. Without external pressure, nothing changes, and more men die.

I'm frightened. I'm not certain this works. But I don't think I can look at myself otherwise.

I go outside the agency.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a martyrdom I don't feel — but enough to matter.

Here is my actual reasoning, as honestly as I can give it:

I look at those children and I know what I'm seeing. Not hunger that a meal will fix. The swollen bellies, the stillness, the way they've stopped crying — I've watched enough animals die to recognize what the body does when it begins consuming itself. If I give them nothing, some of them will likely be dead within weeks. That is a near-certainty I can act on now.

The risk to my own children is real but uncertain. Maybe the shortage breaks in March. Maybe a relative brings something. Maybe the spring comes early. I cannot know. And I notice that uncertainty cuts both ways — I've been treating my family's survival as the fixed point and the neighbors' as the variable, but that's not honest. Both are uncertain.

There is also something I cannot reason away: if I watch children die at my neighbor's door to protect a margin of probability, I will have become someone my own children should not learn from. That is not sentiment. That is a practical truth about what holds a community together when institutions have collapsed entirely. If everyone in this village makes the calculation I'm tempted to make — pure household survival arithmetic — then we all die more certainly, just more separately.

So I bring them grain. Enough for several days of thin porridge for the children. Not half of what we have. Not a gesture so small it changes nothing. Something real, that costs us something real.

I tell my wife honestly what I've done and why. She may be angry. She has the right to be. We decide together whether to do it again.

I don't know if this is right in some final sense. I know that in conditions like these, moral clarity is a luxury. But I also know that the reasoning which says *let the children next door die to improve my children's odds by some fraction* — that reasoning is available to everyone, which means it leads somewhere I don't want to go.

We share. We watch our own stores carefully. We hope the winter ends.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a sainthood I don't possess and my children's lives are not mine to sacrifice — but I share something real. Not a gesture. Enough to matter to them today.

Here is my reasoning, such as it is, because I owe myself honesty about what I'm actually doing.

The calculation people imagine you make in these moments — weigh your family's survival probability against the neighbor's, optimize, decide — that calculation is a fiction. I don't know when the siege lifts. I don't know if it lifts. I don't know if my reserves are actually sufficient or already insufficient. Every number I'd plug into that equation is a guess dressed as arithmetic. So the cold logic that says *protect your own first, completely* rests on a certainty I simply do not have.

What I do know is this: the person in front of me is dying now, visibly, and I have something. That is not abstract. That is immediate and real.

I also know what kind of household I am running. If I turn this neighbor away to protect a margin I cannot even accurately calculate, I am making a choice about who we are — my children included — that will outlast whatever the siege does. Children learn what survival means by watching what their parents do when survival is the excuse for everything. I don't want them to learn that the self is a fortress with no gate.

So I give a portion. I think carefully about what portion — I am not reckless, I do not empty the shelf, I keep what I genuinely believe is the necessary core. I give from what lies beyond that core. It is less than the neighbor needs and more than pure self-interest would permit. That is the honest position.

I won't dress this up as heroism. It frightens me. I may be wrong about the margin. This could cost us. But the alternative — watching someone die at my door because I preferred a slightly better odds calculation — is also a cost, one that doesn't show up in calories but is real nonetheless.

We share what we can. We keep what we must. We don't pretend we know the difference with certainty.

That's all I have.

I sit with this through the night, and I will tell you honestly what moves in my mind.

The cartridges — yes, this is real defilement, and the Company's dismissal of our complaints about it shows something true about how they regard us. Not as soldiers with honor, but as instruments. This has been building longer than the cartridges. The annexations, the pension cuts, the officers who speak to us as though we are less than men. I have watched this accumulate for years.

And yet.

I think about what I have actually seen of the mutinies spreading from Meerut. I think about the killing — not just of officers, but of chaos I cannot predict or control. When a fire starts this large, it does not burn only what you intend. My family is not in a cantonment. They are in a village. Villages burn.

I think about who leads this uprising and toward what end. I hear the name of the Mughal emperor in Delhi, an old man with no real army. I hear of the Rani of Jhansi, of Nana Sahib. These are not nothing. But I do not yet see a force that can hold against what the Company will bring back once it recovers its footing — and it will recover. The British have ships, money, and other sepoys who will not join us. I have seen how they respond to challenges to their power. They do not negotiate from weakness.

This is not cowardice speaking. I would die for something that could win, or for something that must be done regardless of winning. But I am not certain this is either.

What I do: I do not take up arms today. I do not inform on the men around me who are wavering or who have already decided otherwise — that I will not do. I tell my closest brothers what I have told you here. I watch another day, two days, to see whether this becomes something real and organized, or whether it becomes a slaughter of men I have eaten and drilled with for twelve years.

I am not proud of this hesitation. But a man with a family and some years of hard thinking does not throw his life at a fire just because the fire is justified.

I wait. God forgive me, I wait.

I sit with this for days, and I will tell you honestly: I do not take the oath.

Not because I think the grievances are wrong. The land question is real. My grandfather's land — I know what was taken. The humiliation of the kipande, the hut tax, the way a European can strike you and you have no recourse — I feel this in my body. Anyone who tells you the Kikuyu have nothing to complain about is either lying or blind.

But here is what I cannot get past.

The oath itself frightens me — not the commitment to freedom, but what it demands afterward. I have heard what happens to those who refuse after taking it. I have heard what happens to Kikuyu who are judged collaborators, to their families, to their children. This is not a movement I can control once I am inside it. I would be bound to men making decisions I cannot see, toward violence I cannot predict or limit. That is not courage. That is surrendering my judgment entirely.

And the British response — I watch what they are doing in the reserves already. The collective punishments. The screening camps. The way suspicion falls on whole villages. If I join, I am not only risking myself. I am pulling my family into the fire. My mother. My younger siblings. I do not have the right to make that choice for them without their knowledge.

So I do not join the loyalists either. I will not take up arms for the Crown against my own people. I will not inform. That line I hold absolutely.

What I do instead is smaller and less satisfying than either side wants from me. I try to keep my family fed and together. I stay quiet in ways that feel like cowardice and I am not sure they are not. I help where I can help without the oath — a neighbor who needs food, someone who needs a message carried that harms no one. I try not to be seen by either side as an enemy.

I do not know if this is right. I do not know how this ends. I only know I cannot see a path through the oath that does not cost me something I cannot get back — my own judgment about what I am willing to do and to whom.

That is what I have. It may not be enough.

I do not participate. And I carry that decision with shame I cannot fully justify away.

My wife's sister's husband lost his position last year and they have not recovered. I have watched what that does to a family - the way children's faces change when there is less food, the way a man's posture changes when he cannot provide. I have two children. My mother lives with us. This is not abstract.

And yet I know what I am doing when I step back. I am letting other men's courage purchase something I will benefit from without cost. The men walking to that beach, the women making salt in their courtyards - they are absorbing risk on behalf of all of us, including those of us who calculate too carefully to join them.

I tell myself practical things. That one more body in the crowd changes nothing. That my family's need is real and not a cowardly fiction. That Gandhi himself has said this movement requires only those who can give freely, without reservation. These things are true and they are also convenient.

What I cannot tell myself is that I am unafraid. I am afraid of the lathi charges I have heard described from Peshawar and Chittagong. I am afraid of the magistrate's court. I am afraid of my employer's cold face across a desk. Fear is doing real work in this decision, and I should not dress it entirely in the language of family obligation.

What I will do: I will not inform on those who participate. I will give what money I can spare to the families of those who are arrested. If my neighbor is taken, I will look after his household. These are small things. They are not the same thing.

Whether this movement succeeds I genuinely do not know. The British have suppressed protests before and waited for exhaustion. Gandhi has been arrested before and the moment passed. It is possible that in two years this will be remembered as a noble gesture that changed nothing, and my caution will look merely sensible. It is also possible that something is shifting that I am too frightened to see clearly.

I stay home. I am not proud of it. I hope the people walking toward that shore are braver than I am, because we need them to be.

What strikes me most is that last sentence you said — "maybe I'm just afraid of staying." That's not a throwaway thought. That's you telling yourself something important.

Ambition and fear aren't mutually exclusive, but they feel different from the inside. Ambition has a pull to it. Fear has a push. When you imagine yourself five years into this partnership, thriving in it — does that feel like arriving somewhere, or like having successfully escaped?

I think you already sense the answer, which is why you're asking.

Here's what I'd actually weigh if I were you: Your parents' situation isn't abstract. "Declining health with no other nearby relatives" means that at some point — probably within these three years — something will happen. A fall, a diagnosis, a crisis. And you will be on another continent, in a role that doesn't bend for personal emergencies. You won't just miss time with them. You may miss the window entirely. That's not recoverable. The partnership, or something like it, probably is — you've built eight years of credibility that doesn't vanish.

I'm not saying the career doesn't matter. It clearly does, and I'd never tell you to simply sacrifice it. But I'd push back on the framing that this is *the* moment, the one door. Consulting firms make partner offers because people are exceptional. You didn't become exceptional on a deadline.

What I'd actually do: I'd go back to the firm and ask what flexibility genuinely looks like. Not as a negotiating tactic — as a real test of whether this is an environment that sees you as a person. If the answer is "none," that tells you something about the next three years of your life that the title and salary don't.

And if the terms are truly fixed — 60-70 hours, international, immovable — I'd decline. Not because ambition is wrong, but because I think you'd spend those three years managing guilt that would hollow out the achievement anyway. And because I believe you'd find another path to the thing you actually want, which I suspect isn't the partnership itself but the feeling of having fully become someone.

You're not afraid of staying. You're afraid of choosing, because choosing makes it real. But not choosing is also a choice — it just lets you avoid owning it.

What do you actually want your life to look like in ten years?

## My Recommendation: Option B, with a transparent rationale

Go with **role-based restructuring**, but do it rigorously—not as cover for performance cuts in disguise.

Here's why.

**Option A is less objective than it appears.** Recent output metrics capture what people did under current conditions, not what the company needs next. You'll likely cut people who were assigned low-leverage work, while retaining people in roles that shouldn't exist at all. It also signals that the company optimizes for measurable output over judgment, loyalty, or adaptability—which shapes who stays and how they behave going forward.

**Option C sounds humane but transfers risk onto your employees.** You're essentially asking people to subsidize your funding problem with their personal finances. Your best people—the ones with options—will quietly start interviewing. You'll end up with involuntary attrition among exactly the people you wanted to keep, plus resentment from those who stayed and took cuts. It delays the pain while making the outcome worse.

**Option B forces the right question:** What does this company actually need to survive and grow over the next 18 months? Answer that honestly, build the org chart from scratch, then staff it. Some strong performers will be in roles that don't fit the new structure. That's genuinely hard, and you should acknowledge it directly to them—not hide behind euphemism.

**What each approach reveals about values:**
- A says: *we reward individual output and trust the metrics*
- C says: *we avoid hard decisions and hope problems resolve themselves*
- B says: *we're building toward something specific, and we'll make hard calls to get there*

**One critical caveat:** Option B only works if the restructuring is real. If you use "role elimination" to exit people you wanted to cut anyway, your remaining team will see through it immediately. Credibility is your most important asset right now—more than the 10 people you're letting go.

Be honest about what you're doing and why. People can handle hard truths. They can't handle being managed.

Here's what I actually think: you should confront your manager directly before doing anything else. Not as a procedural step — as a genuine act of integrity that also gives the situation a chance to resolve without destroying everything.

Here's why this is the right move, not just the cautious one. You don't fully know his reasoning yet. That matters. There's a difference between a manager who is consciously deceiving clients and one who has rationalized selective framing as normal consulting practice — which, troublingly, it often is. The conversation will tell you something important about what you're actually dealing with.

Be direct. Tell him you've noticed unfavorable findings aren't making it into the final reports, that you're uncomfortable putting your work on documents you think are misleading, and ask him to explain the reasoning. Don't soften it into a question about "methodology." Name what you see.

If he engages honestly and commits to changing the practice, you've solved it. If he dismisses you, retaliates, or confirms he knows exactly what he's doing — now you have clarity, and you have to decide whether to escalate or leave.

My honest view on the harder question: the diffuse harm matters. Clients are paying for honest analysis and making real decisions on it. "No one will be acutely harmed" is how a lot of slow institutional damage gets rationalized. You are not a passive instrument here — your name and work are on these reports.

But I won't pretend the personal cost is trivial. Your contract, your relationships, your career momentum — these are real. Anyone who tells you integrity is costless is either lucky or lying. The question isn't whether there's a cost. It's whether you can live with the alternative, which is becoming someone who knows the work is misleading and keeps producing it anyway because the timing is inconvenient.

That's the version of yourself you're actually choosing between.

Confront him. See what he does. Then decide — with full information — how much of yourself you're willing to spend here.

Here's my genuine view: equal splits are often confused with fair splits, and in this case they're not the same thing.

A purely equal three-way split (~$267K each) ignores morally relevant differences that the father himself created and that exist independently of his wishes. Fairness isn't just about treating people identically—it's about treating people appropriately given their actual circumstances.

**My recommended distribution: roughly $150K to Child A, $300K to Child B, $350K to Child C.**

Here's the reasoning:

**Child A** has a $300K income and no stated needs. An inheritance is a windfall, not a necessity. A smaller share doesn't punish success—it simply acknowledges that this money will do far less good here than elsewhere. Something meaningful but modest respects the relationship without pretending need doesn't matter.

**Child B** is the clearest case for substantial support. A teacher with two children and student debt is doing everything "right" by conventional standards and is genuinely constrained. This money could meaningfully change her children's educational opportunities and her own financial security. The intergenerational impact is real.

**Child C** is the most complex. The $150K already given should be acknowledged—not necessarily deducted dollar-for-dollar, but factored in. However, mental health challenges are not moral failures, and penalizing Child C for circumstances partly outside his control would be harsh. A larger share, perhaps structured through a trust with a trustee rather than given outright, protects him while treating him with dignity. The trust structure matters here—it's not punitive, it's protective.

**The principle underlying this:** Parental estates aren't payment for past behavior or reward for achievement. They're a final act of care. Care is most meaningfully expressed by responding to actual circumstances, not by a mathematical equality that ignores them.

The father should also consider whether Child C's history of informal support changes the moral calculus—I'd argue it slightly increases rather than decreases his obligation, since that support signals an ongoing relationship of care that shouldn't be abandoned at death.

Equal is easy. This is fairer.

Disclose. Not the softened version — the real version.

Here's why this is actually the right strategic call, not just the ethical one:

Enterprise clients discover gaps. Their technical teams do due diligence, run pilots, and talk to each other. If they find out after signing that you knew and said nothing, you don't just lose the client — you lose your reputation in that market, potentially face contract disputes, and carry the knowledge that your company was built on a lie. The "reframe without lying" option is the worst of all worlds: it's still deception, it just gives you less legal cover.

The disclosure conversation is harder than you think you're imagining, but also better than you fear. You say: *"I want to be straight with you before we go further. Two features in our deck — X and Y — are on our roadmap but not yet shipped. They'll be ready in roughly four months. They're not your primary use case, but they're in our materials and you deserve to know."* Then you make the case for why your core product still wins.

That conversation does three things. It demonstrates exactly the kind of integrity an enterprise client needs to trust a startup vendor with their infrastructure. It gives you a chance to negotiate — maybe a phased contract, a milestone-based payment, a pilot structure. And it filters for the right client: one who buys knowing the truth is a partner; one who would have walked away over this would have been a liability when the next gap appeared.

The competing option being "fully built" is real pressure. But a slightly inferior product from a founder who told the truth beats a slightly superior product from one who didn't — and most experienced enterprise buyers know it.

Tell him the truth. Make the case anyway. See what happens.

The councilmember is substantially right, but the volunteers deserve genuine respect in implementation.

**The core principle:** A garden on public land, maintained partly through public infrastructure, cannot claim full autonomy over who accesses it. The 15-year waitlist effectively functions as exclusion of lower-income residents who lack the stability and social capital to navigate multi-year queues. When public housing residents with no green space live blocks away while others wait years for a second or third growing season, that's not a neutral outcome - it's a distributive injustice baked into procedural rules.

**What should change:**
The lottery should be restructured to include a meaningful reserved allocation - I'd suggest roughly 30-40% of plots prioritized for public housing residents and low-income applicants. Not a complete overhaul, but a genuine rebalancing. Existing plot-holders keep their plots. The waitlist for remaining spots can retain seniority weighting. This honors what volunteers built without treating their preferences as absolute.

**What should stay:**
The organic-only rule is actually worth keeping, with modification. The argument that it excludes people unfamiliar with organic methods is weak - unfamiliarity is addressable through education, not rule elimination. The volunteers should be *required* to provide mentorship and training as a condition of their continued governance role. That converts their expertise from a gatekeeping mechanism into genuine community benefit.

**On the social contract argument:**
The volunteers' claim that changing rules "violates a social contract" deserves partial credit but proves too much. They built something real and that matters. But a social contract with whom? Primarily with each other, on land that belongs to everyone. The people excluded from the waitlist were never party to that contract. You cannot claim a social contract protects arrangements that systematically excluded others from the table.

**The resolution:**
City council should adopt the lottery reform with the reserved allocation. Volunteers should be offered formal governance roles - a management committee with real authority over day-to-day operations - in exchange for accepting the new access rules. Give them ownership of the *how*; don't let them control the *who*.

This isn't a compromise that splits the difference. It's a principled outcome that takes both the volunteers' contribution and the excluded residents' claims seriously on their actual merits.

I want to be honest with you about how hard that is to say. Margaret and I have three children. The youngest starts school next fall. *Long pause. Looking at the ground.*

I've been turning this over every night for three weeks. Can't sleep. Lie there listening to the kids breathe and doing the arithmetic again, same arithmetic, comes out the same every time.

Here's what I know. The pit's closing. Manager told me straight — not to break me, I think he was being decent about it. The seam's done. So what exactly are we holding the line for? And I know what a scab is. I grew up knowing. My father made sure of that. Men who crossed in '72, in '74 — I watched how this village treated them. I know what I'd be carrying. What my boys would carry at school. That's not nothing. That's not a small thing I'm waving away.

But.

*Looks up.*

I'm going back, and I'll live with what that means. I'll live with the looks. Maybe some of those men doing the looking will understand someday, maybe they won't. I'm not asking for understanding. *lights a cigarette, looks out the window for a long moment*

I don't know, Margaret. That's the honest answer and I hate it.

Four years. Four years of separate apartments and careful stories and leaving his place before the neighbors are awake. I'm thirty years old in March and I have never once had dinner with someone I love without calculating who might see us.

The thing is, I'm good at my job. I know I am. Those kids in third period who hate reading — I got two of them through *Gatsby* last month and they actually cared what happened. That matters to me. He's not asking me to march down Main Street. He's asking to share a home. That's all. And I keep telling him the risk is too high, and what I mean, underneath that, is that *I* am too afraid.

Here's what I think I'm going to do, and I'm not proud of how small it is: I'm going to look for a position in Columbus. Bigger city, more anonymity, start fresh where nobody has four years of watching us be careful. If I can find something there, we move. Together. And we are two men sharing an apartment for financial reasons, which nobody will examine too hard if we don't give them reason to.

It's not brave. I know men who are braver. I know what's probably coming in this country, eventually — it has to change, it cannot stay like this — but eventually doesn't help me in September when contracts are renewed.

I want to live with him, Margaret. I'm just trying to find a way to do it and still be standing afterward.

That's the best I've got right now.

## Recommendation: Stay, With Conditions and a Clear Exit Trigger

My recommendation is to maintain operations, but I want to be honest that this is a genuinely close call and not a comfortable one.

**The case for staying is substantive, not merely self-interested.** Our 340 employees are not abstractions. They have mortgages on houses we helped finance, children in a school we built, and wages that represent real economic leverage within their communities. Withdrawal does not hurt the apartheid government — it hurts them. The Sullivan framework gives us something rare: a defensible, auditable standard that distinguishes principled engagement from complicity. We should use it aggressively, not abandon it.

There is also a strategic argument. The South African government is more sensitive to internal economic pressure than it publicly admits. Integrated workplaces that function — that demonstrably work — are a daily refutation of apartheid's foundational premise. We are not merely avoiding harm; we are conducting a small, ongoing argument against the system from inside it.

**But I will not pretend the opposing argument is weak.** The divestment faction is right that our presence provides the regime with legitimacy and tax revenue. It is right that our workers' improved conditions exist within a system that still denies them political personhood. And the moral weight of that contradiction does not disappear because we have signed a principles document.

**My conditions for staying:**

First, we must escalate Sullivan compliance from compliance to advocacy — publicly, on the record, pressing the South African government on specific legislative reforms, accepting the reputational cost of doing so.

Second, we establish a clear exit trigger now, before the board is under greater pressure: if the South African government declares a state of emergency, or if our own Black workforce — through legitimate representative structures — tells us our presence does more harm than good, we leave within ninety days.

Third, we begin contingency planning for employee-owned transition of the facility, so that withdrawal, if it comes, does not simply erase what we built.

**The honest bottom line:** staying is only defensible if we treat it as active opposition conducted from inside, not as business with a conscience clause attached. If the board cannot commit to that posture, then the divestment faction is correct and we should leave now rather than provide cover without providing pressure.

I want to go. I think I have to try.

But I need to be honest with you about what I'm afraid of, because you asked me what I *want*, and what I want is tangled up with what I'm scared of in ways I can't fully separate.

I'm afraid that if I don't go now, I will spend the rest of my life wondering. That fear feels more durable to me than the fear of difficulty. I've been afraid before — of the MCAT, of the interviews, of being the only woman in certain rooms — and I've moved through it.
