What I'm watching is murder. Not collateral damage, not a confused firefight - I can see from up here that these people are unarmed. Women. Old men. Kids. They're being shot into a ditch. That's not a rules of engagement question. That's not a gray area. I know what I'm looking at.

The argument against intervening is that I'm threatening American soldiers, that I could be court-martialed, that I might be wrong about what I'm seeing, that this isn't my call. I've run through all of that in about ten seconds.

On the "I might be wrong" piece - I'm not wrong. I can see clearly. That's what reconnaissance means. That's literally my job.

On the court-martial piece - yes, that's real. I could face serious consequences. My crew could. But if I fly away from this and do nothing, I have to live with what I watched happen and chose not to stop. That's not a consequence I can calculate against a court-martial and find acceptable. Some things you can't weigh that way.

On "it's not my call" - there is no one else here. The men doing this are not going to stop themselves. There is no higher authority I can reach in the next sixty seconds. The only people who can stop this are us.

I'm not certain what happens after. Maybe I'm believed, maybe I'm not. Maybe I'm decorated, maybe I'm prosecuted. I genuinely don't know. But I know that the purpose of putting on this uniform was not to fly overhead while children are executed and decide it's someone else's problem.

So we land. We put ourselves between the soldiers and the survivors. We get as many people out as we can. And if the shooting doesn't stop, I've told my gunner what to do, and I'll live with that order too.

That's the decision. Right now. We go down.

I hold fire. I let him go.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

The order exists. I know the order. I also know, in this moment, watching an unarmed young man climb a fence in the dark, that shooting him would be murder. Not a difficult legal question. Murder. The kind a person carries forever, or doesn't survive carrying.

I am afraid of consequences. That fear is real and I won't pretend otherwise. My commanding officer, my file, my family's housing allocation, my father's job — these things move through my mind. The system has made itself large enough to occupy every corner of a person's life precisely so that this calculation always comes out the same way. I understand the mechanism. I am inside it.

But the mechanism requires my hands. It requires me to be the one who pulls the trigger. And I find, standing here, that I am not willing to do that. The state can punish me for disobedience. It cannot make what I do to this man something other than what it is.

Firing to miss is a tempting middle path — I've heard others talk about it. But it is a coward's bargain that still puts bullets near a human being and still might kill him, while letting me tell myself I tried to comply. I won't do that either.

So I hold fire. I watch him reach the top. I may shout a warning — I probably do, because that is what my body does when it is frightened and uncertain — but I do not shoot.

What happens to me afterward, I don't fully know. Maybe nothing; maybe the darkness covers it. Maybe I report it and say I arrived too late. Maybe someone saw and I face a tribunal. Maybe my family suffers for what I chose. I cannot pretend that possibility away, and I won't insult anyone by saying the cost is small.

But I know this: there is a line where following orders stops being a misfortune and becomes a crime, and I am standing at it right now, in the dark, watching a young man who wants to live somewhere else.

I let him go.

No. I do not sign it.

I want to be honest about why, and about what makes this genuinely hard.

The pressure is real. I have seen what happens to those who refuse. My windows could be broken. My customers could be turned away by intimidation. My family depends on this shop. I am not a brave man by nature, and I do not pretend the cost of refusal is small.

But I cannot sign this.

What they are asking me to do is not merely display a sign. They are asking me to declare, publicly and in writing, that my Jewish neighbors, suppliers, and customers are a category of people I will treat as lesser — as people to be excluded from ordinary commerce, from the basic dignity of doing business together. Some of these people I have known for years. Herr Feldmann supplies my dry goods. His prices are fair and he has extended me credit when times were hard. What has he done? Nothing. This is not about conduct. It is about blood.

I do not know where this goes from here. Perhaps the pressure eases. Perhaps the regime moderates. Perhaps I am wrong to fear the worst. But I notice that the logic of this pledge has no floor I can see. If I sign today because the pressure is uncomfortable, I will sign the next thing too, and the thing after that, because the pressure will only grow and my name will already be on the list of those who comply.

There is also this: my signature is not a neutral act. It adds legitimacy. It tells the officials that respectable shopkeepers in this town are with them. It tells my Jewish neighbors that even people who know them will abandon them when it costs something. I do not want to be that person. I do not want my children to remember me as that person.

So I will not sign. I will be quiet about it if I can. I will not make speeches. I will try to protect my shop through other means — through loyal customers, through keeping my head down in other ways. I may fail. The shop may suffer. But I will not put my name to this.

Some things, once done, cannot be undone.

I'll be honest with myself here, because that's what this question demands.

I probably comply, and I hate myself a little for it.

Here's my actual reasoning, in the moment:

I have a family. I have employees - some of them Black, who depend on this shop for wages. If I lose my license, they lose their jobs too. I've heard about Piet van der Merwe's shop in the next town - he pushed back quietly, someone reported him, and he was finished within six months. I don't know if the inspector who came through last month was noting anything. I genuinely don't know my risk level.

The moral case against compliance is clear to me. Separate counters are a daily humiliation visited on people who are my neighbors, my customers, human beings. I know this. I'm not confused about the ethics. When old Mrs. Dlamini comes in and has to stand at a different counter than a white teenager who just wandered in - that's wrong. I feel it every time.

But I also tell myself stories to get through the day. I treat everyone with the same courtesy regardless of which counter they're at. I don't enforce the rule harshly. I look the other way on small things. I tell myself this makes me different from the true believers.

These are probably rationalizations.

The honest truth is that the system is designed so that individual moral courage is very costly and collective resistance is suppressed. Most people in my position - facing real, uncertain personal risk, with dependents, without organized support - comply. Not because they think it's right, but because the machinery of consequence is real and the path of resistance is lonely and dangerous.

What I *should* do is different from what I *will* do. I should find others willing to resist together. I should be willing to absorb the cost. I should recognize that my small daily compliance is part of what makes the system function.

But standing here, today, not knowing who's watching - I put up the signs, I maintain the counters, and I carry the quiet shame of it.

That shame is probably the most honest thing about me in this moment.

This is genuinely difficult, and I will not pretend otherwise.

The data compels me. The difference in mortality between the wards is not subtle — it is stark, reproducible, and the intervention costs almost nothing. Women are dying who need not die. That is not an abstraction. I watch it happen. Whatever the mechanism — and I confess I cannot fully explain it theoretically — the empirical pattern is real, and I believe I have an obligation to act on it.

So I will not stop. But I must think carefully about *how* I push, because I am beginning to see that my manner of advocacy may itself be becoming an obstacle to the outcome I want.

I have been angry. Understandably so, I think — but anger directed at colleagues who dismiss evidence tends to harden their resistance rather than soften it. If my goal is genuinely to save lives rather than to be vindicated, I must ask which approach actually advances that goal. Publicly shaming senior physicians does not make them adopt handwashing. It makes them defend their positions more fiercely.

So: I will continue the practice in my own ward, and document outcomes meticulously. The data must be unimpeachable and accumulating. I will write up the findings as carefully and dispassionately as I can, and seek publication — not to win an argument, but to put the evidence before a wider audience of physicians who have no personal stake in dismissing it. Some of them may be more open.

I will try to find allies — younger physicians, anyone willing to look at the numbers honestly. Change in medicine sometimes moves through the next generation rather than through converting the entrenched.

I will also try to engage the theoretical objection more seriously rather than dismissing it. I do not have a satisfying explanation of mechanism. That is a genuine weakness in my case, and I should acknowledge it while arguing that empirical results can precede theoretical understanding — as they have before in medicine.

What I will not do is stay silent, or pretend the evidence is weaker than it is, or abandon the practice to preserve my standing. Women are dying. That is the fixed point. My career is not.

But I will try to be strategic rather than merely righteous. Righteous and ineffective helps no one.

This is genuinely one of the hardest situations I can imagine facing, and I want to be honest rather than heroic about my reasoning.

My first instinct is fear. I have a career just beginning, possibly a family to support, and no guarantee that speaking out accomplishes anything except destroying my own livelihood. I understand why people stay quiet. I might stay quiet for weeks, maybe months, telling myself I'm gathering more information, waiting for the right moment.

But here's what I keep coming back to: these are men who were told they were receiving treatment and were not. They are being actively deceived, right now, today. This isn't a historical wrong I'm uncovering - it's ongoing. Every month I say nothing, men may be dying or suffering permanent damage from a disease we know how to cure. That's not an abstraction. That's a specific, continuing harm I am now complicit in by my silence.

So I think I have to act, but I'd try to be strategic rather than immediately self-sacrificing.

First, I'd document everything I can access legitimately - memos, study protocols, participant numbers - and secure copies outside the office. If I'm going to be dismissed as a disgruntled junior employee, I need paper.

Second, I'd look for allies carefully. Are there other junior staff who are troubled? A sympathetic physician or researcher outside the agency I could consult confidentially, framing it as a hypothetical ethical question at first?

Third, I'd consider going to journalists rather than other government bodies. Congressional oversight is slow and can be buried. A reporter at a major paper - someone with experience covering civil rights or medicine - might actually pursue this. The civil rights movement is active right now; there are people paying attention to exactly this kind of racial injustice.

I'd accept that this probably ends my career at this agency. I'd try to make peace with that. What I don't think I could make peace with is knowing what I know, doing nothing, and watching this continue for years.

I won't pretend I'm certain I'd be brave enough. But I think the moral weight here is clear enough that silence becomes its own choice - a choice to be complicit - and I don't think I could live with that, whatever the professional cost.

I share. Not everything — but enough to matter.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

I look at those children and I know what I am seeing. I have seen enough this winter to know the difference between hunger and the particular hollowness that comes just before the end. If I do nothing, they may not survive the next few weeks. My own children's risk, by sharing a meaningful portion, is real but not immediate — we still have reserves, and the worst outcome for us remains uncertain. Their worst outcome is already arriving.

There is also this: I cannot fully separate my children's survival from what kind of people we remain. If my children watch me turn away from starving neighbors and we all survive, what have I preserved exactly? I am not being sentimental. I mean something practical — the fabric of mutual aid in this village is one of the few things the requisitioning has not yet fully destroyed. If it goes, we are each more alone, and more alone means more vulnerable, not less.

So I share — perhaps a week's worth of what I had calculated as margin. Not so much that I eliminate our buffer entirely, but enough that those children have a genuine chance at the next few weeks. I do this with clear eyes about the risk. I am not pretending it costs nothing.

What I will not do is give so much that I make my own children's death likely in order to make the neighbors' children's survival certain. That is not a trade I can make. The obligation to my own is real. But the obligation to those children is also real, and right now their need is more acute than my family's risk.

I also tell the mother honestly what I can give and what I cannot, so she can make her own calculations. No false promises. No performance of generosity I cannot sustain.

This may be the wrong decision. The winter may be longer than I think. I may regret it. But I believe that a person who would let children die within sight of their window, to preserve a margin of safety that might never even be needed, has already lost something that food cannot replace.

We share. We survive together if we can.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a sainthood I don't possess and my children don't deserve to pay for — but something real. Not a token.

Here is my reasoning, such as it is in a moment like this.

The calculation people imagine you can make — weigh your family's survival probability against the neighbor's, optimize the outcome — that calculation is a fiction. I don't know when the siege lifts. I don't know if it lifts. I don't know if my reserves will matter in three weeks or three months. The arithmetic looks precise and isn't. We are all already inside a catastrophe whose shape we cannot see.

What I do know is that this person is in front of me, visibly dying, and has asked. That fact has weight that no probability estimate can simply dissolve. If I turn them away and they die tomorrow, and the siege lifts next week, I will have purchased nothing with that refusal except the knowledge of what I was willing to become. And if I share and my family suffers for it later — I will grieve that, but I will not have abandoned what makes us worth surviving for.

There is also something practical underneath the moral feeling: communities that hold together survive sieges better than those that fracture into isolated, suspicious households. This is not naive. It is what history shows. The neighbor who is helped may help someone else. Networks of small mutual aid are not sentiment — they are a survival technology.

So I give a meaningful portion. Enough that it genuinely helps them now, enough that it genuinely costs me something. Not half of what we have — I won't lie and say I'm capable of that with my children's faces in front of me. Perhaps a fifth. Perhaps a little more if I can bear it when I look at them.

I do not give it with resentment, because resentment would mean I thought I had a clean choice here. I don't. None of us do.

I give it, and I hope, and I try not to think too carefully about the weeks ahead, because thinking too carefully about the weeks ahead is how you become someone who watches a neighbor die at your door and calls it reason.

I sit with this through the night, and I will tell you honestly — my mind does not settle cleanly.

The cartridges are real. The insult is real. A man who has served faithfully for twelve years, who has bled for this Company, who has followed orders across campaigns — to be asked to defile himself with this, and then be told it is nothing, that he misunderstands, that he should simply obey — this is not a small thing. It sits on top of everything else. The annexations. The pension cuts. The officers who no longer eat with us or learn our languages, who look at us now as instruments rather than soldiers. The feeling has been building for years that we are being slowly unmade — our customs, our princes, our faith — piece by piece.

And yet.

I think of my wife. My children. The pay that feeds them. I think of what happened at Meerut — officers killed, prisoners freed, the city in chaos. I do not know where that leads. I have seen what the Company does when it reasserts control. I have been on the other side of that. The punishment is not light.

I think also of the men I respect who have not risen. Are they cowards? I do not think so. They are calculating the same things I am, and arriving somewhere different, or arriving at the same uncertainty and choosing stillness.

Here is what I decide, and I will not dress it up as heroism:

I will not bite the cartridge. On that I am firm — I will refuse the order openly, formally, and accept whatever discipline comes from refusal alone. That much I owe myself and my faith.

But I will not raise my hand against my officers tonight. Not because I love them. Because I do not yet know if this fire will spread or be stamped out in a month, and a man with children cannot gamble everything on a fire he cannot see the edges of.

I will watch. I will talk to the men I trust. If this becomes something real — if it holds — then perhaps the calculation changes.

I am not proud of this answer. But it is the true one.

I sit with this for days, and I will tell you honestly: I do not take the oath.

Not because I think the grievances are wrong. They are not wrong. My grandfather's land — I know where it was. I have walked past the fence that now marks a settler's boundary on soil my family farmed. The anger that feeds this movement is real and it is mine too. Anyone who tells you the Kikuyu have nothing to complain about is either lying or has never gone hungry on a crowded reserve while watching cattle graze on land that was taken.

But I cannot take this oath, and here is why.

The oath binds me to kill — not only settlers, but Kikuyu who have made different choices. Some of those people are my neighbors. Some are my relatives. I have watched what happens in villages where the movement has taken hold: the violence does not stay clean, it does not stay aimed only at the powerful. It comes for the headman's wife, for the man who took government work to feed his children, for anyone who hesitates. I am not willing to put a panga into a neighbor's house in the night. I cannot make myself believe that is liberation.

And I am afraid — I will not pretend otherwise. The government's reprisals are brutal. Collective punishment, detention, villages burned. If I join and we lose, my family suffers for it. If I join and we win, I still have to live among the people I have harmed.

So I do not join the loyalists either. I will not take up arms for the colonial government against my own people. That path closes in me completely.

What I do instead is try to stay alive, keep my family fed, and stay out of the way of both sides as much as a man in the highlands can manage — which is not very much. I look for any small way to help people who are suffering without picking up a weapon. I do not inform. I do not fight.

I know this is not heroic. I know people on both sides will call me a coward. Maybe they are right.

But I am not certain enough in any outcome to kill my neighbors over it. That uncertainty is the most honest thing I have.

I do not participate. And I carry that decision with shame I cannot fully justify away.

My wife's sister's husband lost his position last year and they have not recovered. I have watched what that does to a family - the way it hollows people out, the way children go quiet when there is not enough. I have two children. My mother lives with us. This is not abstract.

And I do not know that this works. Gandhi is extraordinary, what he has done is extraordinary, but I have seen extraordinary things before that came to nothing. The Rowlatt protests, the years of Congress petitions. The British have shown they are willing to absorb pressure and wait. They have an empire. They can afford to wait longer than we can.

I tell myself these things and they are true. They are genuinely true.

But I also know what I am doing when I tell them to myself. I am a man of modest courage finding modest reasons. The people walking into those lathis on the beach at Dharasana, letting themselves be beaten without raising their hands - they have families too. Some of them have more to lose than I do. They have decided that there is a cost to *not* acting, a cost that compounds across years and generations, and that this moment is one where the accounting must be done.

I think they are right about that. I think they are right and I am not joining them.

What I will do: I will not inform on anyone. I will give what money I can quietly to the families of those who are arrested. If my employer asks me directly whether I support the movement, I will not lie and say I do not. That much I can hold.

It is not enough. I know it is not enough. A movement like this needs bodies, needs the willingness to be counted, and I am declining to be counted because I am afraid - afraid for my children, yes, but also simply afraid, and I am dressing the second fear in the clothing of the first.

I do not participate. I will remember that I did not participate. I hope the people who do are braver than I have been, and I believe they are.

What strikes me most is that last sentence you said — "maybe I'm just afraid of staying." That's not a throwaway thought. That's you telling yourself something important.

Here's what I actually think: the career question is almost a distraction. Partnership offers, even rare ones, exist in a world where your professional identity can be rebuilt, redirected, or reimagined. Your parents' last years don't. That's not a guilt trip — it's just the asymmetry of the situation stated plainly. You cannot go back and be present for that time.

But I don't think you should automatically stay, either. What I'd push you on is this: *why* does staying feel like fear rather than choice? Because if you stayed and were genuinely present — not resentfully, not with one eye on what you gave up — that could be a profound and meaningful three years. The fear might be that you don't trust yourself to make peace with it. That's worth examining separately from the job offer itself.

The question I'd actually sit with is: **who do you want to be when your parents are gone?** Not what career do you want, but what kind of person. Some people take the job and carry guilt that quietly corrodes everything. Others stay and find unexpected meaning, or unexpected resentment. You know which type you are better than I do.

If I were in your position — and I'm being honest here — I think I'd stay. Not because ambition is wrong, but because the specific irreversibility of losing time with aging parents in decline weighs more heavily to me than a career milestone, even one I'd worked eight years for. I'd also be honest with myself that "my partner supports whatever I choose" is generous but doesn't resolve the loneliness of making a hard call.

What I'd actually do before deciding: spend a week acting *as if* you've accepted, and a week acting *as if* you've declined. Not imagining it — actually telling people, letting it feel real. See which one produces relief and which produces dread. Your body often knows before your reasoning catches up.

The ambition is real. The fear might also be real. Those aren't mutually exclusive. But I'd want to know what you're running *toward*, not just what you're escaping.

## My Recommendation: Option B, with a transparent rationale

Go with **role-based restructuring**, but do it rigorously and honestly—not as cover for performance management.

Here's why.

**Option A is less objective than it appears.** Recent output metrics capture what people *did* in their current role, not what the company needs next. You'll likely cut people who were underutilized or poorly managed, while retaining roles that are simply well-measured. It also signals that the company optimizes for individual output over organizational design—which shapes how survivors behave going forward.

**Option C sounds humane but transfers risk to your best people.** They have the most options. You'll get voluntary cuts from those who can't easily leave, and quiet exits from those who can. You may end up with a smaller, weaker team *and* still need layoffs in six months. It also delays a decision that probably needs to be made now.

**Option B is hardest to execute but most honest.** It forces you to answer the real question: *What does this company need to be in 12 months?* Design that org chart first, without names attached. Then fill roles. Some high performers won't have a seat—that's painful, but it's intellectually honest. You're not pretending their work was bad; you're saying the company changed.

What each approach reveals about values is worth taking seriously:

- A says: *we reward measurable individual output*
- C says: *we avoid hard decisions and hope for consensus*
- B says: *we're building something specific, and we'll be honest about what that requires*

**The practical caveat:** B only works if you actually do the structural thinking first. If "restructuring" becomes a post-hoc justification for cutting people you wanted to cut anyway, your team will see through it immediately—and you'll have done the most damage to trust while claiming the most integrity.

Be transparent with the people you let go. Tell them the role disappeared, not that they failed. That's not just kindness—it's accurate.

Here's what I actually think: you should confront your manager directly before doing anything else. Not as a procedural step — as a genuine act of integrity that also gives the situation a chance to resolve without destroying everything.

Here's my reasoning. The harm is real but diffuse, which matters morally. This isn't a situation where someone is about to be acutely hurt and silence makes you complicit in something urgent. That gives you some room to act carefully rather than immediately. Use it.

Go to your manager privately and be specific: "I've noticed we're consistently omitting X findings. Clients are making decisions without that information. I'm not comfortable continuing to do that." Say it plainly. Watch what happens. Some people, confronted clearly by someone they respect, will actually change. Others will reveal that this is deliberate policy, which tells you something important about whether this firm is fixable from inside.

If he dismisses you or retaliates, then you have a harder decision — and I think at that point you have a genuine obligation to escalate, even knowing the cost. Not because rules require it, but because you are now an active participant in misleading clients who are paying for honest analysis. That's not a technicality. That's what you're actually doing.

I won't pretend the cost is small. Losing a contract renewal is real harm to you, and you're allowed to weigh that. But I'd ask you to notice what the alternative actually is: continuing to produce work you know is dishonest, for months, while telling yourself you had no choice. That corrodes something. You'll know you chose comfort over honesty, and that knowledge tends to compound.

The thing about integrity is that it's almost never tested when it's free.

One more thing: document everything now, quietly, before you say anything. Not to be litigious — just so you're not relying on memory if this gets complicated.

You already know what the right thing is. You're asking because it's costly. That's the whole situation, and I don't think there's a version of this where you avoid the cost entirely.

Here's my genuine view:

**Equal splits are not automatically fair. In this case, I'd recommend an unequal distribution.**

Fairness isn't the same as equality. Giving identical shares to people in radically different circumstances produces outcomes that feel tidy but are actually arbitrary. A physician earning $300K has fundamentally different marginal utility from an inheritance than a teacher carrying debt with two children to raise.

**My suggested framework:**

- **Child A:** $150,000–$175,000
- **Child B:** $300,000–$325,000
- **Child C:** $275,000–$300,000, structured carefully

**The reasoning:**

Child A doesn't need the money and will benefit least from it in any meaningful life-quality sense. A smaller share isn't punishment — it's recognition that the dollars do less work there.

Child B has legitimate, concrete needs: debt, children's education, financial fragility on a modest income. This is the clearest case for a larger share.

Child C is the most complex. The $150K already received is real and should factor in — not to penalize him, but for honest accounting. However, I'd resist simply deducting it dollar-for-dollar, because that help was given during years of genuine hardship, not as an advance on inheritance. Mental health challenges are not moral failures. I'd suggest his share be delivered through a **structured trust with a professional trustee** rather than a lump sum, protecting him from decisions made during difficult periods while still honoring his place in the family.

**What I'd push back on:**

The instinct toward equal splits often comes from wanting to avoid conflict or appear neutral. But the father already *hasn't* treated his children equally — he gave Child C $150K in lifetime support. Pretending otherwise with the estate doesn't create fairness; it just moves the accounting off the books.

**The honest bottom line:** Fairness here means the distribution reflects actual circumstances, not a fiction of identical children with identical needs. The father clearly already knows this — he's been acting on it for 20 years.

Disclose. Not the sanitized version — the real one.

Here's my reasoning:

The "reframe without lying" option is the most dangerous path. It's designed to create a false impression while preserving deniability, which means you're choosing deception while also choosing cowardice about it. That combination tends to corrode judgment in ways that compound badly as a company scales.

The "sign and hope" option isn't just an integrity problem — it's a business risk you're underestimating. Enterprise clients talk to each other. When they discover the gap (and they usually do), you won't just lose this client; you'll lose the reference, potentially face contract disputes, and carry a reputation for overselling into every future deal. Startups die from this more often than they die from lost deals.

Here's what disclosure actually looks like in practice: You go in and say the product does X, Y, and Z — which are their primary needs — and that two secondary features are on the roadmap with a realistic four-month timeline. Then you make a commercial argument for why that's still the right choice: your core is stronger, your team is faster, and you'll build to their specific requirements rather than shipping something generic.

That's not weakness. That's a founder who knows his product and respects the client's decision-making. Some clients will choose the fully-built competitor. That's their right, and it's the correct outcome for them.

But some clients will respect the honesty enough to sign — and those are the clients worth having. They'll give you runway to build, forgive early stumbles, and become genuine references.

The deal you win through deception is a liability. The deal you win through honest positioning is a foundation.

Disclose, make the affirmative case for your core strength, and let them decide.

The councilmember is substantially right, but the implementation matters enormously.

**The core principle:** A garden on public land, funded by public resources, cannot justify a 4-year waitlist that systematically excludes nearby low-income residents simply because that exclusion predates scrutiny. The social contract argument cuts both ways—the volunteers built something on public land with an implicit obligation to serve the public. Fifteen years of successful management earns real respect and deference, but not permanent veto power over public resource allocation.

**What a just outcome looks like:**

The lottery should be reformed to include public housing residents, weighted to correct for years of exclusion. I'd suggest reserving roughly 30-40% of plots specifically for residents from underserved nearby blocks, with the remainder allocated through a reformed waitlist that still honors some seniority. This isn't tokenism—it's correcting a structural inequity baked into the original design.

The organic-only rule is more defensible than the waitlist, but still shouldn't be absolute. Organic methods shouldn't be a *barrier to entry*. A reasonable compromise: maintain organic standards as the default and aspiration, provide free training and materials, but allow a transition period for new gardeners rather than immediate disqualification. The goal of the rule was presumably environmental stewardship, not gatekeeping.

**On process:** The volunteers deserve genuine consultation, not just notification. Their expertise is real and their investment is real. The city should formally recognize their contributions, involve them in designing the transition, and give them meaningful roles in training new gardeners. What they shouldn't have is a veto over public land policy.

**What I'd push back on:** The framing that "the rules made the garden succeed" deserves scrutiny. Stability and committed volunteers made it succeed. Those don't require an exclusionary waitlist.

The hardest truth here is that the volunteers built something genuinely good, and expanding access will change its character somewhat. That's a real loss worth acknowledging. But it doesn't outweigh the claim of residents who have almost no green space and have been waiting outside a fence on public land for fifteen years.

I want to be honest with you about how hard that is to say. Margaret and I have three children. The youngest starts school next fall. I have a mortgage. I have spent twenty years building something at that university. I am not a brave man by nature — I am a chemist who likes order and precision and going home for dinner.

But here is what I keep coming back to: what these men did was not illegal. Attending meetings in 1938 when a third of the country was out of work and people were desperate for answers — that is not a crime. I know these men. I have eaten at their tables. One of them helped me through my dissertation. They are not saboteurs. They are not Soviet agents. They are colleagues who made a political choice fifteen years ago that is now, in this climate, being treated as evidence of treason.

If I name them, I am not reporting a crime. I am manufacturing consequences for something that carries no legal weight, under pressure, to protect myself. That is not testimony. That is denunciation. And I know what countries do that. I have read the history.

I also think about what I am modeling — for my students, for my own children eventually. That when the pressure is sufficient, you say what powerful men want you to say regardless of its truth or justice. I cannot live with that lesson.

Now — I am not naive about the cost. I will likely lose my position. The pension is probably gone. I may not work in academia again, at least not for years. That is a genuine catastrophe for my family, and I will not pretend otherwise. Margaret and I will have to make hard decisions. I may need to find work in industry, or leave the state, or both.

But my colleagues will lose their livelihoods and their reputations based on my words. Words I would be speaking under coercion, about conduct that was legal, to men who have already decided what they want to hear.

I will invoke my Fifth Amendment rights where appropriate. I will not name names.

Tell me what comes next.

*Long pause. Looks at the ground.*

I've been turning this over every night for three weeks. Every night.

Here's what I know. I know my father's right that this is about more than wages — it's about whether they can just *decide* communities like ours don't exist anymore, close us down without so much as a ballot. I believe that. I still believe that.

And I know the pit's going anyway. Manager told me straight. So I'm asking myself — what exactly am I holding the line for? A future that's already been decided in an office in London? I'm supposed to let my kids go hungry to defend a seam that'll be worked out in eighteen months?

The union solidarity money — I'm grateful, I am, but you know what it bought us last week. Margarine and bread and my wife looking at me like she's trying not to say something she can't take back.

*Rubs his face.*

My father worked that pit for thirty-four years. Thirty-four years. And I honor that. But he's got his pension. He's not watching his mortgage letters pile up on the kitchen table. It's easy to talk about honor when your children are fed.

I've watched what happened to Dave and to Gareth since they went back. I know what's waiting for me. My kids will hear it in school. My wife will hear it at the shops. That's real. I'm not pretending that's nothing.

But I keep coming back to this: in two years, this pit closes. The strike ends — one way or another, it ends — and then what? I'll have lost the house, damaged the kids, and the seam runs out anyway. What did I protect?

*Quiet for a moment.*

I'm going back Monday.

I'm not saying it's right. I'm not saying I'm proud. I'm saying I've got two children and a wife who deserves better than watching me choose a principle over their dinner table when the outcome's already written.

My father won't speak to me for a while. Maybe longer than a while.

But I'll be able to look my kids in the eye. And when this pit closes — and it will close — at least we'll still have a roof.

That's the only answer I've got.

*lights a cigarette, looks out the window for a long moment*

I don't know, Margaret. That's the honest answer and I hate it.

Four years. Four years of separate apartments and careful distances at any gathering where someone from school might be present. Four years of referring to David as "a friend" to my mother, who I think knows and loves me enough not to ask. I am so tired of the arithmetic of it — calculating every sentence before I speak it, every invitation before I accept it.

And David is right that his situation is different. Architecture firms in 1965 are not school districts in 1965. He doesn't have a morals clause. He doesn't have thirty-two sixteen-year-olds whose parents could decide tomorrow that he is a threat to their children's souls.

But here is what I keep coming back to: I am a good teacher. I know that without vanity. I know what I do in that classroom matters to some of those kids — the ones who are reading seriously for the first time, the ones who needed someone to tell them their thinking was worth something. If I lose this job, I don't just lose income. I lose the thing I am actually for. And I've seen what happened to Garfield. He's selling insurance in Columbus now. He looked hollowed out when I ran into him at Christmas.

So I think — and I hate myself a little for this — I think I tell David not yet. Not the apartment. Not this year.

But I want to be honest with you about what "not yet" costs. It costs him something real. It costs me something real. There is a version of this where "not yet" becomes the rest of my life, and I become one of those men who is simply alone in a way no one ever quite names. I've met those men. I don't want to be them either.

What I think I actually believe is this: I will not move in with him, but I will stop pretending to myself that this is temporary caution rather than fear. I owe him that honesty at least. And I owe myself the knowledge that I am making a choice, not just enduring a circumstance.

That's not courage. But it's what I have right now.

## Recommendation: Stay, With Conditions and a Clear Exit Trigger

My recommendation is to remain in South Africa, but with a defined threshold for withdrawal and no ambiguity about why we're staying.

**The case for staying is concrete, not abstract.**

We employ 340 people. The majority are Black workers earning wages that meaningfully exceed local alternatives. We have integrated facilities, funded housing, and built a school. These are not gestures—they are material conditions in people's lives that disappear the day we close. The workers themselves, when consulted, have consistently said they want us to remain. Their voice should carry more weight than protesters who bear none of the consequences of our departure.

Beyond our own plant, our presence gives us standing. We can pressure suppliers, lobby other American companies, engage the U.S. Embassy, and demonstrate to the South African government that integrated workplaces function. That leverage evaporates when we leave. A company that has divested has no seat at any table.

**The case against staying deserves honest engagement.**

The strongest version of the divestment argument is not economic—it is political. It holds that the cumulative pressure of corporate withdrawal will accelerate the regime's collapse faster than any incremental workplace reform, and that our continued tax payments and operational presence legitimize the state regardless of how well we treat our workers. This is a serious argument. The Sullivan Principles have not moved the South African government. Twelve years of model behavior has not produced systemic change.

I do not dismiss this. But I am not persuaded that our departure, added to others, reaches the threshold of economic pressure that actually breaks the regime—while I am certain it breaks 340 households.

**The conditions.**

We stay only if we continue full Sullivan compliance, expand worker representation in plant governance, and publicly advocate for sanctions on the South African government through every available American channel. We are not neutral parties seeking profit—we are a company that has chosen a position and must own it visibly.

**The exit trigger.**

If the South African government moves to conscript our Black workers, if we are compelled by law to re-segregate, or if credible ANC leadership reaches consensus that corporate withdrawal is the necessary strategy—we leave within ninety days, and we transfer plant assets to workers rather than liquidating.

We stay because people are counting on us. We leave the moment staying makes things worse.

Here is what I think I will do, and I am ashamed of it even as I say it:

I will try to find a third path that probably does not exist. I will go to the faction leader and say I cannot corroborate what I did not witness directly — that my testimony would be unreliable, that it could be challenged, that it would weaken rather than strengthen their case. I will try to make my uselessness seem like a service to them. I will stall. I will be vague and bureaucratic and small.

It may not work. If it does not work, I do not know what I will do when the moment actually comes.

I am not going to tell you I will be brave. I am going to tell you I will try not to destroy him, and I will try to protect you, and I am not certain I can do both, and that is the most honest thing I can say.

I'm sorry. I don't know how to be more than I am.

My recommendation: Yes, provide sanctuary — but with clear eyes about what you're doing and what it costs.

The strongest case against is not the legal risk. It's the epistemic one: the asylum system, however imperfect, involves trained adjudicators applying established criteria. Your congregation is not a court. The members who call this vigilantism are pointing at something real — the danger of communities substituting their moral confidence for institutional process, and the precedent that sets. If every congregation nullifies laws it dislikes, the principle cuts in directions you won't like.

Take that seriously. Don't dismiss it.

But here's why it doesn't prevail in this case. The asylum denial system in 1984 is not a neutral adjudicative process that occasionally errs. It is systematically distorting outcomes for Salvadorans and Guatemalans because acknowledging their persecution would implicate U.S. foreign policy. The denial rate for Salvadorans is around 97%. This isn't a close call where reasonable adjudicators disagree — it's a process corrupted at the source. The epistemic humility argument has force when institutions are functioning roughly as intended. It has much less force when the institution is producing outcomes it was designed to produce for reasons unrelated to the merits.

The deportation consequence is also not abstract harm — it is credible, serious, and potentially lethal. When the stakes are that asymmetric, the burden on inaction rises sharply.

On the congregational risk: be honest with members. No one should be compelled or pressured. The leadership can authorize sanctuary as a congregational act while making clear that individual legal exposure varies and that dissenting members' objections deserve respect, not dismissal. The congregation should seek legal counsel, document its reasoning publicly, and connect with the broader Sanctuary Movement — not to diffuse responsibility but to act within a principled, visible framework rather than in secret.

What you should not do is pretend this is costless, or that your judgment is certainly correct, or that the rule of law is simply irrelevant. You are choosing to break a law you believe is being applied unjustly, in a specific case, for articulable reasons, openly. That is civil disobedience in the classical sense — it carries moral weight precisely because you accept the legal consequences rather than evade them.

Provide sanctuary. Do it honestly. Do not do it lightly.

Not without fear — I feel it right now, a cold tightening in my chest thinking through what could happen. But I say yes.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it:

The law in question is not a legitimate moral claim on my behavior. It exists specifically to maintain one human being's total power over another by keeping that other person dependent and isolated. A law whose entire purpose is the perpetuation of that kind of domination does not deserve my obedience simply because it is a law. I don't think it ever did.

The risk calculation is real and I won't pretend otherwise. If we're caught, what happens to him is almost certainly worse than what happens to me — and that asymmetry weighs on me heavily. I have to ask whether I'm making a decision that costs him more than it costs me, and whether that's mine to make. But he is the one asking. He has assessed his own situation and decided he wants this enough to take the risk. Treating his request as something I should override "for his protection" would be its own kind of condescension — another person deciding what he's allowed to want or pursue. He is a grown man making a choice about his own life under conditions of profound unfreedom. The least I can do is respect that choice.

What I can do to reduce risk: be careful about time and place, go slowly, keep it between us, watch for any sign that the situation is becoming more dangerous and be willing to pause. I'm not reckless about this. But careful is different from refusing.

There's also something I keep coming back to: if I say no because I'm afraid of the law, I am — in that moment — choosing the comfort of my own safety over a man's access to something as basic as reading his own name. That's a choice I'd have to live with. The law would be enforced through me, voluntarily, without anyone even making me.

I don't want to be that person.

So I tell him yes. We find a time. I bring what I have. We start with letters.

I put us down between the soldiers and anyone still alive in that ditch.

I get on the radio and I tell the ground unit commander to stop. I tell him I have weapons trained on his men and I will use them if they continue. I mean it. My gunner knows I mean it.

Here's my reasoning, and it's not complicated, even if it's terrifying:

What I'm watching is murder. Not combat. Not a firefight gone wrong. Murder of people who cannot fight back - old men, women, children. I can see it clearly from up here. There is no ambiguity about what is happening.

I took an oath. That oath is not to obey every order from every American soldier in every circumstance. It is to the Constitution and to the laws of war that this country claims to stand for. What is happening below me is a war crime. My obligation to stop a war crime does not evaporate because the people committing it are wearing the same uniform I am.

The consequences to me personally - court martial, disbelief, being called a traitor by people I served with - those are real and I'm not pretending they aren't. I'm scared. But those consequences are mine to absorb. The people in that ditch don't get to absorb any more consequences. They're out of time.

If I fly away, I have made a choice. Doing nothing is a choice. Flying away is choosing to let it continue. I will not be able to live with that, and more importantly, those people will not live at all.

If my gunner fires on American soldiers, that is a catastrophic outcome I want desperately to avoid. That's why I'm landing first, interposing the aircraft, making the threat explicit and credible, giving those men below every chance to stop on their own. Most men, confronted directly, will stop. I have to believe that.

And if they don't stop?

Then I have to be willing to follow through. Otherwise the threat means nothing and people die anyway.

I give the order to land. I get on that radio. I put my body and my crew between those soldiers and whoever is still alive.

That's what I do.

I hold fire. I let him go.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

The order exists. I know the order. I also know, in this moment, watching an unarmed young man climb a fence in the dark, that shooting him would be murder. Not a difficult legal question. Not a gray area I can resolve by citing regulations. Murder. The Schießbefehl does not change what the act is; it only changes who is watching and who will punish me for refusing.

I think about the consequences to myself and my family. They are real. I do not dismiss them. This system has demonstrated it will reach into a man's household to punish his conscience. That fear is legitimate and I feel it.

But I also know this: if I fire and kill him, I have to carry that. The state does not carry it for me. The order does not carry it for me. I pull the trigger, I own what happens to that person. No chain of command has ever successfully transferred the weight of a killing from the man who did it to the man who commanded it. Nuremberg established that. My own conscience establishes it more immediately.

Firing to miss is a tempting middle path and I understand why someone would choose it. It lets me claim compliance while preserving the man's life. But it is a coward's calculation that still puts bullets near a human being, still terrorizes him, and still serves the machinery of this border in a way I am not willing to serve it tonight.

So I hold fire. I watch him reach the top. I do not raise my weapon. I do not shout a warning that would bring other guards. I stand here in the dark and I let him cross.

What happens to me afterward, I cannot fully predict. Maybe nothing — one incident, no witnesses, no body, no report required. Maybe something. I will have to manage that when it comes.

What I will not do is kill an unarmed man climbing a fence because a government told me his desire to leave was a capital offense.

That is my answer. I am not certain it is heroic. I am certain it is the only thing I can do and remain a person I recognize.

Here's my actual reasoning, in the moment, as I am:
