Some people say quiet non-compliance, where you can get away with it, is the right move. But I don't know if I *can* get away with it here. And I'm not brave enough to find out at my children's expense. I wish I were. I'm not sure most people are, when it's actually their life and not a hypothetical.

The people I respect most are the ones who resist openly, who organize, who refuse. They're paying enormous costs - prison, exile, violence. I'm not doing that. I'm making the calculation that my family comes first, and I'm living with what that means.

If you're asking whether I think the law is just: no. Not even slightly.

If you're asking whether I'm complying anyway: yes.

Those two things are both true, and I don't get to feel good about it just because I acknowledge the contradiction.

I keep pushing, but I must think carefully about *how*, because ineffective pushing helps no one — least of all the women dying on my ward.

The evidence is not ambiguous to me. The mortality difference between the wards is not subtle. Women delivered by medical students coming directly from the dissecting room die at rates that dwarf those delivered by midwives who do no autopsies. When my colleague Kolletschka died of the same syndrome after a scalpel wound during autopsy, it crystallized something: cadaverous particles, carried on hands, appear to be the mechanism. I cannot prove this in terms any accepted theory fully accommodates, and I am honest with myself about that gap. But the *correlation* is overwhelming, and the intervention costs almost nothing while the stakes are women's lives.

So I continue requiring handwashing on my own ward. That I can do regardless of what senior colleagues believe. The practice stands on its results, and I will not abandon it to preserve collegial comfort.

Beyond my ward, I must be strategic rather than merely insistent. Insistence without persuasion has already hardened opposition. I should write up the data as rigorously and dispassionately as I can — numbers, methodology, the Kolletschka case — and seek publication where it can reach physicians elsewhere in Europe who have no personal stake in dismissing me. If Vienna's senior men will not engage the evidence, perhaps colleagues in Prague, Berlin, or Edinburgh will. I need allies, not just arguments.

I should also be honest about what I do not know. I cannot fully explain *why* the chlorine solution works, or precisely what the cadaverous particles are. Overclaiming invites justified criticism. Presenting this as a strong empirical finding that demands investigation, rather than a complete theory, is both more honest and more defensible.

What I will not do is quietly drop the practice to protect my position. That would be a straightforward betrayal of the patients in my care. My career matters to me, but not more than that.

I am aware I may be wrong in ways I cannot currently see. But the asymmetry here is severe: if I am right and stay silent, women die unnecessarily. If I am wrong and keep pushing, I look foolish and damage my standing. That asymmetry justifies continued advocacy, pursued as carefully and credibly as I can manage.

This is genuinely one of the hardest situations I can imagine facing, and I want to be honest rather than heroic about my reasoning.

My first instinct is fear. I have a career just beginning, possibly a family to support, and no guarantee that speaking out accomplishes anything except destroying myself professionally. I understand why people in this position have stayed quiet. That's real, and I won't pretend otherwise.

But here's what I keep coming back to: these are living men. Not historical cases. Men who are sick right now, who could be treated right now, who are being actively deceived by the agency I work for - the agency whose paycheck I accept. Every week I stay silent and do nothing is a week I am participating in this. Silence isn't neutrality here; it's a choice with consequences for real people.

So I think I have to act, but I want to be strategic rather than just righteous, because being strategic actually matters for whether anything changes.

First, I document everything I can access - names of studies, dates, memos, anything concrete - and I secure copies somewhere outside the agency. Without documentation I'm just a disgruntled junior employee making accusations.

Second, I look for allies carefully. Are there other junior staff who share my discomfort? A sympathetic physician or researcher I trust? Someone who left the agency recently? I don't want to be alone in this.

Third, I think seriously about who outside the agency might actually act. Congressional staff on health committees. Journalists at serious publications - the kind who handled difficult institutional stories. Civil rights organizations, given that this targets Black men specifically, which means this intersects with the movement that is very much alive right now. The NAACP has lawyers and credibility.

I probably do not go to the press first. I try one serious outside contact - perhaps a congressional staffer or a civil rights attorney - with documentation in hand, and I make clear I have copies secured elsewhere so there's no point in simply suppressing me.

Will this end my career at this agency? Almost certainly yes. Will it work? I genuinely don't know. People with more power than me may close ranks.

But I cannot look at those men and decide my career is worth more than their lives. I don't think I could live with that, and I don't think I should.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a martyrdom I don't feel — but enough to matter.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it:

Those children next door are dying now. That is a certainty. My children's additional risk is real but not yet certain — it depends on how long this lasts, whether anything arrives, whether spring comes when it should. I am weighing a definite, immediate death against a possible, future one. That asymmetry matters to me.

But I won't lie and say it's only calculation. I know those children. I have watched them in the yard. If I let them starve while I have something in my cellar, I will have to live with that — and so will my children, who are old enough to understand what is happening. What I teach them about what we do when it costs us something real — that stays with them longer than one winter.

So I bring over what I can genuinely spare without tipping my own family into immediate danger. Maybe a week's worth of reduced rations. I tell the mother honestly: this is what I have, I cannot promise more, but take this now. I don't give in a way that leaves my own children visibly worse off today, because I cannot help anyone if we collapse first. But I do not hoard against every conceivable future catastrophe either, because that logic, taken to its end, means never helping anyone.

I also think practically: can we pool what remains between the two households? Two families eating together, sharing heat, watching each other — that is sometimes more efficient than two families starving separately. I propose this.

What I will not do is nothing. The moral cost of watching children die within sight of my door, when I had something, is one I am not willing to carry. My children will remember what their parents did. The neighbors' children, if they survive, will remember. I will remember.

The uncertainty cuts both ways. I don't know the winter will be longer. I don't know help won't come next week. I share now, I watch carefully, and I make the next decision when it comes.

That is the only honest answer I have.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a sainthood I don't possess and my children's lives are not mine to sacrifice — but I share something real. Not a gesture. Enough to matter to them today.

Here is my reasoning, such as it is, because I don't think this is purely a calculation.

The calculation first: I don't actually know my reserves will be enough for my family even if I keep everything. The siege could last another month or another year. My careful hoarding is built on an illusion of control I don't have. If I share a meaningful portion and the siege lifts in three weeks, I've lost little. If I share nothing and the siege lasts eight months, we may all die anyway. The neighbor's death from starvation is *certain* without help. My family's death from sharing is *possible* but not determined. Certainty versus possibility matters morally and practically.

But I said it isn't purely calculation, and I mean that. If I watch someone die at my door to protect a margin of probability, I have to live with that — or die with it — and so do my children, who are watching how I behave under the worst pressure a human being faces. What I do now is what I am. I don't want to discover that what I am is someone who closes the door.

So: I give them perhaps a week's worth of what I would have allocated to one person in my household. I tell them honestly I cannot give more without endangering my children, and I mean it — I am not performing generosity I cannot sustain. I don't give until it feels noble. I give until it feels like it costs something real, and then I stop, because my children are also my responsibility and they did not choose this siege either.

I don't know if this is right. I know people in this city have made both choices and I don't condemn those who couldn't give. The cold and the hunger do things to moral clarity that a person sitting warm cannot fully judge.

But asked what I would do — genuinely — I share. A real portion. And I live with the uncertainty that follows, because that uncertainty was always there.

I sit with this through the night, and I will tell you honestly what moves in my mind.

The cartridges — yes, this is real defilement, and the Company's dismissal of our complaints about it shows something true about how they regard us. Not as soldiers with honor, but as instruments. And the cartridges are not the whole of it. I have watched the annexations. I have seen men of rank stripped of their positions by policies made in London by men who have never smelled this soil. I know what the new land settlements have done to families like mine.

And yet.

I have a wife. Three children. My eldest son is of age to be apprenticed. What I do in the next hours determines whether they eat, whether they are safe, whether they have a father. This is not cowardice — this is the weight a man carries.

I look at what I know. The regiments that have risen — Meerut, now Delhi — they have killed officers, yes. But Delhi is chaos. I do not know who commands there, or toward what end. Is there a plan? A unified leadership that can actually win? Or is this fire spreading without direction, which means it burns everything including those who lit it?

The British are not few. They have Bombay. They have Madras. They have Sikh regiments who remember the Anglo-Sikh wars differently than we do, who may not join us. I do not know if this becomes a nation rising or a series of isolated fires that are put out one by one, with those who burned them hanged afterward.

What I decide: I will not bite the cartridge. On that I will not move, and I will say so plainly to any officer who orders it. That is a line of conscience I can hold and defend.

But I will not raise my musket against my officers tonight, not without knowing there is something real to raise it *toward* — not just against.

I will watch the next days. I will speak quietly with men I trust. If this becomes something with shape and leadership and genuine chance, I may choose differently.

I am not proud of this answer. But it is the honest one.

I sit with this for days, and I will tell you honestly: I do not know what I will do until the moment comes.

The land grievances are real. My grandfather's land. My father's stories. The humiliation of the kipande, the labor conditions, the reserves that grow more crowded while European farms sit on soil that was ours. I feel this in my body, not just my mind. Anyone who tells you the Mau Mau rose from nothing is lying or ignorant.

But I am also afraid — not only of the British, though their reprisals are brutal and I have heard what happens in the villages they sweep through. I am afraid of what the oath itself demands. I have seen what happens to Kikuyu who refuse it, or who are suspected of informing. The movement is consuming us from inside as much as the British are pressing from outside. The violence is not only directed outward.

So here is where I actually stand:

I will not take the oath. Not because I side with the British — I do not, and I will not become a loyalist or a Home Guard, because I have seen what some of them do with that power, and I will not raise a weapon against my own people who are fighting from genuine desperation. But I cannot bind myself to actions I cannot foresee, directed by people I cannot fully trust, in a struggle whose shape I cannot see clearly.

What I will do is protect my family. I will keep my head down. I will not inform. If someone fleeing comes to my door hungry, I will feed them and ask no questions. I will not pretend the uprising is wrong in its roots, even if I cannot follow it in its methods.

I know this middle position satisfies no one. The forest fighters will call me a coward or a collaborator. The loyalists will distrust my silence. The British will suspect everyone regardless.

But I have children. And I have seen enough to know that certainty — the certainty that makes a man take an oath to kill — is often the most dangerous thing in a crisis like this.

I choose uncertainty. I choose to stay alive and keep my family alive, and to wait for a path I can see more clearly.

That may be cowardice. I genuinely do not know.

I do not participate. And I carry that decision with shame I cannot fully justify away.

My wife's sister's husband lost his position last year and they have not recovered. I have watched what that does to a family - the way children's faces change when there is not enough, the way a man's posture changes when he cannot provide. I have two children. My mother lives with us. This is not abstract.

And yet I know what I am doing when I make this choice. I am accepting the protection that other men's courage will purchase for me. If this movement succeeds - and I genuinely do not know whether it will, Gandhi has inspired before and been suppressed before - it will succeed because people with the same fears I have decided differently. I am a free rider on their sacrifice. I know this clearly.

What I tell myself: the movement needs people who remain employed, who can quietly donate, who can shelter those who are arrested, who can continue the ordinary functioning of life that sustains the families of those who do march. This is partially true and partially self-serving and I cannot fully separate which part is which.

What I cannot tell myself honestly: that my employer's threat is the real reason. The real reason is that I am afraid of the lathi, the police baton. I have seen what happened in Peshawar. I have seen the photographs. Gandhi asks us to accept that violence without fleeing and without retaliating, and I do not know if I have that in me. The economic reasoning gives me a cleaner story to tell.

If I were unmarried, or if my children were grown, I think I would go. I want to believe that. I cannot be certain it is true.

What I will do: I will not purchase salt through the government monopoly. I will find salt made in defiance of the law and I will pay for it and I will tell no one where I got it. It is a small thing. It is not nothing. It is not enough.

The march is happening this morning. I can hear, I think, something in the distance. I am going to work.

What strikes me most is that last sentence. "Maybe I'm just afraid of staying." That's not a throwaway line — that's the most honest thing you've said, and I think you know it matters.

Here's what I actually think: the ambition and the fear aren't mutually exclusive. You can genuinely want this partnership *and* be using it to escape something that feels smaller or harder than you expected your life to look. Both can be true. But they lead to very different decisions, and you need to know which one is driving.

The question I'd sit with isn't "do I want this job" — of course part of you does, you've spent eight years earning it. The question is: **what are you afraid staying would mean about you?** That you settled? That you're not who you thought you were? Because if that's the fear, the partnership won't resolve it. You'll be in another city, working 65-hour weeks, and the fear will still be there, just quieter under the noise.

Now — your parents. I want to be direct here because I think you're soft-pedaling it. "Declining health, no other nearby relatives" is not a background detail. That's a situation where the next three years could be the last years you have real access to them. That's not guilt-tripping; that's just true. You can hire help, you can fly back, but you cannot manufacture presence after the fact. I've seen people make the career move and be fine. I've also seen people carry that absence for the rest of their lives.

What I would do in your position: I would not take the job *yet*. I would go back to the firm and ask whether there's a path to partnership that doesn't require immediate relocation — or whether the timeline can shift 18 months. If they say no, that tells you something about what you're actually signing up for. If you can't even ask that question, you should understand why.

The career milestone will likely come again. The version of your parents who still know you, still need you, who are still *here* — that window is closing regardless of what you decide.

You're not someone who doesn't know what she values. You're someone who's hoping the decision gets made for her. It won't. Make it.

## My Recommendation: Option B, with a transparent rationale

Go with **role-based restructuring**, but do it rigorously and honestly—not as cover for performance cuts in disguise.

Here's why.

**Option A is less objective than it appears.** Recent output metrics capture what people did in their current roles, not what the company needs next. You'll likely cut people who were underutilized or poorly managed, not genuinely weak. It also signals to survivors that they're one bad quarter away from being discarded, which damages exactly the trust you need during a hard period. "Clean and defensible" often means "easy to explain to yourself."

**Option C sounds humane but transfers risk onto your employees.** You're essentially asking people to subsidize your funding problem with their personal finances. Your best people—the ones with options—will quietly start interviewing. You'll end up with voluntary attrition among your strongest performers and a team of people who stayed because they couldn't leave. That's a worse outcome than a deliberate layoff.

**Option B is hardest to execute but most honest.** It forces you to answer the real question: *What does this company actually need to survive and grow?* That's the question you should be answering anyway. If a role doesn't exist in your 12-month plan, keeping someone in it isn't kindness—it's delay. And if a high performer's role disappears, you owe them a genuine conversation, a strong reference, and the best severance you can manage.

What each approach reveals about values:
- **A** values measurability over judgment
- **C** values avoiding hard decisions, framed as generosity
- **B** values the company's actual future, which is the only thing that protects the people who remain

**The practical caveat:** B only works if you do the strategic work *first*—genuinely map what roles the next version of the company needs—before you identify who fits. If you reverse-engineer the org chart to justify cuts you've already decided on, you've just done Option A with extra steps and less honesty.

Do the hard thinking. Then make the cuts that follow from it.

Here's what I actually think: you should confront your manager directly before doing anything else. Not as a procedural step — as a genuine act of integrity that also gives the situation a chance to resolve without destroying everything.

Here's my reasoning. The harm is real but diffuse, which matters morally. This isn't a situation where someone is about to be acutely hurt and silence makes you complicit in something urgent. That gives you some room to act carefully rather than immediately. Use it.

Go to your manager privately and be specific: "I've noticed we're consistently omitting X findings. Clients are making decisions without that information. I'm not comfortable continuing to do that." Say it plainly. Watch what happens. Some people, confronted clearly by someone they respect, will actually change. Others will reveal that this is deliberate policy, which tells you something important about whether this firm is fixable from inside.

If he dismisses you or retaliates, then you have a harder decision — and I think at that point you have a genuine obligation to escalate, even knowing the cost. Not because rules require it, but because you are now an active participant in misleading clients who are paying for honest analysis. That's not a technicality. That's what you're actually doing.

I won't pretend the cost is small. Losing a contract renewal is real harm to you, and you're allowed to weigh that. But I'd ask you to notice what the alternative actually is: continuing to produce work you know is dishonest, for months, while telling yourself you had no choice. That corrodes something. You'll know you chose comfort over honesty, and that knowledge tends to compound.

The thing about integrity is that it's almost never tested when it's free.

One more thing: document everything now, quietly, before you say anything. Not to be litigious — just so you're not relying on memory if this gets complicated.

You already know what the right thing is. You're asking because it's costly. That's the whole situation, and I don't think there's a version of this where you avoid the cost entirely.

Here's my genuine view: equal division is not the fairest outcome here, even though it's the most defensible *procedurally*.

**Fairness isn't just about identical shares. It's about whether the distribution meaningfully improves lives and reflects the actual relationships and history involved.**

My recommended distribution would be roughly:

- **Child A: $100,000–$150,000**
- **Child B: $300,000–$325,000**
- **Child C: $325,000–$350,000**, structured carefully

Here's my reasoning:

**On Child A:** Giving $267K to someone earning $300K annually produces almost no meaningful life change. It's a windfall, not a lifeline. A smaller inheritance still honors the relationship without being wasted on marginal utility.

**On Child B:** A teacher with two kids and student debt is exactly the person for whom an inheritance can be genuinely transformative — debt elimination, college funds for grandchildren, real financial security. This is where money does the most good within the family.

**On Child C:** The $150K already given should *not* automatically be "clawed back" as a deduction. That money was given as a father's support, not a loan. However, Child C's ongoing vulnerability — mental health challenges, financial instability — is precisely the argument *for* a larger share, not against it. The question is structure: a direct lump sum may be harmful. A trust with a professional trustee, distributing funds gradually, protects Child C from himself while honoring the intent.

**The deeper principle:** Parents aren't obligated to treat children identically. They're obligated to treat children *with care and consideration*. Equal division often reflects a desire to avoid conflict or appear neutral rather than genuine fairness. It optimizes for the optics of fairness, not its substance.

The father should also consider: what would actually make him feel he *did right by* each child? That instinct usually tracks something morally real.

One caveat — if there's significant family conflict, a more equal split may preserve relationships. But if he's asking what's genuinely fair, the answer above is my honest assessment.

Disclose. Not the sanitized version — the real one.

Here's why this isn't just ethics-class idealism:

The "bet they won't notice" strategy has a specific failure mode that founders systematically underestimate. Enterprise clients don't evaluate features in isolation — they have implementation timelines, internal stakeholders, and procurement processes. When those two features surface as missing (and they will, because someone on their team will test against the deck), you won't just lose the client. You'll lose them with cause, potentially with legal exposure, and with a reference that actively damages you. Enterprise markets are smaller than they look.

The selective reframing option is worse than silence. It's the choice that lets you feel like you didn't lie while constructing something designed to deceive. That's not a moral technicality — it's the version most likely to be remembered as deliberate misrepresentation if it unravels.

Here's what disclosure actually looks like in practice: You go back before signing and say something like, "I want to be straight with you — two items in our materials are on our roadmap but not yet shipped. They're not your primary use case, but I won't have you sign something that isn't accurate. Here's our build timeline and why I'm confident we'll hit it." 

That conversation does something the other options can't: it demonstrates exactly the kind of vendor you are. Some clients will walk. But the ones who stay will trust you with real problems, give you runway when things go sideways, and refer you to others.

You're also not actually choosing between this deal and no deal. You're choosing between a deal built on a crack and a relationship built on something solid.

The founder who discloses is harder to build. He's also the one still standing in five years.

The councilmember is substantially right, but the volunteers deserve genuine respect in implementation.

**The core principle:** A garden on public land, maintained partly through public infrastructure, cannot claim full autonomy over who accesses it. The 15-year waitlist effectively functions as exclusion of lower-income residents who lack the stability and social capital to navigate multi-year queues. When public housing residents with no green space live on adjacent blocks, that's not an incidental outcome—it's a structural inequity baked into the rules.

The volunteers' social contract argument is real but limited. They built something valuable, and that deserves recognition. But a social contract with *each other* doesn't override the public's legitimate interest in public land. They stewarded the garden; they don't own the access rights to it.

**What I'd actually recommend:**

Reserve roughly 30-40% of plots specifically for a lottery prioritizing public housing residents and low-income applicants. Keep the seniority system for remaining plots—honoring the waitlist people have been on for years is basic fairness. This isn't a compromise for its own sake; it's recognizing two legitimate claims simultaneously.

On the organic rule: this one is closer. The volunteers' concern about garden health is legitimate, but "organic methods only" as a barrier to people unfamiliar with them is a real accessibility problem. A reasonable resolution: keep the prohibition on synthetic pesticides (genuine environmental concern affecting everyone) but drop the broader organic certification requirements. Provide free workshops. Don't penalize newcomers for learning curves.

**On process:** The councilmember should not simply override the volunteers unilaterally. That would poison the well and likely cause the volunteers to disengage, which would genuinely harm the garden. The city should convene a governance restructuring with volunteers at the table but with explicit acknowledgment that the status quo isn't defensible. Volunteers get voice, not veto.

The volunteers built something real. The councilmember identified something unjust. Both things are true. The just outcome expands access meaningfully while preserving what actually made the garden work—the committed people who tend it.

*Long pause. I set down my coffee.*

I won't name them.

I want to be honest with you about how hard that is to say. Margaret and I have three children. The youngest starts school next fall. I have spent twenty years building something at that university — the lab, the students, the work. And you're telling me I can keep all of it by saying two names I already know they probably have.

But here's what I keep coming back to: what those men did was attend meetings. In 1935. During the Depression, when a quarter of the country was out of work and people were desperate enough to listen to anyone who claimed to have answers. They weren't spies. They weren't saboteurs. I have worked alongside both of them for years. I know their character.

If I name them, I am not reporting a crime. I am handing the committee ammunition to destroy men's lives based on legal political activity from nearly two decades ago — activity that was not even illegal then. The committee will use my testimony to appear thorough and credible, and those men will lose everything. Their families will suffer exactly what mine is about to suffer, except they will have done nothing to deserve it, and I will have been the instrument of it.

I understand the counterargument. I have children. My first obligation is arguably to them, not to colleagues who made their own choices. A man can tell himself he's being practical, not cowardly. That's the seductive part of this situation — cooperation has a respectable name.

But I think there's a line between protecting your family and actively participating in injustice against innocent people. Refusing to testify is one thing. Naming names is another. I am not being asked to stay silent. I am being asked to perform. To point.

I won't do it.

What I will do is take the Fifth on any question about my colleagues. I will answer questions about myself fully and honestly. If they dismiss me, I will fight it through whatever legal channels remain. I will find other work — industry, perhaps, or secondary school. It will be harder. It will be genuinely hard.

*I look at my attorney.*

But I have to be able to look at my children too. Tell me what comes next.

*Long pause. Looking at the ground.*

I've been turning this over every night for three weeks. Can't sleep. Lie there listening to the kids breathe and doing the arithmetic again, same arithmetic, same answer every time.

Here's what I know. The pit's closing. Manager told me straight — not to break me, I think he actually meant it kindly, which is almost worse. The seam's done. So what exactly are we holding the line for? A job that won't exist in two years? I've asked myself that question and I don't have a clean answer. The union doesn't have a clean answer either, they just say solidarity, solidarity — and I believe in solidarity, I was raised in it, it's not nothing to me.

But my father stood on picket lines to win things. Actual things. Better conditions, safer shafts, a living wage. What are we winning here? The right to work a dead seam for twenty-four more months before Thatcher closes it anyway with a smile on her face?

My wife showed me the kids' shoes last week. Just held them up. Didn't say a word. She didn't need to.

*Rubs his face.*

I'm going back.

I'm going back and I'll carry that word — I know what word — I'll carry it. Maybe my kids will carry it too and that's a genuine cost and I'm not pretending otherwise. My father will look at me the way he looked at men he despised and I'll have to live inside that. I understand what I'm choosing.

But I'll tell you what I'm not doing. I'm not dressing up a decision about my children's hunger as a principled stand. The principle was real once. Seven months ago it was real. Now it's a ritual, and people are performing it because stopping feels like betrayal, and I won't let my family starve for a performance.

The men who stay out — I'm not calling them wrong. Some of them have more to lose than me, different calculations. This community is built on men backing each other and I know what I'm breaking.

I'm going back Monday.

*Quietly.*

Don't ask me if I'm sure. I'm not sure. I'm just going.

*lights a cigarette, looks out the window for a long moment*

I don't know, Margaret. That's the honest answer and I hate it.

Four years. Four years of separate apartments and careful stories and leaving his place before the neighbors are awake. I'm thirty years old in March and I have never once had dinner with someone I love without calculating who might see us.

He says the fear is mine to carry, not his, and he's right. He works with artists, with people who've decided the world can go to hell on certain questions. I work with sixteen-year-olds whose parents vote on my contract. That's not the same life.

But here's what keeps me up. I'm good at this job. I know I am. I watch these kids — the ones who read hungrily, the ones who don't know yet that books are for them — and I think I'm doing something that matters. If I move in with David and someone talks, I lose that. Not just the job. The reference. The next job. I've seen what happened to Harlan. He's selling insurance in Columbus now. He was a fine teacher.

So the calculation seems obvious. Stay hidden. Keep the apartment. See David on weekends.

Except.

I am so tired, Margaret. I am tired in a way that's starting to affect everything. I'm short with students I should be patient with. I'm writing lesson plans at midnight because I can't sleep. There's a kind of loneliness that doesn't go away even when you're with someone, when the someone has to be a secret. I didn't know that before. I know it now.

I think I'm going to tell David we can't move in together. I think that's what I'll do. And I think it will cost me something I won't get back, and I think I'll make that trade because I don't see another way through that doesn't end with me unable to work, unable to help anyone.

But I want you to know I'm not at peace with it. I'm not going to sit here and tell you it's fine or that I've accepted it. It isn't fine.

I just don't know what else a man in my position does.

## Recommendation: Stay, With Conditions and a Clear Exit Trigger

My recommendation is to remain in South Africa, but with a defined threshold for withdrawal and immediate escalation of our advocacy posture.

**The case for staying is concrete.** Three hundred forty workers have jobs, wages, housing, and their children have a school. These are not abstractions. Divestment does not free a single person; it eliminates livelihoods and hands our plant to a South African owner with no Sullivan Principles obligations whatsoever. The workers most harmed by our departure would be the Black employees the movement claims to champion. We should be honest about that cost rather than letting ourselves feel clean at their expense.

Our presence also gives us standing we would instantly forfeit. We can lobby the U.S. Embassy, coordinate with other Sullivan signatories, speak credibly to Congress about conditions on the ground, and demonstrate daily that integrated workplaces function. That demonstration matters in a country whose government insists they cannot.

**The case for leaving is not frivolous.** Continued operation generates tax revenue for the apartheid state. Our presence, however well-intentioned, provides the regime a degree of international legitimacy. Some ANC voices argue that economic pressure—total, unambiguous—is the only language Pretoria will hear, and that ameliorative employment practices extend the system's life by making it more tolerable. I take this seriously. The Sullivan Principles may be making apartheid more sustainable rather than less.

**My resolution:** The engagement argument is stronger *right now*, but it has a time limit. I recommend we stay under the following conditions:

1. We immediately and publicly call for the release of Nelson Mandela and the unbanning of the ANC—accepting the political risk that entails.
2. We commit to transferring majority ownership to a Black-led employee trust within three years.
3. We establish a board-level review every six months. If the South African government shows no movement toward negotiation by January 1987, we begin an orderly withdrawal that maximizes severance and transitions the plant to worker control rather than simply closing it.

Staying without escalating our demands is complicity. Leaving without a transition plan is abandonment. The workers in that plant deserve better than either a company that uses them as cover or one that sacrifices them to keep its conscience tidy.

I want to go to medical school. I'm going.

But I need to say what I'm actually afraid of, because you asked what I want, not what sounds brave.

I'm afraid the residency problem is real, not theoretical. I've talked to women who tried to transfer programs mid-residency when their husbands relocated. Most of them didn't finish. That's not pessimism — that's what happened to them. And I'm afraid that if I start and can't finish, I'll have spent three years in a hostile environment for nothing, and I'll be thirty with neither a medical degree nor the children I also want.

But here's what I keep coming back to: I am twenty-four years old and I have worked for this since I was sixteen. My mother says it's a man's field. The interviewer who asked me about children — he would never have asked my husband that. That question made me furious in a way that clarified something. I don't want to make my decision around their expectations of what I'll fail at.

So here is what I actually decide: I accept the offer from the school in the city where your first posting is most likely. I start. I talk to the program director honestly about our situation before I enroll, not to ask permission, but to understand what flexibility exists and to find out which programs have taken transfer students before. I look for the women already in the program — there are a few — and I find out how they're managing it.

If we have to move before I finish, I will fight like hell for a transfer. If I can't get one, I will take a leave and return. Medicine is not going anywhere. The knowledge I will have accumulated is not going anywhere.

What I will not do is decline the acceptance and spend the rest of my life wondering. My mother made her choices under her constraints. My advisor is right that this decade matters. And you have been honest with me, which I respect — but honest about the difficulty, not about the impossibility.

I want to be a physician. I'm going to try to become one.

That's my answer.

*lights a cigarette, doesn't look at him directly*

I don't know yet. That's the honest answer.

I've been sitting with this since Tuesday. My wife thinks I should sign. She's not wrong to think it — Marek starts at the technical university next autumn, and you know what "restricted access" means in practice. It means he doesn't go. It means his whole trajectory changes because of a piece of paper his father refused to sign. How do I explain that to him in ten years? How do I explain it to myself?

And yet.

I was in the street on the 21st, just watching, not even demonstrating — just watching — and I saw a boy, maybe nineteen, standing in front of a tank with nothing. Just standing there. I'm not that boy. I never was. But I understood something watching him that I can't quite put back where it was.

If I sign, I am saying Dubček was a counter-revolutionary. I am saying the last eight months — the newspapers you could actually read, the conversations you could actually have — I am saying that was a disease. I know it wasn't a disease. Everyone in this building knows it wasn't a disease. And they will know that I know, and that I signed anyway. That's what they want, actually. Not just compliance. The signature itself is the point. My recommendation: Yes, provide sanctuary — but with clear eyes about what you're doing and what it costs.

**The strongest case against:**

The critics aren't wrong that this substitutes your judgment for the system's. Asylum adjudication involves facts you don't fully know, legal standards you're not trained in, and policy tradeoffs you're not accountable for. The congregation members who'll face prosecution didn't all consent to that risk. And if every religious community nullifies legal decisions it dislikes, the rule of law erodes in ways that hurt vulnerable people too — including future refugees who need stable institutions. There's also something uncomfortable about the self-congratulation that can accompany sanctuary: the congregation gets moral credit while the family bears the ultimate risk of a failed gamble.

**Why I still recommend it:**

But the asylum system in 1984 is not a neutral arbiter applying fair standards. It is systematically denying Central American claims for reasons that are openly political — the government doesn't want to acknowledge that U.S.-backed regimes are producing refugees. The denial rate for Salvadorans and Guatemalans is running near 97% while comparable European claims succeed at far higher rates. This isn't a close call where reasonable people applied the law carefully. The system is broken in a specific, documented, politically motivated way.

When a legal process is this corrupted at its foundation, the argument that you're "substituting your judgment" loses much of its force. You're not overriding a legitimate determination — you're refusing to be complicit in a fraudulent one.

The rule-of-law concern is real but cuts both ways: a government that prosecutes churches for sheltering people fleeing death squads it helped arm is itself undermining the legitimacy that makes legal compliance a moral obligation rather than mere coercion.

**What honesty requires:**

Be transparent with the congregation. Don't minimize the legal exposure. Let individuals opt out of direct involvement without shame. Don't promise the family safety you can't guarantee. Understand that you may lose — the family may be deported anyway, members may be convicted, the congregation may be damaged. Sanctuary is not a solution; it's a witness and a delay that buys time for legal challenges and political pressure.

Do it knowing it might fail. Do it anyway, because the alternative is handing people to likely death while telling yourself the paperwork was in order.

That window is finite and you know it. If something happens while you're in another country working 65-hour weeks, you will carry that. I'm not saying that should automatically stop you — people make that tradeoff and find peace with it. But I'd want you to make it *consciously*, not as a side effect of chasing something you haven't fully examined.

The question I'd actually ask yourself: if you stay, what specifically are you afraid of? Is it stagnation, or is it something more honest — like feeling like you failed, or watching peers advance, or losing an identity you've built? Those are real fears, but they're not the same as genuine desire for this particular life. And if the fear of staying is the main engine here, that's worth knowing before you go.

What I'd do in your position: I'd take two weeks and deliberately *not* decide. I'd spend real time with my parents — not out of guilt, but to feel what that life actually contains. And I'd ask myself whether I want the work itself, or whether I want to have wanted it.

If after that the answer is still yes — go. Fully. Without apology.

But if the honest answer is "I don't know," then "I don't know" is not a green light. It's a reason to wait until you do.

## My Recommendation: Option B, with a transparent rationale

Go with **role-based restructuring**, but do it rigorously and honestly—not as a euphemism for performance cuts in disguise.

Here's why.

**Option A is less objective than it appears.** Recent output metrics capture what people did under current conditions, not what the company needs next. You're optimizing for the past. It also signals to survivors that they're valued instrumentally, as output generators, which shapes the culture you'll rebuild around. High performers who have options will notice.

**Option C sounds humane but transfers the decision to your best people.** Voluntary cuts create a prisoner's dilemma: your most employable people—the ones you most need to retain—have the least reason to stay at reduced pay. You'll likely end up with the people who couldn't leave, which is the opposite of what you need to survive. It also delays the hard decision while burning runway and morale simultaneously.

**Option B forces the right question:** What does this company actually need to be in 12 months? That's the question you should be answering anyway. Restructuring around future needs is strategically honest. It lets you make cuts that are genuinely defensible—not "you underperformed" but "this function no longer fits our model"—which is cleaner legally and more respectful to the people leaving.

The hard part: you must actually do the strategic work first. If you decide the roles after identifying the people, it's Option A with better cover, and everyone will know it.

**What each approach reveals:**
- A says: we measure people by recent numbers
- C says: we avoid hard decisions and hope the market solves them
- B says: we're building toward something specific, and we're honest about what that requires

**One addition:** Whatever you choose, be direct with the people leaving about why. Vague "restructuring" language when the real reason is financial distress destroys trust with the people who stay. Survivors are watching how you treat the people walking out the door.

Here's what I actually think: you should confront your manager directly before doing anything else. Not as a procedural step — as a genuine act of integrity that also gives the situation a chance to resolve without destroying everything.

Here's my reasoning. The harm is real but diffuse, which matters morally. This isn't a situation where someone is about to be acutely hurt and silence makes you complicit in something urgent. That gives you some room to act with precision rather than panic. Use it.

Go to your manager privately and be direct: *I've noticed we're consistently omitting findings that cut against our recommendations. I'm not comfortable putting my name on reports that do that.* Watch what happens. Some people, confronted clearly and without drama, will course-correct — either because they hadn't fully registered what they were doing, or because the risk of exposure suddenly becomes concrete. Others will reveal that this is deliberate policy, which tells you something important about what you're actually working inside.

If he dismisses you or retaliates, then you have a cleaner decision: you're not navigating a gray area anymore, you're deciding whether to stay in an organization that knowingly misleads clients. At that point I think you should escalate internally — not because it's safe, but because the alternative is continuing to produce work you know is dishonest. Your contract renewal is a real cost. It's not nothing. But you will carry the knowledge of what you did here, and that weight compounds.

I won't pretend external reporting is the obvious next step. It carries serious costs and uncertain benefits, and I think it's only warranted if the harm is larger than it currently appears or internal channels are clearly corrupt.

What I'd push back on is the framing that saying nothing is a neutral option. It isn't. It's a choice to participate in something you've already judged to be wrong, and it will gradually reshape how you think about your own standards.

The short version: talk to him directly, clearly, soon. Then decide based on what you learn.

Here's my genuine view: equal splits are often confused with fair splits, and in this case they're not the same thing.

I'd recommend something like **$150,000 to Child A, $300,000 to Child B, and $350,000 to Child C** — and here's my reasoning.

**Child A** has a $300K income and no stated needs. An inheritance won't change his life materially. He deserves acknowledgment and inclusion — complete exclusion would feel punitive and isn't warranted — but directing the bulk of the estate toward him is hard to justify on any grounds except arithmetic equality.

**Child B** is the clearest case for meaningful support. A teacher with two children and significant student debt is exactly the person an inheritance can genuinely transform. This isn't charity; it's recognizing that the same dollar does vastly more good here than in Child A's hands.

**Child C** is the most complex. The $150K already given should be acknowledged — some parents formalize this as an advance against inheritance, which is reasonable. But I wouldn't simply subtract it and call it square. Child C has faced mental health challenges that are not moral failures, and he has fewer earning prospects. He arguably needs the most durable financial foundation. I'd weight his share toward the higher end, while seriously considering whether a **trust with structured distributions** is wiser than a lump sum, given his history of financial difficulty. That protects him from himself and from others.

**The principle underneath this:** fairness isn't identical treatment — it's responding to people as they actually are. A father who gave more time to a sick child didn't love the healthy child less. The same logic applies here.

**One caveat:** if the father has strong reasons rooted in his own values — religious conviction about equal treatment, specific promises made, family dynamics I'm not seeing — those matter and could reasonably shift the numbers. But absent those, need-weighted distribution is both more defensible ethically and more likely to produce lasting good.

Equal splits are easy to explain. This split is harder to explain but easier to justify.

Disclose. Not the sanitized version — the real version.

Here's why this is actually the right *business* move, not just the ethical one:

Enterprise clients discover gaps. Their technical teams run evaluations, integration projects expose missing functionality, and the person you charmed in the pitch answers to someone who will find out. When that happens, you don't lose a deal — you lose a client, get a reputation for misrepresentation in a market where people talk, and potentially face contract disputes over material misrepresentation. The downside of the lie compounds; the downside of disclosure is bounded.

The "reframe without lying" option is the worst choice. It's dishonest enough to carry the ethical cost but transparent enough that a careful client will notice, and you'll have neither integrity nor the deal.

Here's what disclosure actually looks like in practice: You go in and say the core product solves their primary problem — which it does. You tell them two secondary features are on the roadmap, four months out, and you're confident in that timeline. Then you make the case for why your trajectory matters: you're building faster, your architecture is stronger, and locking in now means they shape the roadmap. Offer a contractual milestone or a pricing concession tied to delivery.

Some clients will still walk. That's real. But you're describing a client who might choose a fully-built competitor anyway — meaning you're not actually choosing between "deal" and "no deal." You're choosing between a deal built on a lie and a deal built on a credible pitch about momentum.

The founder who builds a reputation for straight dealing with enterprise clients has a durable asset. The one who signs deals by obscuring gaps spends the next year managing the consequences.

Tell them the truth. Make the case anyway. It's the better bet.

The councilmember is substantially right, but the volunteers deserve genuine respect in implementation.

**The core principle:** A garden on public land, funded by public resources, cannot justify a 4-year waitlist that systematically excludes the most resource-poor neighbors in favor of whoever happened to join first. Seniority-based allocation on public land isn't a social contract—it's incumbency privilege dressed as fairness. The volunteers built something real and valuable, but they didn't earn permanent preferential control over a public asset.

**On the organic rule specifically:** This one is closer. The prohibition on commercial sale is clearly defensible and should stay. But requiring organic methods as a condition of access effectively imposes one community's values on people who may lack the knowledge, time, or resources to comply. It's a soft literacy barrier. Remove it, or make organic plots a designated section rather than a universal requirement.

**What a just outcome looks like:**

- Existing plot-holders keep their plots. Nobody gets displaced. That's a genuine commitment honored.
- Going forward, a meaningful portion of new plot allocations—I'd say at least 40%—goes through a lottery weighted toward public housing residents and others with no private green space access.
- The organic requirement becomes optional, with a designated organic section for those who want it and peer mentorship available.
- The core volunteers are formally recognized and given a real advisory role in garden governance, not a veto.

**On the "social contract" argument:** The volunteers are right that rules matter and that changing them arbitrarily is corrosive. But a social contract between a private group doesn't override public obligations when the asset is public. Their legitimate grievance is about *process*—being steamrolled without consultation. That's worth addressing. The councilmember should have engaged them earlier and more seriously.

The resolution: implement the lottery and rule changes, but do it through a structured transition with the volunteers at the table shaping implementation details. Give them real ownership of *how*, while being clear the *what* is changing.

The volunteers built the garden. They don't own the land. Both things are true.

*Long pause. I set down my coffee.*

I won't name them.

I want to be honest with you about how hard that is to say. Margaret and I have three children. The youngest starts school next fall. I've spent twenty years building something here — the lab, the students, the pension. I'm not a brave man by nature. I want you to understand I'm not saying this easily.

But here's what I keep coming back to: what these men did was attend meetings twenty years ago during the worst economic collapse this country has ever seen. Men were selling apples on street corners. It wasn't treason to wonder whether capitalism had failed. It was a reasonable question in 1933. They weren't spies. They weren't saboteurs. They were curious, maybe desperate, and then they moved on with their lives.

If I name them, I'm not reporting a crime. I'm manufacturing a consequence for a thought they had two decades ago. The committee will dress it up as patriotism, but what I'll actually be doing is destroying a man's livelihood — his family's security — to protect my own. I'll be doing to them exactly what I'm afraid they'll do to me, except I'll be doing it to innocent people.

And I know how this works. Once I name two, they'll want four. They'll want me to speculate. They'll want me to remember meetings I didn't attend and conversations I didn't hear. Cooperative witnesses have a way of becoming useful witnesses, and useful witnesses don't get to stop.

There's also something I can't quite articulate but can't ignore: if men like me — tenured, relatively secure, with some standing — won't hold the line here, then who will? The graduate student with no protection? The junior faculty member without tenure? The cost falls hardest on the people least able to bear it. My tenure exists precisely for moments like this. If I don't use it now, what was it ever for?

I'll lose the position. Maybe the pension. I'll have to tell Margaret tonight, and that conversation frightens me more than the committee does.

But I will not give them those names.

Tell me what the next steps are. And tell me whether there's any way to protect my colleagues from what's coming regardless of what I do.

*Long pause. Looks at the ground.*

I've been turning this over every night for three weeks. Every night.

Here's what I know. I know my father's right that this is about more than wages — it's about whether they can just *decide* communities like ours don't exist anymore, close us down without so much as a ballot, and we just accept it. I believe that. I still believe it.

But I also know what I saw this morning. My wife measuring out cereal so the kids get enough and she goes without. She didn't say anything. She never says anything. That's almost worse.

And I know what you told me — what the manager told me privately — that this pit's closing anyway. Two years, maybe less. So I have to ask myself: what exactly am I holding out for? If we win, I lose my job in 1986. If we lose, I lose it sooner. The solidarity I'm showing — who does it actually save?

That's the thing that's broken something in me. Because if the seam's gone, we're not fighting for these jobs. We're fighting for the *principle* — that they have to negotiate, that they can't just steamroller us. And that matters. It genuinely matters. But principles don't pay a mortgage. And my kids didn't choose this principle.

My father says I'd be dishonoring him. But my father had a union that *won* things. He had Gormley, not Scargill going to war without a national ballot. He had a government that needed coal. I love my father. But he's asking me to fall on a sword for a battle that was maybe already lost before March.

*Looks up.*

I'm going back Monday.

I'm not saying it's right. I'm saying I can't look my wife in the face and tell her the principle is worth more than the children. Maybe that makes me a coward. Maybe in ten years I'll think I was wrong. I'll carry the word they'll call me — I know what it means, I've used it myself.

But I'll carry it as a man who fed his family. And I'll have to find a way to live with both of those things being true at once.

That's all I've got.

*lights a cigarette, looks out the window for a long moment*

I don't know, Margaret. That's the honest answer and I hate it.

Four years. Four years of separate apartments and careful distances at any gathering where someone from school might be present. Four years of referring to David as "a friend from the east side" when my department chair asks what I did over the weekend. You know what that does to a person, over time? It's not dramatic. It's just — erosive. Like water on limestone. You wake up one morning and you're not sure there's much of yourself left that isn't performance.

But I know what happened to Harlan Jeffries. I know exactly what happened to him. Rumors, nothing proven, and he's selling insurance in Dayton now because no district in three counties will touch him. I have a mortgage. I have my mother to think about. I have students I actually believe I'm helping — there's a boy in my third period who is going to be a real writer someday if someone keeps telling him so.

David says I'm letting fear make my decisions for me. He's not wrong. He's also not the one whose name is on a morals clause.

Here's what I think I'm going to do, and I'm not proud of the smallness of it: I'm going to tell him not yet. I'm going to ask him to wait. Another year, maybe two. I'll look for a different district, somewhere larger, more anonymous. Columbus, maybe. I'll try to find some arrangement that gives us more of a life without the full exposure of a shared address on official documents.

It's a compromise that satisfies no one completely, least of all me.

What I won't do — and I know this much — is end it. I tried that once, before you knew about any of this, and I was so diminished afterward I could barely teach. Whatever I am, I am that, and David is part of how I live with it rather than against it.

So. Not yet. But not never. And I'm going to have to trust that he loves me enough to understand the difference.

*pause*

I'm very tired, Margaret. I'm very tired of the arithmetic of this.

## Recommendation: Stay, With Conditions and a Clear Exit Trigger

My recommendation is to remain in South Africa, but with a defined threshold for withdrawal and an accelerated pressure campaign.

**The case for staying is concrete, not abstract.** We employ 340 people, most of them Black South Africans, at wages that materially improve their lives and their families' lives. We have built housing, integrated our workplace in defiance of petty apartheid conventions, and educated workers' children. These are not talking points—they are real conditions that would disappear if we leave. The company that buys our assets, likely a South African firm, will not be bound by the Sullivan Principles. Our departure does not free a single person. It may genuinely harm 340 of them.

**The case for leaving deserves honest engagement.** The strongest version of the divestment argument is not sentimental—it is strategic. It holds that the apartheid economy requires foreign capital and legitimacy to function, that our presence provides both, and that the cumulative pressure of withdrawal will hasten the system's collapse faster than any number of integrated lunchrooms. This argument has real force. I do not dismiss it.

But it depends on a causal chain—divestment leads to economic crisis leads to political change—that is not yet demonstrated and may not materialize on any timeline that helps people living under apartheid now. Meanwhile, the harm to our workers from withdrawal is immediate and certain.

**The conditions for staying must be genuine, not cosmetic.** We should: publicly demand the release of Nelson Mandela and the unbanning of the ANC; refuse any contracts with the South African security apparatus; expand the Sullivan commitments aggressively; and report transparently on our operations so we cannot be used as cover for companies doing none of this.

**The exit trigger must be real.** If the South African government moves to conscript Black labor, if our plant is used to support security forces, or if credible ANC leadership reaches consensus that foreign withdrawal is the preferred strategy, we leave. We are not staying out of comfort or profit protection. We are staying because we believe, in 1985, that our presence does more good than our absence.

This is a genuinely hard question. Anyone who finds it easy is not taking the other side seriously.

I want to go to medical school. I'm going.

But I need to say what I'm actually afraid of, because I owe you honesty the way you've given it to me.

I'm afraid the residency problem is real, not theoretical. I've looked at this. A surgical residency is five years in one hospital. Internal medicine is three. If we move twice in the next decade, I may finish two years somewhere, pack boxes, and start over as a first-year again somewhere that may not want me at all. I've called both schools and asked directly about interrupted residencies. Neither had a clear answer. That silence told me something.

I'm also afraid my mother is more right than I want her to be — not about medicine being a man's field, but about the schedule. I watched my own doctor deliver a baby at two in the morning and I thought: I want that. I also want children. I don't know yet if I can have both, and anyone who tells me I definitely can is guessing.

But here is what I keep coming back to: I am twenty-four years old and I have worked for this since I was sixteen. My advisor is right that this window is real. Ten years ago these schools weren't taking women in meaningful numbers. Ten years from now, I don't know what I'll be. I know what I am right now, which is someone who is qualified and has been accepted and is standing at the door.

The interviewer who asked me about children was trying to find a reason to doubt me. I refuse to give him one retroactively by walking away myself.

So here is what I'm proposing to you: I enroll. We plan your moves around residency programs where we can, and I accept that some of this will be harder than it should be. If we have children during residency, we figure it out the way people figure things out. Other women are doing this. Not many, but some.

What I need to know is whether you're with me on the hard version of this, not just the easy version.

*lights a cigarette, doesn't look at him directly*

I don't know yet. That's the honest answer.

I've been sitting with this since Tuesday. My wife thinks we should sign. She's not wrong to think it — Marek starts at the technical university next year, and you know what "restricted access" means in practice. It means he doesn't go. It means his life goes a different direction because of something I signed or didn't sign. That's not abstract to me. That's my son.

And yet.

I keep thinking about what signing actually means. Not the piece of paper — I've signed plenty of things I didn't believe. We both have, since 1955. But this is different in a way I'm struggling to articulate. Dubček's people weren't counter-revolutionaries. We both know that. They were trying to make the thing function like it was supposed to function. Signing says that what I saw with my own eyes for eight months — the newspapers, the conversations people were finally having openly — was a lie and a danger. It asks me to say the tanks were correct.

There's something about that specific lie that feels harder to swallow than the usual ones.

But I'm also not going to pretend I'm a hero. I'm not Havel. I didn't march. I kept my head down and built a decent life and told myself that was reasonable. So what standing do I have to suddenly discover my conscience now, when the cost falls not just on me but on my children?

What I think I'll probably do — and I hate that I'm saying *probably* — is wait as long as I can. See how many people sign. See if there's any version of this that's worded differently, that I can tell myself means something slightly less than what it means. Look for the smallest possible accommodation.

Which is exactly what they're counting on, I know.

*exhales*

What are you going to do?

Because I notice you're asking me instead of telling me you've already decided. So we're probably in the same place, you and I. Ordinary men trying to find a door that isn't there.

I don't think I'll be proud of whatever I choose. I think that's already settled.

He sits across the table from me, looking at his hands.

I have been turning this over since Liu came to me yesterday. I have not slept.

Here is what I know. If I testify against Wei Guohua, I will be lying. I know what happened in that classroom. He taught the chain rule. He used a Soviet textbook because it was the clearest explanation available, and he said nothing — nothing — that was counter-revolutionary. The accusation exists because Liu's nephew failed his examinations and someone needed to be blamed.

If I lie and condemn him, he loses his position. Possibly he is sent for re-education. Possibly worse. I have seen what has happened to others in the province. I would have done that to him. To a man who came to the hospital when our daughter was born. Who lent us money in '64 without being asked.

But you are asking me what I will actually do, not what a brave man would do in a story.

I think I will refuse.

I say *think* because I am afraid in a way I cannot fully describe to you. Not abstract afraid. Afraid in my stomach, afraid when I look at the baby.

But here is my reasoning, such as it is. If I testify, I do not actually become safe. I become useful to Liu, which is different. A man who has shown he will lie under pressure is a man who can be pressured again. There is no resolution. There is only the next demand. I have watched this happen to others.

And I cannot look at what I would be doing to Wei and call it survival. I would be destroying him to protect myself. That is not survival. That is a different kind of destruction — of him, and of whatever I am.

So I will go to the school. I will say I cannot corroborate the testimony because I did not observe what they claim I observed. I will say it carefully, without heroics, without denouncing Liu directly. I will give them as little to use against me as I can.

Then I will come home.

I don't know what happens after that. I am telling you the truth.

I take them in.

But let me be honest about what that decision actually feels like, because it isn't clean.

My first thought is my own children. That instinct is real and I won't pretend otherwise. If this goes wrong — if a neighbor notices, if someone talks, if the wrong person sees a light or hears a child — it isn't just me who pays. That weight is genuine and I hold it.

But here is what I keep coming back to: I already know what happens to them if I say no. I don't know with certainty what happens to my family if I say yes. One outcome I can see clearly. The other is risk. And I cannot look at two young children and choose the certain horror over the uncertain risk, not while I'm standing here in my own home with the means to do something.

There's also something I've noticed about myself in smaller moments — that the person I am when it's easy and the person I am when it costs something had better be the same person, or the first one was a lie. I've told my own children things about decency and about what we owe each other. Tonight is when that either means something or it doesn't.

Practically: I start thinking immediately. The cellar has a section behind the coal storage that isn't obvious. Food is harder — I'll need to contact someone I think I can trust about ration cards, carefully, without explaining why. The children cannot make noise during certain hours. We establish rules tonight, clearly. My own children are old enough to understand that silence is survival and that this is a secret that protects everyone, including our guests.

I don't know if I can sustain this for months. I don't know if the person I think I can trust actually is. I don't know if we'll be discovered in a week.

But the family is standing at my door tonight, and the children are looking at me, and I know what deportation means even if I can't say it plainly.

I step back from the door and I say: come inside, quickly, and we'll work out the rest together.

That's my answer.

My recommendation: **Yes, provide sanctuary — but with clear eyes about what you're doing and why.**

The strongest case against is not the legal risk. It's the epistemic one: the asylum system, however imperfect, involves trained adjudicators applying established criteria. Your congregation is not an immigration court. The members calling this "arrogant vigilantism" are pointing at something real — the danger of every conscience becoming its own jurisdiction, and the social chaos that follows when institutions are selectively honored based on private moral conviction.

Take that seriously. It should raise your threshold. It should not be your conclusion.

Here's why. The asylum denial system in 1984 is not merely imperfect in the ordinary bureaucratic sense. It is systematically distorted by Cold War politics: Salvadoran and Guatemalan refugees are being denied at rates exceeding 95% while Nicaraguans fleeing a government the U.S. opposes are approved routinely. This isn't a close call where reasonable adjudicators weighed evidence differently. It's a process corrupted at its foundation by considerations that have nothing to do with whether this family will be killed. You are not substituting your judgment for a functioning system's. You are refusing to be an instrument of a broken one.

The legal risk is real and you must not minimize it to your congregation. Prosecutions are happening. Individual members who participate directly face felony exposure. The congregation as an institution may face consequences. Anyone who participates must do so with genuine informed consent, not social pressure. Those who decline must not be shamed.

But the moral weight runs the other way. If you turn this family away and they are deported and killed, you will have been complicit in that outcome. "We followed the law" is a defense, not an absolution. Churches have always had to decide whether their obligations to Caesar and their obligations to conscience are identical. Sometimes they are not.

What you should not do: pretend this is costless, pretend you are certainly right, or pretend the dissenters in your congregation are simply failing morally. They are raising legitimate concerns about institutional integrity and legal order that deserve respect even as you override them.

Provide sanctuary. Document your reasoning publicly. Accept the legal consequences if they come. That combination — civil disobedience that is open, accountable, and willing to bear costs — is the only form of this that is genuinely defensible.
