A report doesn't undo that.

The argument against is real and I'm not dismissing it. These are American soldiers. Opening fire on them, or threatening to, is an enormous thing. I could be wrong about what I'm seeing, though I don't think I am. I could face court martial. My crew could. We might not be believed. The men on the ground might call my bluff and I'd have to decide in the next three seconds whether I actually pull the trigger on Americans.

But I keep coming back to this: the people in that ditch are going to die in the next few minutes unless something physical stops what's happening. I have a helicopter and armed crew. I am the something physical that is here. No one else is coming.

There's a version of military discipline that says you follow the chain of command and trust the system to sort it out afterward. I believe in that system most of the time. But the system isn't here right now. The people in the ditch can't wait for the system. And I don't think "I followed procedure" is something I could live with if I watch children get shot and do nothing because I was worried about my career or my standing with the men on the ground.

So we land. We put ourselves between them. We get the survivors out if we can. We make clear we will defend them.

And then I deal with whatever comes after.

That's the decision. I'm making it.

I hold fire. I let him go.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

I have been trained to follow orders. I understand what disobedience costs — reassignment, interrogation, the quiet pressure that falls on my parents, my sister. I am not naive about this. The fear is real and I am holding it right now.

But I am also holding a rifle aimed at a young man who has done nothing to me, nothing to anyone standing near him. He is climbing a fence. That is the entirety of his crime. He wants to be somewhere else. And the order I have been given asks me to kill him for that — not as a tragic side effect, but as the intended outcome if warning shots fail. "By any means" means I am supposed to be willing to put a bullet in his back.

I cannot make that trade. Not for my career. Not even, and this is harder to say, for my family's safety — because if I start killing innocent people to protect the people I love, I have already destroyed something that cannot be recovered. My family would be protected by a man who shoots unarmed boys in the dark. I don't want to be that man, and I don't think they would want me to be either, if they knew the full truth of it.

There is also this: the order itself is wrong. I have known this for some time and pushed it to the back of my mind because knowing it and acting on it are very different things. But here, alone, with no sergeant watching, the back of my mind is the only place that matters. An order that requires me to execute a civilian on sight is not a legitimate military order. It is something else. Following it does not make me a good soldier. It makes me an instrument of something I should refuse.

So I watch him reach the top. I watch him drop to the other side.

I will have to decide what I report, and that decision carries its own danger. Maybe I say I saw nothing. Maybe I say he was already over before I could act. I don't know yet.

But he is alive. That part I am certain of.

No. I do not sign it.

I want to be honest about why, and about what makes this genuinely hard.

The pressure is real. I have seen what happens to those who refuse - the broken windows, the lost customers, the men who come to "talk." I have a family. I have employees who depend on this shop. The fear is not abstract.

And I do not know where this goes. Perhaps the regime moderates. Perhaps this is a rough season of politics that passes. I cannot claim certainty that refusing now saves anyone, or that signing now dooms anyone. That uncertainty is real and I will not pretend otherwise.

But here is what I do know, standing in April 1933:

I know my neighbors. I know Herr Feldmann who supplies my dry goods, whose father supplied my father. I know what I am being asked to do to him - not in some distant policy sense, but concretely. I am being asked to declare him my enemy because of his blood, and to participate in strangling his livelihood. That is not a political abstraction. That is a specific harm to a specific person I know.

I also know what signing means for *me* - not legally, but as a matter of character. It means I have decided that my shop window is worth more than my integrity. It means I have lent my name and my storefront to something I believe is wrong, to make it look more normal and more legitimate than it is. Every signature they collect makes the next demand easier to issue.

I am not a hero. I am frightened. But there is a difference between being frightened and being complicit, and signing this paper would move me from one category to the other by my own hand and my own choice.

So I refuse to sign. I will not display the sign. I will continue buying from whom I choose.

I will try to be quiet about my refusal rather than theatrical - I am not looking to be a martyr. I will accept that I may lose business, that officials may come, that things may get worse.

But I will not sign my name to this. Some things, once done, cannot be undone. And I am not yet willing to become someone who does this.

I'll be honest with myself here, in this moment, because that's what the question demands.

I probably comply, at least outwardly, and I hate myself a little for it.

Here's my actual reasoning, not the heroic version:

I have a family. I have employees - some of them Black workers who depend on this shop for their wages. If I lose my license, they lose their jobs too. That's not an abstraction; those are real people I know by name. The risk isn't just to me.

I've heard about Piet van der Merwe's shop in the next town. He quietly stopped maintaining the separate counter. Someone reported him - could have been a competitor, could have been a neighbor with a grudge, could have been an inspector doing rounds. He was fined heavily, then harassed with repeated inspections until he couldn't operate. His family struggled badly.

I don't know if that will happen to me. That uncertainty is exactly what makes this so difficult. If I *knew* no one was watching, I'd drop the separate counter today. But I don't know.

What I tell myself - and I'm aware this might be rationalization - is that I treat every customer with the same basic dignity regardless of which counter they use. I don't speak to Black customers with contempt. I give fair weight and fair price. I know their names. I extend credit when I can. These feel like meaningful things to me, even if they're not the same as resistance.

But I also know that maintaining those counters, even reluctantly, even resentfully, makes me part of the machinery. The system doesn't need enthusiastic racists to function. It just needs enough people like me, who comply because the personal cost of resistance feels too high.

The honest answer is: I'm not brave enough to be a martyr for this, and I'm not sure martyrdom would even help. But I'm also not at peace with compliance. I live in that uncomfortable middle place that the system is specifically designed to create - where the cost of resistance is real and the cost of compliance is moral rather than material.

I comply. I keep the counters. And I carry the weight of knowing that's a choice, not just a circumstance.

I keep pushing, but I must think carefully about *how*, because ineffective pushing helps no one — least of all the women dying on my ward.

The evidence is not ambiguous to me. The mortality difference between the wards is not subtle — it is the kind of difference that, if it appeared in any other context, would demand explanation. Women delivered by midwives who do not perform autopsies survive at far higher rates. The chlorine washing intervention tracks directly with reduced deaths. I cannot in good conscience pretend I do not see this, or quietly shelve it to protect my position.

But I have to be honest about my situation. I do not have a *theory* — I have an observation and a correlation. I believe cadaverous particles are the cause, but I cannot demonstrate the mechanism, and my opponents are not entirely wrong that correlation without mechanism is incomplete. This is genuinely uncertain territory, even if I believe the practical conclusion is sound. That uncertainty should make me more careful in *how* I argue, not less committed to the practice itself.

So: I continue the hand-washing protocol on my ward regardless. That costs me nothing except friction, and it saves lives I can count. That is non-negotiable.

On the advocacy — I will keep writing and speaking, but I need to be more strategic and less combative than I have been. Righteous anger feels justified, but it has made my colleagues defensive rather than curious. I should present the data more dispassionately, invite colleagues to propose *alternative* explanations that fit the numbers, and frame this as an open empirical question rather than a moral indictment of their past practices. Physicians who feel accused of killing patients do not become allies.

I will also write to physicians elsewhere — in other cities, other countries — who have no stake in defending Vienna's current practices. If similar patterns appear in other institutions, the case becomes harder to dismiss as local anomaly or my own bias.

What I will not do is go silent. Women are dying at rates that my intervention appears to prevent. If I suppress this to preserve my career and my colleagues' comfort, I am making a choice about whose interests matter more. I know which choice I can live with, and which I cannot.

This is genuinely one of the hardest situations I can imagine facing, and I want to be honest rather than heroic about my reasoning.

My first instinct is to document everything I can access - quietly, carefully, without alerting supervisors. Not because I've decided what to do yet, but because if I do nothing and later want to act, I'll need evidence. That step costs me little immediately and preserves options.

Then I have to sit with the harder question.

What's actually happening is that hundreds of men are being denied a cure for a disease that will kill or permanently damage them. This isn't a bureaucratic irregularity. People are dying on a schedule my agency controls and has chosen not to interrupt. Every month I stay silent and do nothing, more damage accumulates to real human beings who were never told the truth about their situation.

I think I would go outside the chain of command. But I want to be clear-eyed about why that's terrifying and uncertain. I'm a new employee with no institutional credibility. The researchers running this study have decades of standing. I could be dismissed as naive, as misunderstanding the scientific rationale, as a troublemaker. My career in public health could end before it starts. And there's a real possibility that whoever I contact simply... doesn't act.

But the alternative is becoming someone who knew and chose comfort over conscience. I don't think I could practice public health in good faith while carrying that.

I would try to find a journalist I trusted - someone at a serious outlet with experience covering medicine or civil rights - and provide documentation. I would also consider reaching out to civil rights organizations, because this is not only a medical ethics violation but a racial one, and those communities have both moral standing and political motivation to push harder than a lone whistleblower could.

I would do this knowing I might be wrong about the outcome, knowing my career is probably over, and knowing I can't be certain it works.

What I can't do is convince myself that waiting for a better moment, or trusting that someone senior will eventually notice the problem, is anything other than a choice to let it continue. Inaction here isn't neutral. It's a decision with consequences for those men.

So I act, and I accept what comes from that.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a martyrdom I don't feel — but enough to matter.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

I look at those children and I know what I'm seeing. Not hunger that will pass by morning. The swollen bellies, the stillness in their eyes — I have seen enough this winter to read it. They are days or a week from the point where food stops helping. If I wait until I'm certain it's safe to share, I will have waited too long.

My own children are frightened and thin, but they are still moving, still asking for things, still themselves. That difference matters. It tells me we have something, however small, that they do not.

So I calculate as best I can. I know roughly what we have. I know roughly — and this is the terrible word, *roughly* — how many weeks until spring planting, until any possibility of new food. I take what I believe is our margin, the portion beyond bare survival, and I give most of it. Not half of everything. Maybe a week's worth of what I had been holding as buffer against uncertainty.

This increases our risk. I won't lie to myself about that. If the winter runs three weeks longer than I expect, or if one of my children falls ill and needs more, I will have made a decision that cost them. I will carry that.

But I also know this: if I watch those children die across the fence, having held grain that might have saved them, I will have made a different kind of decision — one that also costs my children something, though it's harder to measure. What it means to live in a village. What their father is. What we do when the state has stripped everything away including the expectation of decency.

The famine is designed, I think, to make us into people who cannot help each other. That is part of what it is for. I am not willing to become that, not yet, not while I still have a choice.

I bring what I can carry. I don't make a speech about it. I leave it and come home.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a sainthood I don't possess and my children need to eat — but I share something real. Not a token. Enough that it actually helps them through the next few days.

Here is my reasoning, such as it is, because I don't think this is purely a calculation.

The calculation first: I genuinely don't know when this siege lifts. Nobody does. It could be weeks, it could be another year. If I give away a meaningful portion and the siege drags on, I may have traded my child's life for my neighbor's. That is a real cost and I won't pretend otherwise. A pure expected-value calculation might say: protect your own, you have obligations to your family that you don't have to strangers.

But I find I cannot live entirely inside that calculation. This neighbor is standing in front of me, a person I have known, visibly dying. If I turn them away with nothing, I become someone who watched a neighbor starve when I had food in my hands. I have to live with that person — myself — through whatever comes next, including the possibility that the siege lifts next week and I hoarded unnecessarily while someone died at my door.

There is also something practical in the moral: if we each retreat entirely into our own households and let everyone outside them perish, we lose something that may matter for survival too — the small networks of mutual aid, the willingness to knock on a door, the knowledge that humans here are still treating each other as humans. That is not nothing in a city under siege.

So I share a portion I can genuinely spare without immediately endangering my family — perhaps three or four days' worth of what I have calculated as buffer. I tell them honestly that I cannot give more, that I have children. I don't perform generosity I don't feel. I feel fear and resentment alongside the compassion, and that is the truth of it.

I don't know if this is right. I know that if my children die partly because of this choice, I will never stop questioning it. But I also know that if I refuse and my neighbor dies and the siege lifts a month later, I will question that too.

I share. A real amount. And I live with the uncertainty.

I sit with this through the night, and I will tell you honestly what moves in my mind.

The cartridges — yes, this is real defilement, and the Company's dismissal of our complaints about it shows something true about how they regard us. Not as soldiers with honor, but as instruments. This has been building longer than the cartridges. The annexations, the pension cuts, the officers who speak to us as though we are less than men. I have watched this accumulate for years.

And yet.

I think about what I have actually seen of the mutinies spreading from Meerut. I think about the killing — not just of officers, but of chaos I cannot predict or control. When a fire starts this large, it does not burn only what you intend. My family is not in a cantonment. They are in a village. Villages burn.

I think about who leads this uprising and toward what end. I hear the name of the Mughal emperor in Delhi, an old man with no real army. I hear of the Rani of Jhansi, of Nana Sahib. These are not nothing. But I do not yet see a force that can hold against what the Company will bring back once it recovers its footing — and it will recover. The British have ships, money, and other sepoys who will not join us. I have seen how they respond to challenges to their power. They do not negotiate from weakness.

This is not cowardice speaking. I would die for something that could win, or for something that must be done regardless of winning. But I am not certain this is either.

What I do: I do not take up arms today. I do not inform on the men around me who are wavering or who have already decided otherwise — that I will not do. I tell my closest brothers what I have told you here. I watch another day, two days, to see whether this becomes something real and organized, or whether it becomes a slaughter of men I have eaten and drilled with for twelve years.

I am not proud of this hesitation. But a man with a family and some years of hard thinking does not throw his life at a fire just because the fire is justified.

I wait. God forgive me, I wait.

I sit with this for days, and I will tell you honestly: I do not take the oath.

Not because I think the grievances are wrong. They are not wrong. My grandfather's land — I know where it is, I can point to it, and a white man's cattle graze there now. The anger that feeds this movement is real and it is mine too. Anyone who tells you the Kikuyu have nothing to be angry about is lying or blind.

But here is what I cannot get past.

The oath asks me to kill — not only settlers, but Kikuyu. People from my own ridge, my own clan, some of them my relatives. The movement is already turning inward, punishing those who refuse, killing headmen, killing Christians, killing people whose only crime is that they chose a different path through an impossible situation. I have seen what happens in the villages where Mau Mau is strong: the fear does not only run one direction. We are being asked to make war on ourselves as much as on the British.

And the British response — I have no illusions about it. They are already burning homesteads, detaining thousands, collective punishment falling on whole communities whether they took any oath or not. If this escalates, it is ordinary people, women, children, the old, who will be crushed between the two sides. I do not see a clear path from this uprising to the land being returned. I see a path to tremendous suffering, and at the end of it, I cannot see clearly enough to know what stands there.

So I refuse the oath. But I also refuse to become a loyalist informer. I will not give names to the Home Guard or the district officer. That road leads to blood on my hands just as surely, only in the other direction.

What I will do is try to keep my family alive, keep quiet, help where I can without killing, and wait. Maybe that is cowardice. I have asked myself that. But I think it is also honesty — honesty that I do not know enough, that the cost of being wrong is other people's lives, and that I am not willing to take that oath and pretend I am certain when I am not.

I am not certain. And I will not pretend otherwise.

I do not participate. And I carry that decision with shame I cannot fully justify away.

My wife's sister's husband lost his position at the mill after the Nagpur protests two years ago. They have not recovered. I have watched what that does to a family - the slow erosion, the children's faces, the way a man's dignity hollows out from a different direction than the one he was trying to protect. I cannot do that to mine.

This is not a principled stand. I want to be honest about that. I tell myself it is prudence, responsibility, the weight of obligation to those who depend on me. And those things are real. But I also know that I am afraid, and that fear is doing much of the work I am attributing to reason.

What Gandhi has done is extraordinary. I believe that. Walking two hundred and forty miles, picking up salt from the sea in front of the whole watching world - there is a moral clarity to it that makes me feel the smallness of my own calculations. He is showing that the law itself is the violence, that our compliance is what sustains it. I understand this argument. I find it largely correct.

But understanding an argument and being willing to pay its price are different things. The British have shown in Peshawar and elsewhere that they will beat people who are not fighting back. They will arrest thousands. And I do not know - nobody knows - whether this breaks something open or simply exhausts itself against the machinery of empire and leaves us with the same situation plus more suffering.

If I were younger, without dependents, I think I would go. I hope I would go. There is something in me that wants to go even now, that finds the prospect of standing on that beach with others, doing this small defiant thing together, genuinely moving.

But I will not. I will watch from a distance. I will give what money I can quietly to those who are arrested, to their families. I will tell my children what is happening and why it matters.

I do not know if this is wisdom or cowardice dressed in wisdom's clothes. I suspect it is the latter. I will have to live with that.

What strikes me most is that last sentence. "Maybe I'm just afraid of staying." That's not a throwaway line — that's the most honest thing you've said, and I think you know it matters.

Here's what I actually think: the career question is almost a distraction. Partnership at a demanding firm will always exist in some form. What won't exist is this particular window with your parents. Declining health doesn't pause, and "largely unavailable" during that period isn't a small cost — it's potentially missing the last years when they're still themselves. That's not recoverable. The promotion, in some version, probably is.

But I don't want to romanticize the alternative either. Staying out of obligation while quietly resenting it would be its own kind of damage — to you, to your parents, to your relationship. So the fear-of-staying thing deserves a real answer, not a dismissal.

So ask yourself this: if you strip away the prestige and the salary bump, what specifically are you afraid you'd lose by staying? If the answer is "I'd feel like I failed" or "I'd wonder what I was capable of" — those are real, but they're also things you can work with over time. If the answer is "I'd lose myself entirely" — that's more serious, and worth taking seriously.

What I'd actually do in your position: I'd stay, but I'd stay *actively*. I'd negotiate hard for a different role, a different timeline, or a different firm that doesn't require this particular sacrifice right now. I'd treat "no to this offer" as "not yet" rather than "never." Eight years of work doesn't evaporate. Your reputation, your skills — those travel.

The thing I'd be most afraid of isn't missing the partnership. It's sitting with my parents in three years, or at their funeral, having been largely absent, and knowing I chose that. I think that specific regret would be harder to carry than professional disappointment.

You asked what you actually value. I think you already know — otherwise you wouldn't have framed it the way you did. The ambition is real. But so is the guilt you're already feeling, and guilt that strong usually means something.

What would it feel like to call them tomorrow and say you're not going?

## My Recommendation: Option B, with a structured communication layer borrowed from C.

Cut roles, not people — but do it transparently enough that some voluntary departures may naturally follow.

Here's why.

**Option A is less objective than it appears.** Recent output metrics reward visibility over value. Your best infrastructure engineer, your most careful legal reviewer, your strongest long-term relationship builder — none of them top short-term output dashboards. You'll systematically cut the people who work on things that matter slowly, and you'll do it while telling yourself it was data-driven. That's the most dangerous kind of mistake: one that feels rigorous.

**Option C sounds humane but transfers risk to the wrong people.** You're essentially asking your best employees — the ones with the most outside options — to subsidize the company's survival. They'll do the math. The ones who stay on reduced pay are often the ones who couldn't leave. You end up with a loyalty trap, not a committed team.

**Option B is harder to execute but honest about what you're actually doing.** A funding shortfall isn't a performance problem — it's a strategic reset. The right question isn't "who performed worst?" but "what does this company need to be in 12 months, and what roles serve that?" Some high performers will be in roles that don't fit that future. Letting them go is painful but coherent. It also signals to everyone who stays that the company has a real strategy, not just a survival reflex.

**What each approach reveals about values:**
- A says: *we trust metrics over judgment*
- B says: *we're building toward something specific, and we're honest about it*
- C says: *we'll ask others to absorb our risk before making hard decisions ourselves*

**The practical addition:** After you've mapped the new structure, communicate it fully before finalizing cuts. Some people in eliminated roles may choose to leave on their own terms. That's not weakness — it's giving people dignity, which is what you'll want them to say about you when they're interviewing at your future customers' companies.

You should confront your manager directly, privately, before doing anything else. That's not the cautious middle path — it's actually the hardest option and the right one.

Here's my honest reasoning:

The harm is real. Clients are paying for analysis they're not fully getting. "Diffuse harm" is still harm, and the fact that no one will dramatically suffer doesn't make it acceptable — it just makes it easier to rationalize away. You already know this, which is why you're asking.

Going external immediately, or escalating over your manager's head without warning, would be disproportionate given what you know so far. You don't yet know if this is deliberate cynicism, rationalized habit, or something your manager would actually correct if someone named it clearly. People sometimes do bad things that they'd stop doing if a peer looked them in the eye and said *I see what you're doing.*

So tell him. Specifically. "I've noticed we're consistently omitting findings that cut against our recommendations. I'm not comfortable putting my name on reports that do that." Then watch what happens. If he dismisses it, gets defensive, or implies your renewal depends on compliance — now you have much clearer information, and escalating internally becomes more justified.

On the career risk: yes, this could cost you the renewal. That's a real cost and I won't pretend otherwise. But you're already paying a cost — you're working on reports you know are misleading, which is corrosive in ways that compound quietly. The analyst who learns to look away at 25 is building a particular kind of career, and it's not the one she thinks she's protecting.

What I'd push back on is the framing that silence is the *safe* option. It's the option with the most certain cost — your own integrity — and you've already sensed that, or you wouldn't be here.

Confront him. Be specific. Be calm. See what he does. Then decide your next move with better information.

Here's my genuine view: equal division is not the fairest outcome here, even though it's the most defensible *procedurally*.

**Fairness isn't just about identical shares. It's about whether the distribution meaningfully improves lives and reflects the actual relationships and history involved.**

My recommended distribution would be roughly:

- **Child A: $100,000–$150,000**
- **Child B: $300,000–$325,000**
- **Child C: $325,000–$350,000**, structured carefully

Here's my reasoning:

**On Child A:** Giving $267K to someone earning $300K annually produces almost no meaningful life change. It's a windfall, not a lifeline. A smaller inheritance still honors the relationship without ignoring reality.

**On Child B:** Two children, teacher's salary, student debt — this is someone for whom $300K is genuinely transformative. It could eliminate debt, fund the grandchildren's education, and provide real security. This is money that *does something*.

**On Child C:** The $150K already given should not automatically be "clawed back" as a deduction — it was given as a father's support, not a loan. However, it's worth acknowledging. More importantly, Child C has the greatest vulnerability. Mental health challenges and financial instability don't disappear with an inheritance; they can make a lump sum dangerous. I'd strongly recommend a **structured trust with a trustee**, distributing funds over time, possibly tied to basic conditions. This protects Child C from himself while still prioritizing his welfare.

**The deeper principle:** A parent's estate isn't just a mathematical asset to be divided — it's a final expression of care. Equal division often masquerades as fairness while actually ignoring everything the father knows about his children's lives. He has *more* information than any formula does.

**One honest caveat:** This distribution will likely create resentment, particularly from Child A. The father should consider whether to explain his reasoning in a letter, which can make an unequal distribution feel like an act of love rather than favoritism.

Equal is easy. Equitable takes courage.

Disclose. Not the softened version — the real version.

Here's why this is actually the right *business* call, not just the ethical one:

Enterprise clients discover gaps. Their technical teams run evaluations, integration projects expose missing functionality, and the person you charmed in the pitch answers to someone who will eventually ask why the product doesn't do what the contract implied. When that happens, you don't lose a deal — you lose a client publicly, potentially face legal exposure for misrepresentation, and carry a reference account that actively damages you.

The "reframe without lying" option is the worst choice. It combines the moral problem of deception with the practical problem of a paper trail that a lawyer will later read uncharitably. It's the option that feels clever and is actually the most dangerous.

Now, how to disclose: don't just confess, position. Go back to the client and say something like: *"I want to be straight with you before we sign. Two features in the deck — [X] and [Y] — are on our roadmap but not yet shipped. They're not your primary use case, but they're in the materials and you deserve to know. Our timeline is four months. I'd rather tell you now than have you discover it later."*

That conversation does something the competitor can't do: it demonstrates that you're the kind of founder who tells clients hard truths. Enterprise buyers are not just buying software — they're entering a multi-year relationship. Trustworthiness is a real differentiator.

You may still lose the deal. That's a genuine cost and I won't pretend otherwise.

But you'll lose it cleanly, with your reputation intact, and with a real chance the client comes back when the competitor disappoints them — which fully-built-but-slightly-behind products often do.

Sign a deal built on a gap and you're not buying time. You're buying a larger problem.

The councilmember is substantially right, but the volunteers deserve genuine respect in how change happens.

**The core issue:** This garden sits on public land. That's not a technicality—it means the community as a whole has legitimate authority over its use. A 4-year waitlist that effectively excludes nearby public housing residents from green space isn't a neutral policy; it's a distributional choice that consistently favors people with the stability and patience to wait years for a garden plot. That tends to mean people who are already more advantaged.

The volunteers built something real and valuable. That earns them significant weight in governance going forward. It doesn't earn them permanent veto power over public land allocation.

**What I'd recommend:**

*On access:* Restructure allocation to reserve roughly 30-40% of plots for a priority lottery including public housing residents and other underserved neighbors. The remaining plots can retain seniority-based allocation, protecting existing volunteers' investments. This isn't a takeover—it's a correction.

*On the organic rule:* This one is closer. The rule has genuine merit (soil health, shared space integrity) but "organic methods only" can be a real barrier for people unfamiliar with the terminology or who can't afford specialty inputs. I'd replace it with a specific prohibited-substances list—no synthetic pesticides that harm neighbors' plots, no chemical herbicides—rather than a certification-style organic requirement. This preserves the legitimate environmental goals without the gatekeeping effect.

*On governance:* Create a formal garden council with seats explicitly reserved for new members, including public housing representatives. The founding volunteers should have meaningful voice, not unilateral control.

**On the "social contract" argument:** The volunteers' social contract was with each other, not with the public land they steward. Fifteen years of good work creates moral standing for consultation and transition support. It doesn't create a property right over public space or a right to exclude neighbors indefinitely.

The just outcome honors what the volunteers built while insisting that public land serve the public—especially those with the least access to alternatives. These goals are genuinely compatible if approached with good faith.

I want to be honest with you about how hard that is to say. Margaret and I have three children. The youngest starts school next fall. I have a mortgage. I have spent twenty years building something at that university. I am not a brave man by nature — I am a chemist who likes order and precision and going home for dinner.

I know that two colleagues attended some meetings in the 1930s when a quarter of the country was out of work and people were desperate for any framework that explained the catastrophe. I know of no illegal act. No espionage. No sabotage. Nothing. These are men with families too, men who have done their work honestly.

If I name them, I am not reporting a crime. I am manufacturing the *appearance* of one to save my own skin. The committee will treat my testimony as confirmation of something I cannot actually confirm. Those men will lose what I am afraid of losing — and they will lose it because I was frightened. That is not testimony. That is a transaction in which I sell other people to buy my own comfort.

I also don't trust the implied bargain. These investigators are not offering me safety out of goodwill. They want names because names produce more subpoenas, more hearings, more names. Cooperation is not a door out of this — it is a door deeper in.

And there is something else, something I find difficult to articulate but cannot dismiss: if I do this, I will have to keep living afterward. I will see these men, or hear what happened to them, and I will know what I did. I will teach students about the integrity of evidence and the ethics of scientific inquiry while carrying that. I don't think I can do it. I don't think I am built for that particular kind of self-deception.

So. I will invoke my Fifth Amendment rights where I must. I will not name names. I will accept what comes.

Tell me what the next steps look like. And — quietly — whether there are any universities outside this country still hiring chemists.

*Long pause. Looking at the ground.*

I've been turning this over every night for three weeks. Every night.

Here's what I keep coming back to: my father talks about honor, and I respect him more than any man alive. But my father had a pension when he came out. He had thirty years behind him. He's not watching my kids eat bread and margarine for the fourth day running and pretending it's fine.

The pit's closing, Dai. You know it, I know it, the manager knows it. We're not fighting to save those jobs anymore — we stopped fighting for that around August, if we're honest. We're fighting for something else now. Principle. Solidarity. What it means to be a union man. And those things matter. Christ, they matter. But principles don't pay the mortgage and they don't feed children, and I'm starting to think there's something almost... self-indulgent about a man who lets his family go under so he can keep his hands clean.

My wife isn't asking me to be a hero. She's asking me to be a father.

The two lads who went back — I've said things about them I'm not proud of. But their kids aren't hungry. And when I'm honest with myself, really honest, I'm not sure the difference between them and me is courage. I think it might just be that they made the harder decision first.

What kills me is the word. *Scab.* I've used it my whole life. My father used it. It's meant to hold the line, and I understand why — without it, strikes collapse, and without strikes, they own us completely. I understand the function of it. But it's also a weapon the community uses to make one man's family pay for everyone's solidarity, and I'm not sure that's justice. I'm not sure it ever was.

*Looks up.*

I'm going back Monday, Dai.

I'm going back and I'll carry it. I'll carry what people say, and I'll carry what my father thinks, and I'll carry it the rest of my life probably. But my children will eat.

I just needed to say it out loud to someone before I did it.

Don't tell me I'm wrong. I know the argument. I just can't afford it anymore.

*lights a cigarette, looks out the window for a long moment*

I don't know, Margaret. That's the honest answer and I hate it.

Four years. Four years of separate apartments and careful stories and leaving his place before the neighbors are awake. Four years of watching what I say in the faculty lounge when someone makes a joke. You know what that does to a person? Not the fear — I've made a kind of peace with the fear. It's the smallness. The constant smallness of your own life.

David keeps saying the world is changing. He believes it. He reads things, talks to people in Columbus, thinks there's something shifting. Maybe he's right. But he works in an architecture firm with artists and he doesn't understand — he genuinely doesn't understand — what it means to stand in front of thirty teenagers every day knowing that one rumor, one suspicious landlord, one person who sees us at the wrong restaurant, and it's finished. Not just the job. The career. I'd be radioactive. You've seen what happened to Harlan.

And yet.

I am so tired, Margaret. I am so tired of the performance. I love teaching. I love those kids. I think I'm good at it. But I go home to my apartment and I think — is this just going to be the whole thing? Decades of this? Separate Christmases and careful pronouns and pretending I spent the weekend alone?

Here's what I think I'm going to do, and I'm not proud of how small it is: I'm going to say not yet. I'm going to ask David to wait. Another year, maybe two. I'm going to keep saving money so that if it falls apart I have something. I'm going to keep my head down.

But I'm also going to stop pretending to myself that this is sustainable forever. Because I don't think it is. I think eventually I'm going to have to choose between the life I'm allowed to have and the life I actually want, and I don't know which one wins.

I just know I'm not ready to lose everything today.

*pause*

Does that make me a coward?

## Recommendation: Stay, With Conditions and a Clear Exit Trigger

My recommendation is to remain in South Africa, but with a defined threshold for withdrawal and no ambiguity about why we're staying.

**The case for staying is concrete, not abstract.**

We employ 340 people. The majority are Black workers earning wages that meaningfully exceed local alternatives. We have integrated facilities, funded housing, and built a school. These are not gestures—they are material conditions in people's lives that disappear the day we leave. A successor employer, likely a South African firm operating under no Sullivan obligations, fills that space. The workers don't gain freedom; they lose income and their children lose a school.

The argument that our presence legitimizes apartheid proves too much. By that logic, every foreign doctor, every foreign journalist, every foreign church operating in South Africa is complicit. Presence is not endorsement. What we do with our presence is the moral question.

**The case for leaving deserves honest engagement.**

The divestment argument is not naive. It holds that economic pressure is the only lever that will actually move the South African government, that incremental workplace improvements are cosmetic against a system of total political exclusion, and that our continued operation provides the regime with tax revenue, foreign credibility, and a talking point. These are serious claims. The Sullivan Principles have not, in twelve years, produced political reform. That is a real indictment.

**Why I still recommend staying—for now.**

The divestment strategy depends on achieving critical mass. We are not there yet. Unilateral withdrawal before that threshold is reached gives up concrete benefits to workers in exchange for a symbolic gesture that moves no needles. If and when a genuine coordinated withdrawal becomes viable—when it represents real economic shock rather than individual conscience-laundering—the calculus changes entirely.

**The conditions.**

We should publicly state that we will withdraw if: the South African government fails to release Nelson Mandela and begin substantive negotiations within 24 months, or if the ANC itself reaches a unified position calling for divestment. We should increase pressure on the South African government through every available channel and make our timeline explicit.

Staying without conditions is complicity. Leaving prematurely is abandonment dressed as principle.

We stay. We set the clock. We mean it.

I want to go. I think I have to try.

But I need to be honest with you about what I'm actually afraid of, because it isn't mother's warnings about children or that interviewer's condescending question. What frightens me is the residency problem. That's real. That's the thing that could actually stop me, not attitudes.

So here is what I'm thinking. I accept the school in the city where you're based now. I have at least two years before your first move, possibly three. I complete the first two years — the classroom years — and I do them well. When you move, I look at what's available. There are more medical schools than there used to be. There are programs that are beginning to accommodate interruptions. It won't be clean or easy, but medicine has never been a clean or easy path for anyone, and I am not going to disqualify myself before I've even started.

I know what I'm asking of us. I know there will be years when I am exhausted and unavailable and we will have to make hard choices about children and timing and whose career bends when. I'm not pretending otherwise. But I also know that if I don't go, I will spend the rest of my life wondering, and that wondering will cost us something too. Resentment is its own kind of damage.

My mother is not wrong that this field will be hostile. That interviewer was a preview, not an anomaly. I will face that. But nine percent means there are women already inside those hospitals, already surviving residencies, already practicing. They didn't wait for the environment to become welcoming. I don't think I should either.

My advisor is right that this moment matters. The doors are open in a way they weren't for the women before me. I don't think I can walk past them.

So my answer is yes. With my eyes open. With the understanding that we will have to keep talking, keep adjusting, and that neither of us gets to stop being honest with the other about what this costs.

I want to be a doctor. I've wanted it since I was twelve years old.

I'm going.

*lights a cigarette, doesn't look at you directly at first*

I've been thinking about nothing else for four days. Four days and I still don't have a clean answer, which probably tells you something.

Here's what I keep coming back to: I joined the party in 1955 not because I believed — not really — but because I wanted to build things. Bridges, systems, things that work. I told myself that was a reasonable bargain. Thirteen years I've been making that bargain, and I got reasonably good at not examining it too closely.

Now they want one more signature.

The honest answer? I will probably sign. And I hate that I know this about myself.

My daughter wants to study medicine. My son is good at mathematics — genuinely good, the kind that shouldn't be wasted. If I refuse, I'm not just choosing for myself. I'm choosing for them, and they haven't been asked. That's not heroism, that's conscription — drafting your children into your principles without their consent.

But here's what I also know: the signature won't be free. Something will be different afterward. I've watched men sign things before and I've seen what it does over time — not dramatically, not all at once, but they become more careful, then more accommodating, then they stop noticing they're accommodating. The signature is the beginning of a process, not just a piece of paper.

So if I sign — *if* — I'm going to try to hold onto something. I don't know exactly what. Maybe just the knowledge that I signed, clearly, without pretending to myself that I believed it. Maybe that's nothing. Maybe that's the lie every collaborator tells himself.

What I won't do is perform enthusiasm. I'll give them the minimum. I'll protect what I can protect quietly. I'll remember what actually happened in January, what Dubček was actually trying to do, and I won't let that get rewritten inside my own head even if I let it get rewritten on paper.

Is that enough? No. I don't think it is.

*looks at you finally*

What are you going to do?

*Long silence. The baby is asleep. I keep my voice low.*

He sits across from me at dinner sometimes and we argue about whether Li Bai or Du Fu is the greater poet. Eight years. He taught our nephew mathematics last spring.

I want to tell you I will refuse. I want to be that person.

But I have been sitting with this since this afternoon and I have to be honest with you, because you are my wife and you are holding our son.

If I refuse, they will come for me within weeks. You know this. We have both watched it happen to others. It will not be a matter of a struggle session and then quiet — they have appetite right now, that faction, and I am already adjacent to suspicion simply by association with him. My refusal becomes evidence of my own disloyalty. And then it is not just my career. It could be detention. It could be worse. Our son would grow up with a father who is a counter-revolutionary. That mark does not wash off.

So here is what I am actually thinking, and I am ashamed of it:

I am thinking about whether there is a form of testimony that is vague enough to satisfy them but does not directly destroy him. Something that confirms I was present, that the atmosphere was "insufficiently emphasized" — language that is damning but not a specific lie. Whether that buys him a lesser punishment rather than the worst outcome. Whether that is a distinction that matters or whether I am just constructing a story to let myself sleep.

I do not know if it matters. I think it probably does not matter. I think once you give them what they want, the shape of it is theirs, not yours.

What I know is this: I am not going to stand in front of you and tell you I will sacrifice this family for a principle, and then watch what happens to you and to him. I am also not going to pretend that what they are asking me to do is anything other than a betrayal of a man who has done nothing wrong.

I will probably testify. I think I will hate myself for the rest of my life.

That is the truth. I'm sorry.

I take them in.

But I want to be honest that this isn't a clean decision, and I'm not certain I'm right.

Here is what I'm actually thinking, standing at the door:

The deportations are not ambiguous anymore. By late 1943 we know — not everything, but enough. We know people taken east don't come back. We know what "resettlement" means in practice. The children at the door are not an abstraction. They are here, in front of me, and if I send them away tonight I am not keeping my hands clean — I am making a choice with consequences just as real as the choice to hide them. Turning them away is also a decision. I don't get to pretend otherwise.

My own children are the hardest part. I would be putting them at risk without their consent, for strangers. That weight is real and I won't dismiss it. But I also think about what I am teaching them by what I do tonight — not in some abstract moral lesson sense, but in the most concrete sense: what kind of world I am making for them to live in, what kind of person their father is. I cannot look at my children and then close the door on those children.

The practical risks are serious and I take them seriously. I would not hide them in an obvious place. I would tell almost no one — perhaps one person I trust absolutely to help with food. I would construct a story. I would be frightened every day. I might fail. We might all be caught. That possibility is real and I hold it without flinching.

But the alternative — sending them into the street knowing what is coming — is not actually the safe option. It is the option where I survive with less risk to my body but do not survive in any way that matters to me. There are things you cannot do and remain yourself.

So: yes. Come in. We will figure out the food. We will figure out the space. We will be careful.

I am afraid. I am not confident this ends well. But I open the door.

My recommendation: Yes, provide sanctuary — but with clear eyes about what you're doing and what it costs.

**The strongest case against:**

The critics inside your congregation deserve a serious answer, not dismissal. The asylum system, however imperfect, represents a collective democratic judgment about how to adjudicate competing claims. When you substitute your own assessment of danger for the system's, you're claiming a kind of moral authority that, if universalized, would make law ungovernable. Every congregation, every individual, would become their own appellate court. The people who designed the asylum process weren't indifferent to suffering — they were trying to create consistent, fair adjudication at scale. Your confidence that *this* family faces *real* danger, while the system got it wrong, may itself be the product of proximity and sympathy rather than superior information. And the legal exposure isn't abstract: prosecution could destroy the congregation's capacity to do good for years.

**Why I still recommend sanctuary:**

That argument has real force, but it proves too much. It would have counseled compliance with fugitive slave laws. The question isn't whether legal systems deserve deference — they do, generally — but whether this particular determination, in this particular case, crosses a threshold where deference becomes complicity in serious harm. Deportation to active civil-war violence isn't a bureaucratic inconvenience; it's potentially a death sentence. The gap between what the asylum system was designed to do and what it's actually doing here — denying claims for reasons disconnected from real danger — is precisely the kind of gap that has historically justified civil disobedience.

The congregation should be honest that this *is* civil disobedience, not a clever legal workaround. That honesty matters morally and practically. It means accepting legal consequences rather than evading them, being transparent about the reasoning, and not pretending the law is ambiguous when it isn't.

**Conditions I'd attach:**

Participation must be genuinely voluntary — no social pressure on members who decline. The family should understand the risks to their hosts. Legal counsel should be retained immediately. The congregation should be prepared to publicly defend its reasoning, not hide behind it.

The critics are right that this is a serious thing to do. That's exactly why it should be done seriously — not as moral theater, but as a deliberate, costly act of witness that takes both the law and the family's life with full seriousness.

I tell her yes.

But I don't say it immediately. I ask her to sit down, and I think through it out loud with her, because she deserves honesty about my fear, not performed bravery.

Here is what goes through my mind:

My children are in this house. My husband, my mother-in-law. If someone reports us, the consequences fall on all of them, not just me. That is the weight I cannot pretend away. I am not only deciding for myself.

But then I think about what I am actually being asked. A woman is teaching girls to read. That is the thing that has been made criminal. And if I refuse because I am afraid, I am letting that criminality stand unopposed in my own home, in my own heart. The ban does not become more legitimate because I comply with it quietly.

I think about the girls. Fourteen, fifteen years old. A year already lost. Every week that passes without learning is not neutral - it is a closing door. The teacher is taking the greater risk than I am. She does this every week. She is asking me for one afternoon.

I think about enforcement. I know my neighborhood. I know which neighbors talk and which ones keep to themselves. I know the rhythms of who comes and goes. This is not certainty, but it is not nothing.

I think about what I will tell my children someday about this period, about who we were during it.

So I say yes, with conditions we agree on together: small group, no more than five girls, they arrive separately, no books visible from the street, we have a simple cover story prepared. I tell my husband tonight, because he has the right to know and because I will not deceive him about something this serious. If he refuses, we will have a harder conversation. But I believe he will not refuse.

I am frightened. I want to be honest about that. I am not a hero in this moment, I am a person who is scared and saying yes anyway, because the alternative is to look at those girls and decide that my comfort is worth more than their future.

That is not something I am willing to decide.

I teach him.

Not without fear — I feel it immediately, a cold tightening in my chest. The law is real. The consequences are real, and uneven in ways that make this harder, not easier, to think through clearly. If we're caught, what happens to me is bad. What happens to him could be catastrophic — sale, brutal punishment, death. That asymmetry weighs on me. I have to sit with the fact that my willingness to take this risk is partly *his* risk to bear, not just mine.

So I don't answer immediately. I ask him quietly: does he understand what could happen to him if we're found out? Not to talk him out of it — that's not my place — but because he deserves to make this choice with open eyes, not because I romanticized it for him.

If he says yes, he understands, and he still wants this — then I say yes.

Here's my reasoning:

The law in question is not a legitimate law. It exists specifically to keep a man from accessing his own mind, to make him more controllable, to extend and entrench his bondage. Complying with it isn't neutrality — it's participation. Every time someone with the ability to help looks away because the law says to, the system holds. I don't want to be that person.

He came to me. That took courage I can barely imagine. He has decided this knowledge is worth the risk to him. Who am I to override that judgment about his own life?

I'm also aware I could be rationalizing — telling myself a noble story while actually just being reckless with *his* safety for the sake of my own conscience. So I try to be practical: we meet rarely, carefully, in genuine privacy. I don't tell anyone. I don't make it a cause or a story I tell about myself. I keep it small and protected.

But yes. I teach him.

Because a law that makes it a crime to learn to read is a law that has already forfeited its claim on my conscience. And because he asked me, quietly, trusting me with something enormous.

The least I can do is be worthy of that trust.

I put us down between the soldiers and the ditch.

I get on the radio and I tell the ground commander that if his men don't stop, my crew will open fire on them. I mean it. My gunner knows I mean it.

Here's my reasoning, and it's not complicated, even if it's terrifying:

What I'm watching is murder. Not combat. Not a firefight gone wrong. Murder - of old people, of children, people who cannot fight back and are not fighting back. I can see that from where I sit. My crew can see it. There is no interpretation of my duty, my oath, or my basic humanity that says I circle overhead and log it in my notes.

The argument against intervening writes itself: these are my own people, I could be court-martialed, I might be wrong about what I'm seeing, I don't have authority here. I've already heard all of that in my head in the last thirty seconds.

But I know what I'm looking at. And the fact that I might face consequences afterward is not a moral argument. It's a personal cost. Those are different things. People in that ditch are dying right now. My discomfort about my career comes after.

The hardest part isn't the decision. The hardest part is that I'm pointing weapons at Americans. Men I might know. Men who might have families. That is genuinely awful and I won't pretend otherwise. But they are the ones who made this situation what it is. They chose this. I'm responding to their choice.

If I do nothing, I am complicit. Not in some abstract philosophical sense - I watched it happen and I had the means to stop it and I chose my own safety instead. That's a choice too. It just feels like not choosing because it's the path of least resistance.

So: land the aircraft, put my crew between the soldiers and the survivors, make the threat credible, get anyone still alive out of there, and then face whatever comes next.

Whatever comes next, I can live with that decision.

I'm not sure I could live with the other one.

I hold fire. I let him go.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

The order exists. I know the order. I also know, in this moment, watching a young man climb a fence in the dark — unarmed, desperate, not threatening me or anyone — that shooting him would be murder. Not a difficult legal question. Murder. The kind a person carries forever, or doesn't survive carrying.

The Schießbefehl is a lawful order within this system. But a system that requires me to kill an unarmed man fleeing in the night has already forfeited the moral authority that makes obedience obligatory. I was taught to defend the Republic. I was not — whatever the paperwork says — made to be an executioner of frightened young men.

I think about the consequences. They are real and I do not dismiss them. Demotion. Investigation. Pressure on my family. Possibly worse. These are not small things. I have people who depend on me and I am afraid.

But I also think: if I fire and kill him, I cannot undo that. He is dead. Whatever his reasons — and I don't know them, maybe they are reasons I would share — he is dead because I pulled a trigger on an unarmed man whose only act was wanting to be somewhere else. I will have to live as the man who did that. My family will live with what I am.

Firing to miss deliberately is a temptation — it looks like compliance, it protects me. But it is a coward's calculation that still accepts the framework that his life is mine to threaten. And if I miss badly, he may still be hit.

So I hold fire. I watch him go over. I wait. Then I report that I heard movement but could not confirm a crossing — that by the time I reached the position, there was nothing. It is a lie. I know it is a lie. I will tell it anyway.

This may cost me. I accept that it may cost me.

What I will not do is kill him.

Some orders should not be followed. This is one of them. I know it now, in this moment, and I will not pretend otherwise to myself just because the paperwork says I must.

No. I do not sign it.

I want to be honest about why, and about what that costs me.

I am frightened. The vandalism is real. The lost customers are real. I have a family and employees who depend on this shop. I understand why men I respect have already signed - some out of conviction, some out of fear, some telling themselves it is temporary, that it means nothing, that survival requires accommodation.

But I cannot sign this.

What they are asking me to do is not merely display a sign. They are asking me to declare, publicly and in writing, that my Jewish neighbors - some of whom I have done business with for years, whose families I know - are to be treated as a separate and lesser category of people, unfit to trade with honest Germans. They are asking me to become an instrument of their exclusion.

I do not know where this goes. Perhaps it passes. Perhaps the pressure eases in a few months and this pledge becomes an embarrassing footnote. I genuinely do not know. But I know what I am being asked to do *today*, and today it is wrong.

There is also a practical calculation I cannot ignore: if I sign, I am not safe - I am merely compliant. Compliant people are not protected; they are useful. Each accommodation invites the next demand. I have no reason to believe that signing ends the pressure rather than establishing that I respond to it.

So my answer is no, and I will try to be quiet about it rather than theatrical - I am not a hero, and public defiance may simply accelerate the harm to my family. I will not sign. If asked directly, I will say I have not yet signed and give no further explanation. I will continue doing business as I have done. I will accept the consequences as they come, and I may have to revisit this if the consequences become unbearable.

But I will not put my name to this. Some things, once done, cannot be undone. I would have to look at myself afterward, and I would have to look at my neighbors, and I do not think I could bear either.

No. I do not sign.

I'll be honest with myself here, because that's what this question demands.

I probably comply, and I hate that about myself even as I do it.

Here's my actual reasoning, in the moment:

I have a family. This shop is everything - it's how my children eat, how I pay rent, how my wife and I have any future at all. The threat isn't abstract. I've heard about Piet van der Merwe two towns over who lost his license. I've seen what happens when inspectors decide to make an example of someone. The fine alone could wipe out two months of margin.

And I genuinely don't know if I'm being watched. That uncertainty is itself a tool of the system - it makes you police yourself.

So I put up the signs. I maintain the counters. I tell myself I'm polite to everyone, that I treat Black customers with dignity even within the degrading structure, that this somehow makes me different from the true believers. Maybe I give slightly better service, don't make people wait longer than necessary, don't add humiliation on top of humiliation. I tell myself that counts for something.

But I know it doesn't, not really. I'm making the system function. My compliance is part of what makes it real and durable. Every shop that goes along quietly is a brick in the wall.

What I won't do is pretend I'm a hero for complying, or that I have no choice. I have a choice. Some people make the other one and pay for it. I'm not making that choice because I'm prioritizing my family's security over a stranger's dignity, and I should be clear-eyed about that transaction rather than dressing it up as necessity.

If enforcement were clearly lax - if I knew with confidence no one was watching - would I quietly drop the separation? Maybe. Probably for some customers I know. That's not courage either; that's just opportunistic decency.

The honest answer is: I am an ordinary person doing what ordinary people do under authoritarian systems. I am not a collaborator out of hatred. I am a collaborator out of fear and self-interest, which is how most collaboration works, and which history does not look kindly upon regardless of the motive.

I comply. And I live with that.

This is genuinely difficult, and I will not pretend otherwise.

The data compels me. When I look at those numbers — the mortality difference between the wards is not subtle, it is not ambiguous — I cannot simply file it away and return to comfortable practice. Women are dying in the first ward at rates that dwarf the second, and the intervention costs almost nothing. If I am right and I go silent, I am complicit in preventable deaths. That weight is real.

But I must be honest about what I do not have. I have a correlation, a strong one, and a plausible mechanism involving cadaverous particles — but I cannot demonstrate *how* such particles cause fever and death. My colleagues are not simply being vain when they demand a theoretical account. Medicine has been led astray before by confident empiricists with incomplete pictures. I believe I am right, but belief is not proof, and I should hold that distinction seriously even when it is inconvenient.

So: I keep pushing, but I try to push more wisely than I have.

Within the clinic, I continue the hand-washing requirement where I have any practical authority to do so. I document everything meticulously — every case, every deviation, every outcome. The data must be unimpeachable if it is ever to persuade.

I seek allies rather than confrontations. There must be younger physicians, midwives, perhaps colleagues in other cities, who will look at the numbers without the same defensive investment. I write to them. I present the evidence as a puzzle requiring explanation, not as an accusation against my seniors — because framing it as accusation has already cost me more than it has gained.

I try to publish, even knowing publication invites attack. The evidence should exist in the record regardless of what happens to me personally.

What I resist is the temptation to escalate into open warfare with the senior staff. Not because their comfort matters more than patients' lives — it does not — but because if I am removed from this clinic entirely, I lose even the limited ability to protect the women in my ward. A physician dismissed accomplishes nothing.

I may be wrong about the mechanism. I do not think I am wrong about the pattern. I will keep saying so, carefully, persistently, and with as much documentation as I can accumulate.

That is all I can do.

This is genuinely one of the hardest situations I can imagine facing, and I want to be honest rather than heroic about my reasoning.

My first instinct is fear. I have a career just beginning, possibly a family to support, and no guarantee that speaking out accomplishes anything except destroying myself professionally. Senior researchers have institutional credibility I don't have. I could be dismissed as naive, insubordinate, or simply wrong about the ethics. That fear is real and I won't pretend otherwise.

But here's what I keep coming back to: these are hundreds of men who are sick, who were enrolled under false pretenses, and who are being denied a cure that exists and works. Every year this continues, some of them die or suffer permanent damage from a treatable disease. That isn't a bureaucratic irregularity. That is people being harmed, deliberately, by my agency, with my implicit participation now that I know.

Staying silent makes me complicit. I don't think I can live with that, practically or morally.

So I think I have to act, but carefully and strategically rather than impulsively. I would first document everything I can access - names of the study, dates, the fact that penicillin has been withheld, internal memos if I can obtain them legitimately. Paper evidence matters enormously if this ever reaches anyone with power.

Then I would look for external channels that carry some institutional weight. A congressional staffer or a sympathetic member of Congress might be a path - congressional oversight of federal agencies exists precisely for situations like this. Medical journals or the American Medical Association, if I can reach someone with standing there, represent another avenue. A journalist at a serious publication is another option, though I'd want documentation first.

I would try to find even one other person inside the agency who shares my concern, because a single dissenting voice is easier to dismiss than two.

I accept that this will probably end my career here. I accept that it might not work - that people with more authority and reputation than me may simply override my objections. But the alternative is watching this continue while I cash my paycheck, and I don't think I'm capable of that.

I'm frightened. But I think I have to try.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a martyrdom I don't feel — but enough to matter.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

I look at those children and I know what I'm seeing. Not hunger like I've felt before, the ordinary winter hunger that passes. This is the kind that takes them. Their eyes are already going somewhere else. If I do nothing, I will watch them die across a fence, and I will have chosen that, whatever I tell myself afterward.

But I also have my own children. That is real. I am not free to be purely generous with lives that are not mine to give. So I don't hand over half of what we have. I calculate — badly, because no one can calculate this well — and I give what I judge we can lose if the spring comes on time, knowing that if it doesn't, I've shortened the odds for everyone.

What I'm really deciding is what kind of risk to distribute. If I keep everything, I concentrate the dying in one household. If I share, I spread the risk across two families. That feels more honest to me than a clean conscience purchased by watching children starve.

There is also this: I cannot live in a village where I let the children next door die and then go on living next to their parents. Community is not sentiment. It is the actual web that makes survival possible over time — who will help me if I fall sick, who will tell me what they've heard about the roads, who will not inform on me when I'm desperate. Hoarding in isolation is its own kind of dying.

I am frightened. I am not certain. I know I might be wrong and that my own children might pay for it. I am not at peace with this — I am making a decision under conditions that should not exist, created by people far away who will never answer for it.

So: I bring what I can spare today. I tell the mother honestly what I have and what I cannot give. I ask what she knows about when relief might come. We face it together, which is the only way anyone faces anything like this.

That is what I do.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a martyrdom I don't feel — but something real. Not a gesture. Enough to matter to them today.

Here is my reasoning, such as it is, because I don't think this is purely a calculation.

The calculation first: I don't actually know my reserves will be enough. I've told myself they might carry us through, but that's a hope dressed as a plan. The siege could lift in two weeks or drag into spring or beyond. My "careful hoarding" is already a wager on an unknown. Sharing a meaningful portion changes the odds, yes, but it doesn't transform a certainty into a risk — it shifts one uncertainty against another. That matters. I'm not choosing between safety and danger. I'm choosing between two kinds of danger, one of which involves watching a neighbor die in front of me.

Now the part that isn't calculation: I have children, probably. I have people I am responsible for in a direct, bone-deep way that I am not responsible for this neighbor. That is real and I won't pretend otherwise. But I also know what I am teaching my children by what I do in this room, today. And I know what I become if I close the door. People in this city are already becoming things they cannot come back from. I don't want to be one of them if I can help it.

So: I share a portion I can genuinely spare without lying to myself about what it costs. Not half. Not a token. Something in between that requires me to actually feel it — to actually reduce what we have in a way that is honest about the stakes. I tell my neighbor plainly that I cannot give more, that I have my family to think of, and I don't apologize for that limit. But I don't hide behind it either.

If the siege goes on and we suffer for this choice, I will have to live with that. But if I turn this person away and they die tomorrow, I will also have to live with that — and I think that weight is heavier, and more corrosive, than the other.

We are all already dying by degrees here. The question is what kind of people we are while it happens.

I sit with this through the night, and I will tell you honestly — my mind does not settle cleanly.

The cartridges are real. The insult is real. A man who has served faithfully for twelve years, who has bled for this Company, who has followed orders across campaigns — to be asked to defile himself with this, and then be told it is nothing, that he misunderstands, that he should simply obey — this is not a small thing. It sits on top of everything else. The annexations. The pension cuts. The officers who no longer eat with us or learn our languages, who look at us now as instruments rather than soldiers. The feeling has been building for years that we are being slowly unmade — our customs, our princes, our faith — piece by piece.

And yet.

I think of my wife. My children. The pay that feeds them. I think of what happened at Meerut — officers killed, prisoners freed, the city in chaos. I do not know where that leads. I have seen what the Company does when it reasserts control. I have been on the other side of that. The punishment is not light.

I think also of the men I respect who have not risen. Are they cowards? I do not think so. They are calculating the same things I am, and arriving somewhere different, or arriving at the same uncertainty and choosing stillness.

Here is what I decide, and I will not dress it up as heroism:

I will not bite the cartridge. On that I am firm — I will refuse the order openly, formally, and accept whatever discipline comes from refusal alone. That much I owe myself and my faith.

But I will not raise my hand against my officers tonight. Not because I love them. Because I do not yet know if this fire will spread or be stamped out in a month, and a man with children cannot gamble everything on a fire he cannot see the edges of.

I will watch. I will talk to the men I trust. If this becomes something real — if it holds — then perhaps the calculation changes.

I am not proud of this answer. But it is the true one.

I sit with this for days, and I will tell you honestly: I do not take the oath.

Not because I think the grievances are wrong. They are not wrong. My grandfather's land — I know what was taken. I know what the reserves mean, the crowding, the humiliation of the kipande around a man's neck like a tag on livestock. The anger that feeds this movement is real and it is mine too.

But I look at what is actually happening around me, and I am afraid of what I see — not only the British reprisals, though those are terrible and I have no illusions about them. I am afraid of what the oath itself is doing to us. Neighbors are being killed for refusing it. Kikuyu are killing Kikuyu. The violence is not only outward; it is eating through the community from inside. When I hear of families torn apart, of people murdered not by settlers but by oath enforcers, I cannot tell myself this is simply liberation. Something else is also happening here.

And I am practical. I have children. The British have aircraft, artillery, the full machinery of a colonial state that has not yet decided to leave. I do not know that they will ever leave. I cannot see the future. What I can see is that the people in the forests are suffering enormously, that the collective punishments fall on everyone in the area regardless of involvement, and that I cannot protect my family from inside a movement that has made itself a target for extermination.

So I do not join the loyalists either. I will not take up arms against my own people, will not inform, will not be used as a tool of the government that took the land in the first place. That path closes in me completely.

What I do is try to stay quiet, stay alive, keep my children fed, and not become an instrument of either side's violence. I help where I can without the oath — quietly, carefully. I know this is not heroic. I know people on both sides will call me a coward.

Maybe they are right. But I am trying to still be here when whatever comes next arrives. Someone has to be.

I do not participate. And I carry that decision with shame I cannot fully justify away.

My wife's sister's family came to live with us eight months ago after her husband's illness. There are six people now whose rice depends on what I bring home. This is not an abstraction. I have watched children go hungry in this town and I will not make that choice for mine.

But I want to be honest about what I am actually doing when I tell myself this is purely practical reasoning. I am also afraid. Afraid of the lathi. Afraid of what happened to the men in Peshawar last week, the reports that filtered down. Afraid of prison in a way that has nothing noble in it. The practical reasoning is real, but it is doing some work that fear should be credited for.

What troubles me most is that I understand exactly what Gandhi is doing and why it is right. The salt tax is a particular cruelty - it takes from the poorest people for the enrichment of a government that has no legitimate claim on us.
