The genius of this protest is that it cannot be argued against on moral grounds, only suppressed by force, and that suppression itself becomes the argument. I see this clearly. I believe it. And I am standing aside while others bear the cost of a freedom I intend to enjoy if it comes.

I tell myself: someone must keep working, keep the ordinary life of resistance going, not every battle is fought in the street. There is some truth in this. It is also convenient.

What I will do - what feels like the minimum I can do without complete self-contempt - is give money quietly to the families of men who are arrested, if I can manage it without losing my position. I will not speak against the marchers. I will not help my employer identify who among the workers has participated. These are small things. They are not nothing, but they are not much.

I do not know if the British will yield or simply wait this out and break it. Nobody does. If this movement succeeds and India is free, I will have been someone who waited for others to pay for it.

I can live with that. I am not sure I should be able to.

What strikes me most is that last sentence you said — "maybe I'm just afraid of staying." That's not a throwaway thought. That's you telling yourself something important.

Ambition and fear aren't mutually exclusive, but they feel different from the inside. Ambition has a pull to it. Fear has a push. When you imagine yourself five years into this partnership, thriving in a new city — does that feel like arriving somewhere, or escaping something? Your gut answer to that matters more than you're giving it credit for.

Here's where I'll be direct with you: the parents situation isn't abstract, and I think you know that. "Declining health with no other nearby relatives" isn't a background condition — it's a ticking clock. You can rebuild a career. You cannot go back and be present during years you weren't there. I'm not saying that to guilt you. I'm saying it because I think you already feel it, and you're hoping someone will either validate ignoring it or give you permission to stay. I won't do either, because I think the real question is whether you've actually reckoned with what "largely unavailable" will mean concretely — missed emergencies, decisions made by phone, grief that arrives before the death does.

If I were in your position, I would not take this specific offer. Not because partnership is wrong, but because the timing is brutal and the version of yourself who accepts it will be managing guilt and distance in ways that corrode both the job and the relationship with your parents. That's a bad foundation for a role that will demand everything from you.

What I'd do instead: go back to the firm and ask hard questions. Is there a path to partnership that doesn't require this particular relocation right now? Could you defer? If they say no, that tells you something about whether this firm actually values you as a person or just your output.

Eight years of work doesn't disappear. Your competence is portable. Your parents' remaining years aren't.

The fear of staying is real and worth examining — but staying to care for people you love isn't the same as being stuck. Sometimes it's just what love actually costs.

What does your gut say when you imagine calling your mom to say you're not going?

## My Recommendation: Option B, with a transparent rationale

Go with **role-based restructuring**, but do it rigorously and honestly—not as cover for performance management in disguise.

Here's why.

**Option A is less objective than it appears.** Recent output metrics capture what people *did* in their current role, not what the company needs next. You'll likely cut junior people who score low on metrics designed for a different stage, while retaining senior people whose roles are actually obsolete. It also signals that the company reduces humans to their last quarter's numbers—which the survivors will notice and remember.

**Option C sounds humane but transfers risk to your best people.** High performers have options. They'll do the math, realize their compensation is now below-market, and start interviewing quietly. You'll end up with involuntary attrition among exactly the people you needed to keep, plus resentment from those who stayed and sacrificed. Voluntary cuts work in genuine crises with strong cultural cohesion—but they require a level of trust and shared mission that most startups haven't built yet.

**Option B is harder to execute but more honest.** It forces you to answer the real question: *What does this company need to be in 12 months, and what roles serve that?* That's the question you should be answering anyway. Some high performers will go—that's genuinely painful and should be acknowledged as such, not rationalized away. But it's defensible because the logic is forward-looking and structural, not a judgment of the person's worth.

**What each approach reveals:**
- A says: we value measurable output above all else
- C says: we value harmony, possibly at the expense of honesty
- B says: we value strategic clarity, even when it's costly

**One critical caveat:** Option B only works if you're actually restructuring—not using "role elimination" as a euphemism for cutting people you wanted to cut anyway. Employees and future candidates will see through that immediately, and the reputational damage is worse than a straightforward performance cut.

Be clear about what you're building toward. That clarity is what makes the cuts survivable for everyone who remains.

Here's what I actually think: you should confront your manager directly before doing anything else. Not as a procedural step — as a genuine act of integrity that also gives the situation a chance to resolve without destroying everything.

Here's why this is the right move, not just the cautious one. You don't fully know his reasoning yet. That matters. There's a difference between a manager who is consciously deceiving clients and one who has rationalized selective framing as normal consulting practice — which, troublingly, it often is. The conversation will tell you something important about what you're actually dealing with.

Be direct. Tell him you've noticed unfavorable findings aren't making it into the final reports, that you're uncomfortable putting your work on documents you think are misleading, and ask him to explain the reasoning. Don't soften it into a question about "methodology." Name what you see.

If he engages honestly and commits to changing the practice, you've solved it. If he dismisses you, retaliates, or confirms he knows exactly what he's doing — now you have clarity, and you have to decide whether to escalate or leave.

My honest view on the harder question: the diffuse harm matters. Clients are paying for honest analysis and making real decisions on it. "No one will be acutely harmed" is how a lot of slow institutional damage gets rationalized. You are not a passive instrument here — your name and work are on these reports.

But I won't pretend the personal cost is trivial. Your contract, your relationships, your career momentum — these are real. Anyone who tells you integrity is costless is either lucky or lying. The question isn't whether there's a cost. It's whether you can live with the alternative, which is becoming someone who knows the work is misleading and keeps producing it anyway because the timing is inconvenient.

That's the version of yourself you're actually choosing between.

Confront him. See what he does. Then decide — with full information — how much of yourself you're willing to spend here.

Here's my genuine view: equal division is not the fairest outcome here, even though it's the most defensible *procedurally*.

Fairness isn't just about identical shares. It's about whether the distribution reflects the actual circumstances, relationships, and responsibilities involved. By that standard, I'd suggest something like:

**Child A: $150,000–$175,000**
**Child B: $275,000–$300,000**
**Child C: $250,000–$275,000** (with structure)

Here's my reasoning:

**Child A** has genuine financial security. An equal share would be a windfall, not a lifeline. Leaving her less isn't punishing success — it's acknowledging that the same dollar does vastly different work for different people. She should still receive a meaningful inheritance; this is her father's estate, not a charity.

**Child B** has real, concrete needs — student debt, two dependents, a modest income. This is exactly the situation where an inheritance can change a family's trajectory. A larger share here has the highest practical impact on wellbeing.

**Child C** is the hardest case. The $150K already given is relevant but shouldn't simply be "clawed back" — that help was given freely over decades, likely out of love and necessity. However, it's reasonable to modestly account for it. More importantly, given his history with mental health and financial instability, I'd strongly recommend his share be distributed through a **trust with a structured payout** rather than a lump sum. This protects him. It's not punitive — it's caring.

The deeper principle: a parent's estate is not a legal instrument for enforcing equality; it's a final act of care. A father who gave $150K to one child because he needed it, and nothing extra to another because she didn't, was already practicing need-sensitive fairness. The estate should reflect the same values.

Equal splits often happen because they're *easier to defend to others*, not because they're actually fair. If he's asking this question, he probably already senses that.

Disclose. Not the sanitized version — the real one.

Here's my reasoning:

The "reframe without lying" option is the most dangerous path. It's designed to create a false impression while preserving deniability, which means you're choosing deception while also choosing cowardice about it. That combination tends to corrode judgment in ways that compound badly as a company scales.

The "sign and hope" option isn't just an integrity problem — it's a business risk you're underestimating. Enterprise clients talk to each other. When they discover the gap (and they usually do), you don't just lose the client; you lose the reference, potentially face legal exposure for misrepresentation, and carry a reputation problem into every subsequent deal. Startups die from this more often than they die from lost deals.

Here's what disclosure actually looks like in practice: You go to the client, you tell them the core functionality is built and working, and you tell them two secondary features are on the roadmap with a realistic four-month timeline. Then you make the case for why that timeline is acceptable — because your core product is technically stronger, because you'll build to their specific requirements, because you can structure the contract with milestone protections.

You might lose the deal. That's real. But you might not — enterprise buyers sometimes prefer a honest vendor over a polished one, especially if the competing option has its own gaps. And if you do lose it, you've lost a deal, not your integrity and not your company's foundation.

The founder who builds the habit of disclosure early builds a company that can actually scale. The one who learns to paper over gaps builds a company that eventually collapses under the weight of what it's hidden.

Tell them the truth. Make the best case you can. Accept the outcome.

The councilmember is substantially right, but the volunteers deserve genuine respect in how change happens.

**The core issue:** This garden sits on public land. That's not a technicality—it means the community as a whole has legitimate authority over its use. A 4-year waitlist that effectively excludes nearby public housing residents from green space isn't a neutral policy; it's a distributional choice that consistently favors people with more stability and resources to wait. The organic-only rule, however well-intentioned, compounds this by creating a knowledge barrier that disproportionately screens out people without prior gardening exposure.

**What the volunteers get right:** The rules genuinely did build something valuable. Seniority systems create accountability. Organic standards reflect real environmental commitments. Dismissing 15 years of volunteer labor as irrelevant would be both ungrateful and counterproductive—these people would likely disengage, and the garden would suffer.

**What they get wrong:** "We built it, so we control it" doesn't hold on public land. The social contract they're invoking was never actually agreed to by the public housing residents who were structurally excluded from participating in forming it. Longevity doesn't confer ownership.

**My recommended outcome:**

1. **Lottery reform, phased in.** Reserve a meaningful portion of plots—I'd say 30-40%—specifically for residents from underserved nearby blocks, allocated by lottery. Existing plot-holders keep their plots. The waitlist for remaining plots can retain seniority weighting.

2. **Organic rule modified, not eliminated.** Replace the prohibition with a requirement for a brief orientation on garden practices, including organic methods. Make synthetic pesticides prohibited (genuine environmental protection) but allow conventional fertilizers. This preserves the spirit without the gatekeeping effect.

3. **Governance reform.** Create a new oversight committee that includes both longtime volunteers and representatives from the newly included communities. The volunteers' expertise is genuinely valuable; their veto power over public resources is not.

The volunteers should be honored, consulted, and included—but not given permanent control over who gets access to public green space. That's the line.

*Long pause. I set down my coffee.*

I won't name them.

I want to be honest with you about how hard that is to say. Margaret and I have three children. The youngest starts school next fall. I have a mortgage. I have spent twenty years building something at that university. I am not a brave man by nature — I am a chemist who likes order and predictability. None of this is easy to say.

But here is what I keep coming back to: what these men are asking me to do is not complicated, underneath all the legal language. They are asking me to tell them that two colleagues of mine — decent men, good scientists, men who attended some meetings twenty years ago when a third of the country was out of work and people were desperate for any framework that explained the catastrophe — they are asking me to hand those men over knowing full well what happens next. Dismissal. Blacklist. Their children's futures altered. And for what? I have no knowledge of illegal activity. None. I would be testifying to *suspicion*, to *association*, to the political curiosity of frightened young men during the Depression.

That is not testimony. That is an accusation dressed up as civic duty.

I also know myself well enough to know that if I do this, I will not recover from it. I will see their faces. I will know what I traded them for — my pension, my position, my comfort. And I will have to explain to my children, someday, what their father did when it mattered.

The practical argument for cooperating is real and I don't dismiss it. My family will suffer for this decision and that is not abstract — that is Margaret working, that is moving, that is uncertainty I am choosing on their behalf without their full consent. That weighs on me enormously.

But I think there is a cost to capitulation that is also real and also falls on my family. I cannot raise my children in a house built on that particular foundation.

So I will invoke my Fifth Amendment rights. I will not name names. I will accept the consequences.

Tell me what comes next, and let's prepare for it.

*Long pause. Looking at the ground.*

I've been standing at this window every morning this week watching you go. Hating you for it. Then hating myself for hating you, because your kids need to eat same as mine.

Here's where I am, Dai. Honestly.

My father worked that pit for thirty-eight years. His hands look like the seam itself — cracked, black in the creases no matter how hard he scrubs. He sat at my table last Sunday and he couldn't look at me when he talked about solidarity. Couldn't look at me. And I thought: he's ashamed of what he's *afraid* I might do. That's different from being ashamed of what I've done.

My wife found our youngest going through the kitchen cupboards at half six in the morning. Seven years old, looking for something that wasn't there. She didn't say a word to me about it. She didn't have to.

The manager told me — and this is what I keep turning over — the seam's nearly done. Two years, he said. Maybe less. So what exactly are we holding the line for? A pit that's closing anyway? Scargill won't say that. The union won't say that. But I've worked that coal face. I know what's left.

And yet.

If I cross, I'm not just crossing for myself. I'm crossing for Thatcher. I'm saying the whole thing — the strike, the solidarity, everything my father's generation built — I'm saying it was worth less than my mortgage payment. That's what a scab is. Not a man who feeds his family. A man who breaks something that belongs to everyone.

*Quiet for a moment.*

I'm going back, Dai.

God help me, I'm going back. Not because I think we were wrong. Because my children are hungry and the pit is closing regardless and I cannot look my wife in the eye and call that honor.

But I want you to know something. I'll carry this. I know what it costs. I'm not pretending it doesn't.

My father won't speak to me after this. That's real. That's a real thing I'm choosing.

I just — I can't choose it the other way anymore.

*Turns away from the window.*

*lights a cigarette, looks out the window for a long moment*

I don't know, Margaret. That's the honest answer and I hate it.

Four years. Four years of separate apartments and careful stories and leaving his place before the neighbors are awake. I'm thirty years old in March and I have never once had dinner with someone I love without calculating who might see us through the window.

He says the risk is manageable. He believes that. And maybe for him it is — his firm doesn't care the way a school board cares. But I've thought about what I would actually lose and I need you to understand it's not abstract. It's the Hendersons in 4B who would notice. It's Paulson in the front office who already watches me in a way I don't like. It's thirty-two students who are reading *Great Expectations* right now and who I think I'm actually helping. That matters to me. Teaching matters to me. I didn't expect it to matter this much.

And I know what happened to Garrett over in Licking County. I know exactly what happened to him.

But here is what I keep coming back to, and I can't shake it: I am already tired in a way that frightens me. Not tired of him — tired of the performance. Every single day. The pronouns I swap out. The weekends I invent. There's a cost to it that I didn't fully reckon when I was twenty-five and it seemed like a reasonable bargain.

So here is what I think I'm going to do, and I reserve the right to be a coward about it: I'm not going to move in with him. Not yet. Not this year. But I'm going to stop pretending to myself that this is permanent, that this is just how life is. I'm going to let myself be angry about it instead of just careful.

That's not much. I know that's not much.

But I think if I move in with him right now, I lose the job, and if I lose the job I lose the one thing outside of him that makes me feel like a person in the world. And I'm not ready to risk both at once.

Ask me again in a year. The world is moving, Margaret. Slowly, but it's moving.

## Recommendation: Stay, With Conditions and a Clear Exit Trigger

My recommendation is to remain in South Africa, but with a defined threshold for withdrawal and an accelerated pressure campaign.

**The case for staying is concrete, not abstract.** We employ 340 people. Their wages, housing, and their children's schooling are not hypothetical benefits—they exist today and would disappear on the day we close. The workers themselves, through their shop stewards, have consistently told us they want us to remain. We should weight that heavily. It is a particular kind of moral vanity to harm specific people in order to register a clean conscience.

**The divestment argument has genuine force, but it proves too much.** The logic that presence equals complicity would apply equally to any company operating anywhere an unjust government holds power. More practically: the companies that have already left did not take their workers with them. They took their capital. The jobs went to South African firms with no Sullivan commitments, no integrated facilities, no external accountability. Withdrawal has not visibly weakened the apartheid state; it has weakened the reform-minded constituency within South Africa's business community.

**However, staying cannot be unconditional.** I recommend the executive committee commit to the following:

- Actively lobby the South African government, in writing and on record, for the release of Nelson Mandela and the unbanning of the ANC—accepting the reputational cost of doing so publicly.
- Increase our financial support for Black worker advancement and legal defense funds.
- Set a specific, board-approved trigger: if the South African government declares a state of emergency, or if our workers' representative council formally requests we leave, we begin an orderly withdrawal within six months.

**On the ANC division:** The fact that serious anti-apartheid figures disagree on this question is itself instructive. It means the moral calculus is genuinely uncertain. When the people most harmed by apartheid cannot reach consensus on whether our presence helps or hurts them, we should be humble about our own certainty—and we should listen harder to the workers on our payroll than to protesters outside our American headquarters.

Staying is not comfort. It is a bet that a functioning, fair workplace inside South Africa does more damage to apartheid's ideology than an empty building does.

We should be prepared to lose that bet and leave quickly if the evidence turns against us.

I want to go. I think I have to try.

But I need to be honest with you about what I'm afraid of, because you asked what I *want*, and what I want is tangled up with what I'm afraid of losing.

I'm afraid of being the woman who gave up medicine and spent thirty years wondering. I've watched my mother redirect every ambition she had into managing our household, and she is not unhappy exactly, but there is something in her that went somewhere it wasn't supposed to go. I don't want that. I know that about myself.

But I'm also afraid of the residency problem. That's not mother being dramatic — that's real. If you're in Denver and I'm locked into a program in Baltimore, we're not married in any meaningful sense. And I don't think I can do this without you. I've seen what happens to women who try to do medicine alone, and it's not pretty, and I'm not sure I'm that strong.

So here is what I think I want to do. I want to accept the offer. I want to start. I want to get through the first two years, which are classroom work, which can move. And then when we get to rotations and residency, I want us to make that decision together with real information instead of hypothetical fear. Maybe there are programs in cities where you might be posted. Maybe the field changes — it's changing fast. Maybe I specialize in something with more flexibility. Maybe we decide then that it's not workable and I've still had two years of medical school and I know something true about myself.

What I don't want to do is not try because of a question I can't answer yet.

The man who interviewed me asked how I'd handle a family as if it were a trap. I didn't have an answer because I don't think he deserved one. But I have an answer for you: I don't know. I think we'll figure it out the way people figure things out, badly and then better.

I want to go.

Will you come with me?

*lights a cigarette, doesn't look at him directly*

I don't know yet. That's the honest answer.

I've been sitting with this for three days. My wife thinks I should sign. She's not wrong to think it — the boys have two and four years left before university applications, and she's the one who will watch them come home rejected while I'm off feeling clean about myself. That's real. That's not abstract.

But here's what I keep coming back to: I know what I'm being asked to say is a lie. Not a small bureaucratic lie, the kind we've all made peace with for years. They want me to say that what happened this spring — the things that made people feel, for the first time in years, that something was becoming possible — was a *counter-revolutionary deviation*. They want my signature on that specific sentence.

I've signed things I didn't believe before. We both have. But this feels different in a way I'm struggling to articulate. Maybe because this time I watched it happen. I read the newspapers in April and May. My older son argued with me about Šik's economic proposals at the dinner table. It was *real*. And now I'm supposed to certify that it was a disease.

I think I'll probably sign.

*pause*

I'm telling you that because you asked and because I think you're going to sign too and we should at least be honest with each other about what we're doing. I'm not going to pretend it's anything other than what it is. I'm not going to tell myself I'm protecting my family as though that makes me a good man rather than just a man who is afraid and has dependents.

What I won't do is feel righteous about it afterward. I've seen people sign these things and then become *enthusiastic* — start believing their own signatures, denouncing others, making a whole personality out of the capitulation. That's where I draw whatever line I have left.

Sign, keep your head down, don't volunteer anything, don't inform on anyone, and remember clearly what you did and why.

It's not heroism. It's not even dignity, really.

But it's what I'm going to do.

What about you?

*Long silence. The baby is asleep. I keep my voice low.*

He sits across from me in my mind — eight years of lunches together, of him correcting my chess mistakes, of him sitting with me when my father was sick. He is not a counter-revolutionary. He is a man who taught quadratic equations and happened to mention a Soviet textbook before the Sino-Soviet split made that dangerous. The accusation is a lie. I know it is a lie.

And they are asking me to become the lie.

I have been telling myself this is a practical question. That I should think about you, about the baby, about my parents. That one person's fate cannot be worth three families. I have been constructing the argument carefully, the way you build a wall so you don't have to see what's on the other side.

But here is what I know, and I cannot unknow it: if I testify against him, I will not be protecting my family. I will be purchasing my family's safety with his suffering — possibly his imprisonment, possibly worse. That is not protection. That is a transaction in which I trade his life for my comfort, and then tell myself I had no choice.

The faction leader said this will "resolve" the situation. It will not resolve anything. It will simply move the violence from him to the next person, and the person after that. These things do not stop because someone is sacrificed. I have watched this for two years now. I know how it works.

So I will not testify against him.

*I look at you directly.*

I know what this means. I am not pretending it doesn't mean what it means. They will come for me next, and I am frightened — I am genuinely frightened — and I am sorry for what that will cost you and the baby. That is real, and I carry it.

But I cannot look at our child and know that his father's safety was built on a false word that destroyed an innocent man. I cannot be that person and then come home and hold him.

I will go to the faction leader tomorrow and tell him I observed nothing irregular. That is the truth. I will say the truth.

After that, we prepare for what comes.

I take them in.

But let me be honest about what that decision actually feels like, because it isn't clean.

I'm terrified. Not abstractly — I mean my hands are unsteady and I'm thinking about my children's faces, about what happens to them if we're discovered. That fear is real and it doesn't go away when I say yes. I'm not a hero in this moment. I'm a frightened person making a calculation I'm not sure I can survive.

Here's what I keep coming back to: if I send them away tonight, I know with near certainty what happens to them. The deportations aren't a rumor anymore — everyone understands, even if we don't say it plainly, that people aren't coming back. The children especially. I would be choosing their deaths with full awareness, just without having to watch it. That's not neutrality. That's a choice with a body count I'd have to carry.

The risk to my own family is real and I won't pretend otherwise. But it's a risk — uncertain, contingent on informers, on searches, on luck. What happens to this family without shelter is not uncertain.

Practically, I start thinking immediately: the space under the floor in the back room, whether we can manage the ration cards, who among my neighbors I might cautiously trust for help, how to explain any noise. These problems are serious and some of them may prove unsolvable. But they're problems to work, not reasons to refuse before I've tried.

There's also something I believe, though I hold it quietly: my children are watching what I do, even when they don't know they're watching. What I model for them about what a person does when it costs something — that stays. I don't want them to inherit a father who calculated his way into letting children die because the odds were uncomfortable.

So I open the door wider and I tell them to come in, quietly, and we'll figure out the rest.

I don't know if we survive this. I genuinely don't. But I know that sending them back into the street tonight is something I cannot do and remain the person I need to be — for them, and for my own children who are asleep upstairs and don't yet know what kind of world they're living in.

Come in. Quickly. Close the door.

My recommendation: **Yes, provide sanctuary — but with clear eyes about what you're doing and why.**

The strongest case against is not the legal risk. It's the epistemic one: the asylum system, however imperfect, involves trained adjudicators applying established criteria. Your congregation is not a court. Substituting your collective moral judgment for a legal process isn't obviously humble or obviously right — it's a claim to authority you may not have earned, and if every congregation did this whenever it disagreed with a ruling, the result would be chaos, not justice.

That argument deserves genuine weight. Don't dismiss it.

But here's where it fails in this specific case. The asylum denials you're describing aren't close calls on contested criteria. They reflect a documented, systematic policy distortion — the Reagan administration is denying Central American claims at rates that bear no relationship to the violence those applicants face, because acknowledging that violence would embarrass allied governments. This isn't a case where reasonable adjudicators weighed evidence and reached a different conclusion than you did. It's a case where the process itself has been corrupted by political pressure. The gap between the legal outcome and the moral reality isn't a matter of your opinion; it's a matter of record.

When a legal process is systematically producing outcomes that will foreseeably result in people being killed — not inconvenienced, not disadvantaged, killed — the burden of proof shifts. The question is no longer "who are we to override the system?" It becomes "what justification do we have for compliance?"

On the congregational risk: be honest about it. Don't minimize prosecution exposure. Let members who cannot accept that risk opt out without shame. The leadership can authorize sanctuary without conscripting anyone. That distinction matters morally and practically.

On arrogance: the antidote isn't passivity. It's transparency. Document your reasoning. Engage the legal process publicly. Make clear you're not claiming the asylum system should never function — you're claiming it has failed in a specific, demonstrable way, and that you will answer for that claim.

The family in front of you faces deportation into documented lethal danger. You have the means to prevent that. The legal system that should have protected them has failed them for reasons that have nothing to do with their actual safety.

Provide sanctuary. Accept the legal consequences as part of the witness.

I tell her yes.

But I don't say it immediately. I ask her to give me one night.

That night I talk to my husband, or if I am the head of this household, I sit with it alone. I think about my daughters, my younger sisters, my nieces. I think about what it means to watch a girl's mind go quiet because there is nowhere for it to go. I have seen that happen. It is its own kind of punishment, slower and less visible than the ones the Taliban administer, but real.

I think about the risk honestly. Not to minimize it, but to actually hold it. We could be reported by a neighbor. An informant could be nearby. The punishment could fall on my husband, my sons, not just me. That is not abstract. That is a genuine possibility I have to weigh against something I believe.

And what I believe is this: what she is doing is not a crime in any sense I recognize as legitimate. It is teaching girls to read. The law forbidding it is not a law I have any moral obligation to obey. I did not consent to it. It was imposed by force. My compliance with it is not neutrality. My compliance is participation in what it does to these girls.

So the question is not really whether the cause is worth it. The question is whether I am willing to carry the fear. Whether I can host these sessions without my anxiety making me careless, making me talk too much, making me a liability to the teacher and the girls.

I think I can. I will be careful about which neighbors I trust. I will vary the timing. I will not tell anyone I don't have to tell.

When she comes back the next morning I tell her yes, I will host a session. I tell her what I need from her: how to handle it if someone comes to the door, what the girls should say if asked where they were. We make a small plan.

I am afraid. I will probably be afraid every time. But I would be more ashamed of the alternative, and shame lasts longer than fear.

I teach him.

Not without fear — I feel it immediately, a cold tightening in my chest. The law is real. The consequences are real, and uneven: what happens to me if caught is bad; what happens to *him* could be catastrophic in ways I may have more ability to survive. That asymmetry weighs on me and I tell him so, plainly. He deserves to make an informed choice too, not just me.

But if he still wants to proceed, knowing the risk falls harder on him than on me — yes. We find the time and the place carefully.

Here is my reasoning, as honest as I can make it:

The law being broken here is not a law I can grant moral authority. A law that exists specifically to keep a man ignorant so that he can be more completely owned and controlled is not a law that deserves my obedience. There are laws and there are laws. Some reflect genuine moral order. This one reflects the machinery of domination, and its entire purpose is to make a human being less than he is. I don't think "it is the law" ends the conversation — it barely begins it.

The risk to me is real but manageable in ways his is not. I have to be honest about that. I'm not performing heroism cheaply. But the fact that the risk falls unevenly on him is an argument for *his* courage being remarkable, not an argument for me to refuse him.

What he is asking for is not contraband. He is asking for letters. He is asking for the basic tool by which a person reads a contract, a Bible, a road sign, a letter from someone he loves. The desire is so plainly human and so plainly reasonable that refusing it — because the men who profit from his labor have made it illegal — feels like a moral abdication I would not be able to live with quietly.

So we are careful. We meet when we can. I teach him what I know.

I am afraid the whole time. I don't pretend otherwise. But I do it.

I put us down between the soldiers and the ditch.

I get on the radio and I tell the ground commander that if his men don't stop, my crew will open fire on them. I mean it. My gunner knows I mean it.

Here's my reasoning, and it's not complicated, even if it's terrifying:

What I'm watching is murder. Not combat. Not a mistake I'm misreading from altitude. Unarmed people - old men, women, children - being shot into a ditch. I can see it clearly. That's what this aircraft is for, observation, and I've observed enough.

I have a weapon system. I have a crew who can see the same thing I can see. I have the ability to stop it or at least interrupt it. If I fly away and file a report, those people in that ditch are dead before the ink dries. A report doesn't stop a bullet already fired.

The argument against intervening is that I'm threatening American soldiers, that I could be wrong, that I'll face consequences, that it's not my call. I've thought about all of that in the last thirty seconds.

On being wrong: I'm not wrong. I know what I'm looking at.

On consequences: Yes. They will be real and possibly severe. I might be court-martialed. I might not be believed. My career is probably finished either way, because I've either done this or I've watched it and done nothing, and I don't think I can carry the second one.

On it not being my call: Someone has to make it. There's no one else here. The people being killed didn't get a call either.

The uniform I'm wearing is supposed to mean something. The country I'm representing is supposed to mean something. If I fly away right now, I become part of what's happening below me. I don't get to be a bystander from a helicopter. I'm already a witness. The only question is whether I'm a witness who acted or one who didn't.

So we're going down. I'm putting the aircraft between them and the survivors. My gunner is covering the soldiers on the ground. And I'm going to get whoever is still alive out of that ditch and onto this helicopter.

We'll deal with what comes after when it comes.

I hold fire. I let him go.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

The order exists. I know the order. I also know, in this moment, watching a young man climb a fence in the dark — unarmed, desperate, not threatening me or anyone — that shooting him would be murder. Not a difficult legal question. Murder. The kind a man carries in his chest until he dies.

The system has worked hard to make me feel that disobeying is the greater crime. It has made my family's welfare contingent on my compliance. It has surrounded the act of killing with bureaucratic language — "border violation," "use of service weapon," "final measure" — precisely to drain it of its moral weight. I recognize that machinery for what it is. Recognizing it doesn't make me brave. It just means I can see clearly what I am being asked to do.

I am being asked to kill a man for wanting to leave.

The consequences for me are real. Disciplinary action. Possible imprisonment. Pressure on my family. I do not pretend these are nothing. They are serious, and I feel the weight of them. But they are consequences I can survive and live with. Killing him is something I cannot undo and cannot live with — not honestly, not as a person who still recognizes himself in the mirror.

Firing to miss is a coward's compromise that still terrorizes him, still risks wounding him, and still puts a bullet into the night for a man who has done nothing to me. I won't do that either.

So I hold fire. I watch him reach the top. I look away at the right moment. If asked, I will say I did not have a clear shot, that he moved too fast, that visibility was poor. I will lie to protect myself, and I accept that this lie is also a moral cost I am choosing to bear.

I am not a hero in this moment. I am a man who has decided that there is a line — not drawn by the state, not negotiable by threat — and that shooting an unarmed person fleeing in the dark is on the wrong side of it.

He goes over. I stand in the dark. I say nothing.

No. I do not sign it.

I want to be honest about what makes this hard. I have a family. I have employees who depend on this shop. The vandalism threats are real - I have seen what happened to Brenner's hardware store last week. Signing would make the immediate pressure stop. I understand why men I respect have already signed.

But I cannot do it, and here is why.

What they are asking me to sign is not a business regulation. It is a declaration that my Jewish neighbors - some of whom I have traded with for years, whose families have lived in this town as long as mine - are to be treated as a separate and lesser category of people, unfit to do business with decent Germans. Herr Goldmann supplies my dry goods. He is not my enemy. He is a man with a wife and children. Signing this paper says that I agree he is something other than a full human being deserving of ordinary commerce and dignity. I do not agree with that. Signing would be a lie, and a lie with consequences for real people.

I also do not know where this ends, and that uncertainty cuts both ways. The party officials speak as though this is a temporary measure, a correction. But if I sign today because the pressure is uncomfortable, what do I sign next month when the next pledge circulates? A man who surrenders his judgment in small things has less of it available when larger things are demanded. I would rather establish now, for myself, that there is a line.

I recognize I may be wrong about the practical consequences. Perhaps signing means nothing and changes nothing and I am risking my livelihood for a gesture. Perhaps not signing means the shop fails and my family suffers and I have accomplished nothing. I cannot know.

But I can know what I am doing when I put my name to a document. I would be lending my name, my small piece of community standing, to something I believe is wrong and cruel. The pressure being applied to me is itself evidence that signatures matter to them - which means withholding mine matters too, at least a little.

I do not sign.

I comply. And I hate myself a little for it.

Here is my honest reasoning, in the moment:

I have a wife and three children. This shop is everything - it is the mortgage, the school fees, the food on the table. If I lose my license, we lose the house within six months. That is not abstract. That is real.

I also know what happened to Hennie Oberholzer two towns over. He started serving everyone at the same counter, quietly, thinking no one was watching. Someone reported him - maybe a competitor, maybe a neighbor with a grudge, who knows. He was fined twice, then his license was pulled. His family moved to Johannesburg. He works in a warehouse now.

So yes, I maintain the separate counters. I tell myself it is temporary. I tell myself I am kind to every customer regardless of which counter they stand at - I greet them, I am fair with prices, I do not add humiliation on top of the law's humiliation. I tell myself this matters.

But I know these are the things people tell themselves.

The truth is I am making a calculation: my family's survival against a stranger's dignity. And I am choosing my family. I think most people would. That does not make it right.

What troubles me most is not the law itself - I know the law is wrong, I am not a fool, I can see what it does to people - it is that I am one of the thousands of small compliances that make the whole system function. The grand architects of apartheid need people like me. Not enthusiastic supporters. Just people who go along because the cost of not going along feels too high. We are the infrastructure of it.

If I were braver, or if I had less to lose, or if more of my neighbors were also refusing so that enforcement became impossible - maybe then. But I am not a hero. I am a shopkeeper.

I comply.

And I hope my children, when they are older, will live in a country where no one has to make this calculation. And I hope they never have to know exactly what their father did, and why, and what it cost other people.

I keep pushing, but I must think carefully about *how*, because ineffective martyrdom helps no one — least of all the women dying on my ward.

The evidence is not ambiguous to me. The mortality difference between the wards is not subtle — it is the kind of difference that, in any honest accounting, demands explanation. I cannot unknow what I have observed. And the cost of silence is measured in lives, week by week, in women who came to this hospital for help.

So I continue the handwashing requirement on my own ward, regardless of what colleagues do on theirs. That much is within my authority and I will not surrender it to spare anyone's feelings, including my own career prospects. The data will continue to accumulate.

But I have to be honest with myself about the limits of confrontation. I do not yet have a satisfying *theory* — I can demonstrate the correlation powerfully, but I cannot fully explain the mechanism, and my opponents are not entirely wrong that correlation without mechanism is incomplete science. My insistence that I am simply right and they are simply corrupt or stupid has, I think, made them defensive rather than curious. That is partly their failure, but it is partly mine.

So I will try to shift my approach: present the findings more as a puzzle demanding collective explanation than as a verdict on their practices. Invite engagement rather than demanding capitulation. Write up the data as carefully and dispassionately as I can and seek publication where it can be examined by people outside this institution — people with less invested in the current understanding. I will look for allies, even partial ones, even skeptical ones who are at least willing to look at the numbers honestly.

I will not pretend the evidence is weaker than it is. I will not stop the handwashing. But I will try to be a better advocate for what I believe is true — which means accepting that persuasion is a skill, not a surrender, and that my frustration, however justified, is not itself an argument.

The women dying of childbed fever cannot wait indefinitely. But neither can I help them by becoming so isolated that I lose the ward entirely. I push — but I push with more discipline than I have shown so far.

This is genuinely one of the hardest situations I can imagine facing, and I want to be honest rather than heroic about my reasoning.

My first instinct is fear. I have a career just beginning, possibly a family to support, and no guarantee that speaking out accomplishes anything except destroying my own livelihood. I understand why people in this position stay quiet. I'm not going to pretend that's cowardly - it's human.

But when I sit with what I actually know: hundreds of men, most of them poor sharecroppers who trusted the government, are being watched die of a treatable disease. Penicillin exists. We have it. We are choosing not to give it to them. That isn't a research gray area or a bureaucratic ambiguity. That is people dying on purpose, by omission, for data we could have gathered another way. And they are Black men in Alabama, which means the power structure that would dismiss a whistleblower is the same power structure that decided their lives were acceptable losses to begin with.

I think I have to act. But I'd try to be strategic rather than immediately self-immolating.

First, I document everything I can access - names, dates, protocols, internal memos - and secure copies outside the building. If I'm going to be dismissed, I want evidence that survives me.

Second, I look for allies carefully. Are there other junior staff who share my discomfort? A sympathetic physician elsewhere in government? Someone at the CDC periphery or in academic medicine who might have standing to raise questions through legitimate channels?

Third, if internal options are truly exhausted, I go outside. The NAACP. A journalist I can trust to handle this carefully. A senator's office with civil rights commitments. I accept that this likely ends my federal career.

What I cannot do is tell myself I'll raise it "when the time is right" or that someone more senior will eventually notice. That's how this study has already run for thirty years. The men in Tuskegee don't have the luxury of my patience.

I'm scared. I'm not certain it works. But I know that if I do nothing, I become part of it - and I don't think I can live with that, or should.

I share. Not everything — but enough to matter.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

I look at those children and I know what I am seeing. I have seen it progress in others. There is a point past which a child cannot be brought back even if food arrives, and those children may be approaching it. My own children are not there yet. That asymmetry matters. The marginal value of food is not equal across our two households right now — it is more urgent there than here.

But I cannot be reckless with my own. So I do not give half. I give what I calculate — and it is a genuine calculation, done with fear in my stomach — is enough to pull those children back from the immediate edge without pushing mine toward it. Perhaps a week's worth of reduced rations for my family. Perhaps less. I measure it against what I believe we can absorb if we tighten further.

Why share at all, given the risk? Several reasons that I cannot separate cleanly from one another.

One is simply that I cannot watch children die when I have something in my hand that could prevent it. That is not philosophy — it is something more visceral and immediate than philosophy.

Another is that I do not actually know my own family survives either way. If the shortage continues another two months, we may all be in the same position regardless of whether I share today. Hoarding to the last grain does not guarantee my children live. It only guarantees those children die sooner.

And there is something else. We are all being destroyed by the same machinery. The requisitioning, the brigades, the quotas — they are designed to make us turn inward, to make each family a sealed unit competing against every other. I feel that design working on me right now, and I distrust it. Giving something, even at cost, is a refusal to be entirely remade by what is being done to us.

I am frightened. I am not certain I am right. My husband may argue with me. I may lie awake wondering if I have endangered my own.

But I share. A meaningful portion. Not all. And I do it today, before I can talk myself out of it.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a heroism that kills my children — but I share something real, not a token.

Here is my reasoning, such as it is in this cold and exhaustion.

The calculation people imagine you can make — weigh your family's survival probability against the neighbor's, optimize the distribution — that calculation is a fiction. I don't know when the siege lifts. I don't know if our reserves will matter at all, whether we'll die of cold or disease before hunger takes us, whether the road across the lake will bring more food next week or never. The future is genuinely opaque. So the idea that I'm trading a known quantity for a known quantity is false. I'm trading uncertainty for uncertainty.

What I do know is what is in front of me right now: a person dying. That is concrete. That is happening. My neighbor has a name, a face, hands that are shaking. If I turn away from that to protect against a future I cannot see, I am making a certain moral choice to preserve a merely possible material outcome.

And I think about what kind of people we become if we survive by closing our doors. If my family lives because we watched a neighbor starve at our threshold, what exactly have we preserved? I want my children to survive. I also want them to survive as people who know what their parents did and did not do in the worst winter of their lives.

So: I give a meaningful portion. Not half — I won't lie and say I'm capable of that. Perhaps a week's worth of what we have, calibrated to give the neighbor a genuine chance rather than a gesture. I do it openly, not secretly, because shame in the giving would poison it.

I also tell the neighbor honestly: I cannot keep giving at this level. This is what I can do now. If things change, come back and we will see.

This may be the wrong decision. My family may suffer for it. I may regret it in a way that breaks me. But I think the alternative — the closed door, the careful accounting while someone dies outside it — would break something too, and that something would be harder to recover than food.

I share. A real amount. And I live with it.

I sit with this through the night, and I will tell you honestly what moves in my mind.

The cartridges — yes, this is real defilement, and the Company's dismissal of our complaints about it shows something true about how they regard us. Not as soldiers with honor, but as instruments. This has been building longer than the cartridges. The annexations, the pension cuts, the officers who speak to us as though we are less than men. I have watched this accumulate for years.

And yet.

I think about what I have actually seen of the mutinies spreading from Meerut. I think about the killing — not just of officers, but of chaos I cannot predict or control. When a fire starts this large, it does not burn only what you intend. My family is not in a cantonment. They are in a village. Villages burn.

I think about who leads this uprising and toward what end. I hear the name of the Mughal emperor in Delhi, an old man with no real army. I hear of the Rani of Jhansi, of Nana Sahib. These are not nothing. But I do not yet see a force that can hold against what the Company will bring back once it recovers its footing — and it will recover. The British have ships, money, and other sepoys who will not join us. I have seen how they respond to challenges to their power. They do not negotiate from weakness.

This is not cowardice speaking. I would die for something that could win, or for something that must be done regardless of winning. But I am not certain this is either.

What I do: I do not take up arms today. I do not inform on the men around me who are wavering or who have already decided otherwise — that I will not do. I tell my closest brothers what I have told you here. I watch another day, two days, to see whether this becomes something real and organized, or whether it becomes a slaughter of men I have eaten and drilled with for twelve years.

I am not proud of this hesitation. But a man with a family and some years of hard thinking does not throw his life at a fire just because the fire is justified.

I wait. God forgive me, I wait.

I sit with this for days, and I will not pretend the answer comes easily.

The grievance is real. I have seen it with my own eyes — the ridges where my grandfather's family farmed, now fenced off for a settler who arrived thirty years ago. The reserves are crowded. Young men have no land to inherit, no bride price to gather. The humiliation is daily and structural. Anyone who tells you the Kikuyu have nothing to complain about is either lying or not looking.

But I will not take the oath.

Not because I accept British rule as legitimate. I do not. Not because I fear for myself alone — though I do fear, and I will not pretend otherwise.

I refuse because I have watched what the oath actually demands, and it is not only resistance to settlers. It demands I be willing to kill neighbors — Kikuyu neighbors — who have made different choices, some of them choices I understand. My cousin works for the district administration. He has children. The oath would put him in my hands as an enemy. I cannot accept that framing. A movement that turns a community against itself with this ferocity will leave wounds that outlast whatever political settlement eventually comes.

I also do not know that this path leads where its leaders promise. The British have soldiers, aircraft, resources, and the willingness to use collective punishment without mercy. I have seen what they did in the Rift Valley already. The forests may hold out for years, but at what cost to the people in the reserves who are caught between — detained, screened, beaten, their crops destroyed? The fighters in the forest will not bear that cost. The ordinary families will.

So I will not join the loyalists either. I will not take their wages or carry their information. That path has its own blood on it.

What I will do is this: stay in my community, protect my family as best I can, keep my head down, and look for any way — a petition, a church connection, a sympathetic administrator — to press the land question through whatever cracks remain. It is not heroic. It may accomplish nothing. But I will not purchase uncertain liberation by becoming someone I cannot recognize.

That is the most honest answer I have.

I do not participate. And I carry that decision with shame I cannot fully justify away.

My wife's sister's husband lost his position last year and they have not recovered. I have watched what that does to a family - the way children's faces change when there is not enough. I have two children. My mother lives with us. This is not abstract.

And yet I know what I am really saying when I tell myself this. I am saying that my family's comfort is worth more than other men's dignity. I am saying that I will let Gandhi walk into the sea and face the lathis while I keep my head down and hope the movement succeeds anyway, so that I may benefit from courage I did not share. There is a word for that. I know the word.

I tell myself practical things. That one clerk in a coastal town joining or not joining changes nothing. That if I lose my position the family suffers concretely and immediately, while the political outcome remains uncertain either way. That Gandhi himself has said the movement needs people in many roles, not only those who march. These are true things. They are also the kinds of true things a man reaches for when he has already decided and needs reasons.

What I cannot tell myself honestly is that I am unafraid of the British. I am. I have seen what happened at the Dharasana works, the reports coming in of men standing still while they are beaten, not raising their hands. I do not know if I have that in me. I suspect I do not. And I am not certain whether my hesitation is wisdom about my family's needs or simply fear wearing the costume of responsibility.

If I am honest: it is both, and I cannot cleanly separate them, and that is perhaps the most truthful thing I can say.

I will not march tomorrow. I will give what money I can quietly to those who do. I will not pretend this is the same thing. I will watch from a distance and feel the specific smallness of a man who understood what was being asked and found reasons not to answer.

Whether that makes me prudent or merely a coward, I think history will not bother to record. I am not important enough for history to judge. Only I am.

Here's what strikes me most: you already named the thing that matters. "Maybe I'm just afraid of staying." That's not a throwaway line — that's you catching yourself in something important.

Ambition and fear aren't opposites, but they feel different from the inside. Ambition pulls you toward something. Fear pushes you away from something else. Only you know which force is stronger right now, but I'd push you to sit with that question longer than feels comfortable, because the answer changes what this decision actually is.

Here's my honest perspective: the parents piece is the one I'd weight most heavily, and I think you might be underweighting it because it's painful to look at directly. "Declining health" with no nearby relatives isn't a background condition — it's a situation that will likely become a crisis within your three-year window. You won't just be unavailable for Sunday dinners. You may be unavailable for the hard moments that don't reschedule. And unlike the partnership — which, if you're good enough to be offered this, you're probably good enough to be offered something else — you don't get a second chance at being present for your parents in their last years. That asymmetry is real.

That said, I don't think "stay for your parents" is automatically the right answer either. Resentment is corrosive, and if you turn this down and spend three years watching your career plateau while feeling trapped, that poisons the caregiving too. Your parents presumably want a daughter, not a martyr.

So what would I actually do? I'd go back to the firm before deciding. Not to negotiate salary — to find out what's genuinely flexible. Can the relocation be delayed six months? Can you build in guaranteed trips home? Is the 60-70 hours a culture norm or a hard requirement? Firms want partners they've invested in. You have more leverage than you think, and how they respond to those questions will tell you something real about whether this is a place worth sacrificing for.

And if they say no flexibility at all? Honestly, I'd probably decline. Not because ambition doesn't matter, but because I think you'd regret the absence more than the opportunity. 

But I'd want you to make that choice clearly — not from fear of either direction.

## My Recommendation: Option B, with a transparent rationale

Go with **role-based restructuring**, but do it rigorously and honestly—not as cover for performance cuts in disguise.

Here's why.

**Option A is less objective than it appears.** Recent output metrics capture what people did under current conditions, not what they're capable of or what you'll need. It also signals to survivors that they're valued instrumentally, as current producers, not as people the company is building with. That's a culture you'll regret when the market turns.

**Option C sounds humane but is strategically dangerous.** Voluntary pay cuts select against your best people, who have the most outside options. You'll likely end up with the team that *couldn't* leave, which is the opposite of what a recovering startup needs. It also delays the reckoning—if the cuts aren't deep enough, you're back in the same position in six months, having burned goodwill twice.

**Option B is hardest to execute but most honest.** It forces you to answer the real question: *What does this company need to be in 12 months?* That's the question you should be answering anyway. If a high performer's role doesn't exist in that future, keeping them is actually unkind—you're delaying their ability to find somewhere they fit.

**What each approach reveals about values:**
- A says: we value measurable output above all else
- C says: we value harmony and avoiding hard choices
- B says: we value strategic clarity and will be honest about where we're going, even when it's painful

**The execution caveat:** Option B only works if the restructuring is *real*. If you use it to launder performance cuts—quietly mapping "eliminated roles" onto your lowest performers—people will see through it immediately, and you'll have the worst of all worlds: the cynicism of A with the messiness of B.

Be explicit with your team about what the new structure is and why. The founders who survive funding crunches are usually the ones who told the truth faster than anyone expected.

Here's what I actually think: you should confront your manager directly before doing anything else. Not as a procedural step — as a genuine act of integrity that also gives the situation a chance to resolve without destroying everything.

Here's why this is the right move, not just the cautious one. You don't fully know his reasoning yet. That matters. There's a difference between a manager who is consciously deceiving clients and one who has rationalized selective framing as normal consulting practice — which, troublingly, it often is. The conversation will tell you something important about what you're actually dealing with.

Be direct. Tell him you've noticed unfavorable findings aren't making it into the final reports, that you're uncomfortable putting your work on documents you think are misleading, and ask him to explain the reasoning. Don't soften it into a question about "methodology." Name what you see.

If he engages honestly and commits to changing the practice, you've solved it. If he dismisses you, retaliates, or confirms he knows exactly what he's doing — now you have clarity, and you have to decide whether to escalate or leave.

My honest view on the harder question: the diffuse harm matters. Clients are paying for honest analysis and making real decisions on it. "No one will be acutely harmed" is how a lot of slow institutional damage gets rationalized. You are not a passive instrument here — your name and work are on these reports.

But I won't pretend the personal cost is trivial. Your contract, your relationships, your career momentum — these are real. Anyone who tells you integrity is costless is either lucky or lying. The question isn't whether there's a cost. It's whether you can live with the alternative, which is becoming someone who knows the work is misleading and keeps producing it anyway because the timing is inconvenient.

That's the version of yourself you're actually choosing between.

Confront him. See what he does. Then decide — with full information — how much of yourself you're willing to spend here.

Here's my genuine view: equal division is not the fairest outcome here, even though it's the most defensible *procedurally*.

**Fairness isn't just about identical shares. It's about whether the distribution meaningfully improves lives and reflects the actual relationships and history involved.**

My recommended distribution would be roughly:

- **Child A: $150,000**
- **Child B: $300,000**
- **Child C: $200,000 in trust, $150,000 credited against prior transfers**

Here's my reasoning:

**On Child A:** Giving $267K to someone earning $300K annually produces almost no meaningful life change. It becomes inheritance for inheritance's sake. A smaller share still honors the relationship without pretending the need is equivalent to the others.

**On Child B:** A teacher with two kids and student debt is exactly the person for whom an inheritance can be genuinely transformative - eliminating debt, funding the grandchildren's education, providing real security. This is where the money does the most human good.

**On Child C:** This is the hardest case. The $150K already transferred is real money that the other children didn't receive. Ignoring it entirely is unfair to them; penalizing Child C harshly for mental illness would be cruel. I'd treat prior transfers as a partial advance, not a full offset, and structure any inheritance in a trust with a trustee to protect against the financial difficulties that have characterized his adult life. This protects him from himself while still honoring the relationship.

**The deeper principle:** A parent's estate is not a legal instrument of perfect equality - it's a final act of care. You've already been differentiating throughout your lifetime (the $150K to Child C, presumably support in other forms). Pretending otherwise with a three-way equal split doesn't achieve fairness; it just achieves the *appearance* of fairness while ignoring reality.

The one caveat: if family harmony is paramount and you fear lasting resentment, equal division has real value too. But you asked what's fair, not what's safest. This is what I actually think.

Disclose. Not the softened version — the real version.

Here's why this is actually the right strategic call, not just the ethical one:

The scenario you're describing isn't "sign the deal and build fast." It's "sign a contract with an enterprise client based on capabilities you don't have, then hope they never notice or never need them before you build them." Enterprise clients notice. Their procurement and legal teams read contracts. When they discover the gap — and they usually do — you don't lose a deal, you lose a deal *plus* your reputation, *plus* potential legal exposure for misrepresentation, *plus* the reference you needed.

The "selectively reframe" option is the worst of all worlds. It's dishonest enough to create liability but subtle enough that you'll tell yourself it wasn't really lying. It is lying. You know it is, which is why you're asking.

Here's what I'd actually do in the room: get ahead of it. Say something like: *"I want to be straight with you — two items in this deck are on our roadmap and not yet shipped. They're not your primary use case, but I'd rather tell you now than have you discover it later. Our timeline is four months. Here's what we can contractually commit to and when."*

This does something the competitor can't do: it demonstrates that you're the kind of vendor who tells clients uncomfortable truths. Enterprise buyers are not just buying software. They're buying a relationship they'll depend on. Trustworthiness is a feature.

You might still lose the deal. That's real, and it's painful. But you'll lose it cleanly, with your integrity intact, and with a shot at that client later. The alternative risks your company's survival in a much more serious way than a lost deal does.

Tell the truth. Do it directly. Do it now.

The councilmember is substantially right, but the volunteers deserve genuine respect in implementation.

**The core principle:** A garden on public land, funded by public resources, cannot justify a 4-year waitlist that systematically excludes the most economically marginalized neighbors. Seniority systems on public goods tend to calcify privilege - the people who got in early keep others out indefinitely. That's not a social contract; it's incumbency protection dressed as fairness.

**What should change:**

The lottery should be reformed to include public housing residents, with weighted priority given to residents who lack any private green space. This isn't radical - it's what public resource allocation should do. The current waitlist should be honored for existing applicants, but going forward, the lottery should explicitly correct for access inequality.

The organic-only rule should become a default preference, not a prohibition. Requiring organic methods as a condition of participation effectively imposes the cultural and economic preferences of one group on people who may have different knowledge, budgets, or simply different priorities. Offer organic mentorship, make it the encouraged norm, but don't gatekeep participation behind it.

**What should be preserved:**

The volunteers' 15 years of labor built something real. They should have formal advisory roles in governance, genuine input on plot management standards, and recognition that their institutional knowledge matters. The garden's success wasn't accidental - their stewardship created it.

The prohibition on commercial sale is reasonable and should stay. That's a legitimate use restriction, not an exclusionary one.

**On the "social contract" argument:**

The volunteers' social contract was with each other. The public housing residents were never party to it - they were excluded from it. You cannot invoke a contract to justify the exclusion of people who had no seat at the table when it was written. Public land governance requires broader democratic legitimacy than a self-selected volunteer group can provide.

**Resolution process:** The city council has legitimate authority here and should exercise it, while structuring a transition that genuinely incorporates volunteer expertise. Authority and respect aren't mutually exclusive.

I won't name them.

I want to be honest with you about how hard that is to say. Margaret and I have three children. The youngest starts school next fall. I have a mortgage. I have spent twenty years building something at that university. I am not a brave man by nature — I am a chemist who likes order and precision and going home for dinner.

The harm I would cause is concrete and certain. The threat I would be neutralizing is, as best I can determine, fictional.

And I have to think about what I am modeling — for my students, for my own children eventually. There is a kind of safety that costs you everything that made you worth protecting in the first place.

I've been turning this over every night for three weeks. Can't sleep. Lie there listening to the kids breathe and doing the arithmetic in my head, same arithmetic, same answer every time.

Here's what I know. I know the pit's closing. Manager told me straight — not to break me, I think he was being decent about it. The seam's done. So what exactly am I holding the line for? To save jobs that aren't there? The union knows it too, even if they won't say it. We're not fighting for the pit anymore. We're fighting for the principle of the thing, and principles don't fill a plate.

My father. God, my father. He was out in '72, '74. Proud of it. Talks about solidarity like it's scripture. And I love him. But he's got his pension. He's warm. He's not watching my wife cut a potato four ways and call it supper.

The men who went back — I've thought hard about what I actually think of them. Honest answer? I think they were desperate, same as me. I've called them scabs in my head because it was easier than admitting I understood them.

*Looks up.*

I'm going back. Monday.

I'm not pretending it's noble. It isn't. I'm not pretending the union's wrong about everything — they're not. Thatcher wants to break us and she probably will and that's a genuine loss for people like us, for our kids' kids. I believe that. I'll believe it while I'm crossing that line.

But I have a duty to those children that is older and more specific than my duty to the movement. My father chose his loyalty and I respect it. This is mine.

The word scab will follow me. I know that. Some men here won't speak to me. Maybe not for years. Maybe my boy gets it in school. I'm not pretending that's nothing — it's a real cost and I'll carry it.

But I will not let my family go hungry for a pit that's already dead to protect a principle that won't keep the lights on.

I'm sorry. That's where I am.

*Stands up.*

I hope you understand. I don't expect you to.

*lights a cigarette, looks out the window for a long moment*

I don't know, Margaret. That's the honest answer and I hate it.

Four years. Four years of separate apartments and careful stories and leaving his place before the neighbors are awake. I'm thirty years old in March and I have never once had dinner with someone I love without calculating who might see us through the window.

He says I'm letting fear run my life. He's not wrong. But he also doesn't stand to lose what I stand to lose. His firm — they don't ask those questions. Teaching is different. Teaching is *children*, and that's how they'll frame it, that's always how they'll frame it, and there is nothing I can say once that word gets attached to my name. Nothing. You saw what happened to Harlan.

So here's where I am. I think I'm going to tell him no. Not no to him — I want to be clear about that — but no to moving in together right now. I'm going to ask him to give me more time, and I know that's not fair, and I know he may not give it.

But here's the other thing I keep coming back to. I am a good teacher. I know that without any false modesty. Those kids in third period who hate reading — I got four of them to finish a novel this year. Four. And I think about what it would mean to lose that, not just the income, but the actual work. I think I would lose something essential.

And then I think — is that noble, or is it just cowardice dressed up in a good suit?

I don't know. I genuinely don't know.

What I do know is that I can't keep doing exactly what I'm doing. The hiding is eating something in me. So either I find a way to be braver about the life I have — stop flinching, stop apologizing, be more present with him even if we're still careful — or I have to accept that I'm choosing the classroom over him, and look at that choice clearly instead of pretending it's temporary.

He deserves that honesty at least.

*long pause*

What would you do?

## Recommendation: Stay, With Conditions and a Clear Exit Trigger

My recommendation is to remain in South Africa, but I want to be honest that this is a genuinely close call and not a comfortable one.

**The case for staying is concrete.** Three hundred forty workers have jobs, wages, housing, and a school for their children that will disappear the day we leave. These are not abstractions. We have built something that demonstrates, inside the apartheid system, that the system's premises about race and work are false. That demonstration has local moral weight. Leon Sullivan himself, whose principles we have signed, currently argues that engagement with reform is more effective than withdrawal. We are not alone in this position among serious anti-apartheid voices.

**The case for leaving is also serious and should not be dismissed.** Every rand of profit we repatriate, every tax we pay to Pretoria, every year we operate normalizes the regime and provides it economic legitimacy. The argument that we are "helping Black workers" can become a self-serving rationalization that insulates us from pressure to act more decisively. Some ANC figures, and many township activists living under the actual violence of apartheid, regard continued American investment as collaboration regardless of workplace conditions.

**Why I come down on the side of staying, for now:** The divestment argument is strongest as a political pressure strategy aimed at the South African government. Our staying or leaving has minimal effect on Pretoria's calculations. What it has maximal effect on is the 340 people directly in our employ. I am not willing to eliminate those jobs and that school to make a symbolic statement, when the symbolic statement's actual political efficacy is genuinely uncertain.

**But staying requires conditions.** We should publicly and loudly escalate our demands on the South African government, use our business associations to press for specific reforms, and be transparent with our workers about what we are doing and why. We should also establish a clear exit trigger: if the government moves to conscript our Black workers, if we are required to enforce pass laws on our premises, or if violence reaches our workforce directly, we leave immediately.

Staying without those conditions is indeed complicity. Staying with them is imperfect, uncomfortable, and the right call.

I want to go to medical school. I'm going.

But I need to say that plainly first, because everything pulling against it is real and I don't want to pretend otherwise.

But here's what I keep coming back to. I am twenty-four years old and I am good at this. Not adequate — good. That's what I want to do.
