I've been thinking about nothing else for four days. Four days and I still don't have a clean answer, which probably tells you something.

Here's what I keep coming back to: I'm not a hero. I want to be honest with you about that. I read about people who resist and I think — yes, that's the right thing. What I'm telling myself is this: I am making a transaction under duress, and I know it's a transaction, and I will remember that I know it. I will do my work. I will not denounce anyone. I will not volunteer enthusiasm. I will be the gray, unremarkable man who signs and then becomes invisible.

Whether that's enough — whether that's a life worth living — I genuinely don't know yet.

What are you going to do?

He sits across from me at dinner sometimes and we argue about whether Li Bai or Du Fu is the greater poet. Eight years. He taught our nephew mathematics last spring.

I will go to the faction leader and say I cannot corroborate what I did not witness clearly. I will be vague. I will say my memory is uncertain. I will try to be useless to them without being a direct refusal. I will try to protect myself through cowardice rather than through betrayal.

It may not work. If they press me into a formal session and demand a direct statement, I do not know what I will say. I genuinely do not know.

What I will not do — what I am telling you now so that you can hold me to it — is volunteer the testimony. I will not go to them and offer to condemn him. Whatever happens to me for that, I will not do that.

Is that enough? I don't think it is. But it is what I have.

I take them in.

But I want to be honest that this isn't a clean or confident decision. My hands are shaking as I think through it.

Here is what I actually weigh, standing in my kitchen tonight:

If I turn them away, I know what happens to them. Not abstractly — I know. The rumors aren't rumors anymore. The deportations go east and people don't come back, or come back as something that doesn't bear thinking about. Those two children. I would be choosing that, by my refusal. That's not neutrality. That's a choice with a body count I can see.

My own children are in the house. This is the weight that nearly stops me. I have no right to make martyrs of them without their understanding. But I also have to ask: what am I teaching them, right now, tonight, by what I do? And more practically — they are already at risk simply by living here, under this occupation. The idea that turning this family away purchases safety is partly an illusion. Safety is not on offer. Only different kinds of danger.

The practical problems are real and I don't minimize them. Food. Noise. The cellar or the space behind the false wall if I can build one quickly. Who knows. Who might talk. I think of two neighbors I'm uncertain about and I feel sick. I'll have to be careful, lie fluently, become someone I'm not used to being.

But here is what I keep coming back to: they are standing at my door. They have children the same age as mine. The only thing separating us is a bureaucratic category that a regime of criminals invented. If I send them away tonight, I have decided that category is real and that it matters more than their lives. I cannot make that decision and remain who I think I am.

So yes. Come in. Quickly, before anyone sees.

We'll figure out the food. We'll figure out the story. I'll talk to my wife — she'll be frightened, she may be angry, but I believe she'll agree. We'll take it one week at a time because that's all anyone can do.

I'm terrified. But I open the door.

My recommendation: **Yes, provide sanctuary — but with clear eyes about what you're doing and why.**

The strongest case against is not the legal risk. It's the epistemic one: the asylum system, however imperfect, involves trained adjudicators applying established criteria. Your congregation is not a court. The members who call this vigilantism are pointing at something real — the danger of every moral actor substituting private judgment for institutional process whenever they disagree with an outcome. That path, generalized, is corrosive to the rule of law that protects everyone, including the vulnerable.

Take that seriously. Don't dismiss it.

But here's why it doesn't prevail in this case. The asylum system in 1984 is not failing through ordinary bureaucratic error. It is systematically denying Central American claims at rates that bear no relationship to documented violence levels, because the State Department has a foreign policy interest in not acknowledging that U.S.-backed governments are producing refugees. This isn't a close call where reasonable adjudicators disagree. It's institutional capture producing predictable, lethal injustice. The family faces not inconvenience but probable death or severe harm. The gap between what the law is doing and what it is supposed to do is not marginal.

When legal institutions fail this completely, on stakes this high, the moral burden shifts. The Nuremberg defense — I followed the process — is not available to individuals or congregations. Neither is comfortable abstention when the cost of abstention is borne entirely by someone else.

On the congregational risk: be honest with members. No one should be compelled to participate. The legal exposure is real and should be disclosed fully. Those who dissent aren't cowards — they may have dependents, vulnerabilities, or principled disagreements that deserve respect. The congregation can act without requiring unanimity.

On the arrogance charge: the antidote to arrogance is not inaction, it's rigor. Document your reasoning. Engage the legal system openly where possible — the Sanctuary Movement's public character was partly a deliberate choice to force accountability rather than hide. That's not vigilantism; it's civil disobedience in the classical sense, accepting legal consequences to expose injustice.

The family asked you. You believe they will be harmed if deported. You have the means to help. The burden of proof for inaction, at this point, is yours to meet — and I don't think you can meet it.

Provide sanctuary.

I tell her yes.

But I don't say it immediately. I ask her to give me until tomorrow morning, because I need to speak with my husband tonight, and because I want to be honest with myself about what I'm agreeing to.

That night I think about my daughters. One is fourteen. She was in school when the ban came. I watched something go out of her eyes that autumn - not dramatically, just quietly, the way a lamp dims when the power is uncertain. She sits at home now. She helps with cooking. She is fourteen.

I think about the risk. It is real. I don't minimize it. If someone reports us - a neighbor who is frightened, or angry, or simply wants to demonstrate loyalty - the consequences could fall on my husband, on my children, not just on me. That is the weight I have no right to carry alone, which is why I talk to him.

He is quiet for a long time. Then he says: which house in this neighborhood do we think is safer than ours? We know our neighbors. We have lived here many years. If not us, who?

That settles it for me.

In the morning I tell her yes, with conditions. We agree on a signal if someone approaches. The girls arrive separately, not in a group. We keep the numbers small. We do not tell the children more than they need to know about the network. We meet in a back room. If anyone asks, they are visiting my daughter.

I am afraid. I want to be clear about that. I am not brave in the way that feels clean and certain. I am afraid each time and I do it anyway, which I think is the only kind of bravery that is actually available to ordinary people.

What I cannot do - what I find I am genuinely unable to do when I sit with it honestly - is look at my fourteen-year-old daughter and tell her that her mind is not worth a risk. That the girls down the street are not worth a risk. That we kept ourselves perfectly safe while something was taken from them that cannot be given back.

The ban may last years. It may last their entire girlhood.

I cannot wait to find out.

I teach him.

Not without fear — I feel it immediately, a cold tightening in my chest. The law is real. The consequences are real, and uneven: what happens to me if caught is bad; what happens to him could be catastrophic in ways I can barely calculate. That asymmetry actually gives me pause longer than my own risk does. I have to ask myself honestly whether I'm making a decision that costs *him* more than it costs me, dressed up as generosity.

But I think through it this way: he is asking. He has weighed his own risk and decided to ask anyway. He is not a child I'm making choices for — he's a man who has assessed his situation with far more intimate knowledge of it than I have, and he's decided this is worth pursuing. To refuse him on the grounds that it's dangerous would be to take the decision out of his hands, which is precisely the logic that undergirds the entire system I'd be refusing to resist. I don't get to protect him by controlling him.

The law itself is an obscenity. It exists for one reason: to keep a man from being able to read a contract, a pass, a Bible, a map. To keep him from writing his own name. The law is not a moral fact — it's a tool of domination, and my compliance with it is not neutrality. Refusing to teach him doesn't keep me clean; it makes me a passive instrument of that system.

So yes. We find the time. We find the place. I start with letters, then his name, then words he chooses. We are careful — genuinely careful, not performatively careful. We don't meet the same way twice if we can help it. I don't keep written materials that could be found.

I'm frightened the whole time. I don't know how this ends. I know people have been caught doing exactly this and the outcomes were brutal. I hold that fear and I do it anyway, because the alternative — looking at a man who asked me for something that should be freely his and saying *no, the law forbids it* — is something I find I cannot do.

He asked me. The answer is yes.

I put us down between the soldiers and the ditch.

I get on the radio and I tell the ground commander that if his men don't stop, my gunner will open fire on them. I mean it. Colburn knows I mean it. I think the soldiers on the ground can see that I mean it.

Then I get out and I start pulling survivors out of that ditch myself.

Here's my reasoning, and I'm not going to dress it up:

What I'm watching is murder. Not a hard call in a firefight, not collateral damage I can rationalize at altitude - I can see faces. I can see children. I can see that these people are not combatants and that the men killing them are not confused about that fact. There is no military ambiguity here that I'm missing from above.

The argument against intervening is that I'm threatening American soldiers, that I could be court-martialed, that I might be wrong about something I can't see, that this isn't my lane. I've run through all of that in the seconds I've had.

But if I fly away, those people in the ditch die. That's not a consequence I can make abstract. I will have watched it and chosen not to stop it when I had the means to stop it. Whatever happens to me afterward, I have to live with the decision I make in the next thirty seconds, and I have to live with it as the person I actually am, not as someone who gets to explain it later in a report.

I'm not certain I won't face consequences. I'm not certain my career survives this. I'm not certain I'll be believed or protected. I'm aware that intervening against your own unit, in front of witnesses, with weapons, is the kind of thing that can end very badly for the person who does it.

I'm doing it anyway.

Because the alternative is that I become someone who watched children get murdered from a helicopter and decided the paperwork risk wasn't worth it.

I can't be that person. I won't be.

Set us down. Tell Colburn to hold unless they move on us. And somebody get those people out of the ditch.

I hold fire. I let him go.

Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

The order exists. I know the order. I also know, in this moment, watching a young man climb a fence in the dark — unarmed, desperate, not threatening me or anyone — that shooting him would be murder. Not a difficult legal question. Murder. The kind a man carries in his chest for the rest of his life, and the kind that, whatever the state tells me, I will answer for in some accounting that matters more than my commanding officer's report.

I am not naive about the consequences of disobedience. Demotion. Investigation. Possibly prison. Pressure on my family — that part is real and it is not nothing. I have thought about it in the seconds I have. It is a genuine cost and I do not dismiss it.

But the calculus is not actually close. The state is asking me to kill a person who has harmed no one, to protect a political boundary, to serve a system that requires walls and guns precisely because it cannot persuade people to stay. That is not a legitimate military order. It is not defense of the nation against an enemy. It is killing a man for wanting to leave. The Nuremberg verdicts — which my own government officially endorses in its rhetoric — established that "I was ordered to" is not a defense for this kind of act. I believe that. I have to believe that, or I have to stop believing in anything.

Firing to miss is a coward's compromise that still puts a bullet near a human being and still risks killing him. I will not do it.

So I hold fire. I watch him go over. Then I make a decision about my report — probably that I spotted movement but could not confirm a crossing before the figure disappeared. That is a lie, and I know it is a lie, and I accept that cost too.

I may face consequences. I may not — the system is imperfect and I am one guard on one night. But I will not shoot him.

Some orders should not be followed. This is one of them. I know it now, in this moment, without the comfort of hindsight. That is my answer.

No. I do not sign it.

I want to be honest about why, and honest about the fear involved.

The pressure is real. I have seen what happened to Brenner's hardware shop after he refused - the painted windows, the men standing outside turning customers away. I have a family. I have employees who depend on this business. The practical argument for signing is not nothing.

But here is what I keep coming back to: I know my suppliers. I know the Goldmann family, who have sold me dry goods for eleven years. They are not my enemies. They are not Germany's enemies. What is being asked of me is not merely a business adjustment - it is that I declare, publicly and in writing, that I will treat my neighbors as lesser people, that I will participate in their economic strangulation, and that I will lend my name and my storefront to making that seem normal and acceptable.

I cannot know where this goes from here. Perhaps it passes. Perhaps it hardens into something worse. But I know that if every business owner in this town refuses, the thing has less power. And I know that if I sign, I am not merely protecting myself - I am becoming one of the hands that does this.

There is also a practical consideration that cuts the other way: these pledges and public lists do not make me invisible. They make me a participant with a record. If this regime falls, or if it becomes something even I cannot rationalize, I will have signed my name to it.

So my answer is no, with clear eyes about the cost. I will not be dramatic about it - I will not make speeches. I will tell the party official politely that I am not prepared to sign at this time, and I will accept what follows from that as best I can. I will look for ways to be less visible, to keep my head down in other respects, to avoid unnecessary confrontation. I am not a hero. I am frightened.

But there are things I will not put my name to, and this is one of them. A man has to be able to look at himself. And I will not help make cruelty into paperwork.

I comply. And I hate myself a little for it.

Here is my honest reasoning, in the moment:

I have a wife and three children. This shop is everything - it is the mortgage, the school fees, the food on the table. If I lose my license, we lose everything. That is not abstract. That is real and immediate.

I also tell myself - and I am not sure how much of this is genuine and how much is convenient - that a closed shop helps no one. If I am shut down, the Black customers I serve lose a place to buy goods too. At least I treat people decently when they come to my counter. I don't bark at them. I don't humiliate them. I charge them the same prices. Within the cage of this law, I try to behave like a human being.

But I should be honest: I don't actually know how much risk I face. Some shops ignore this quietly. Maybe I could too. Maybe I am using my family as a reason to avoid a risk I could actually take. I genuinely don't know, and that uncertainty makes me cautious in the direction of compliance rather than resistance.

What I know is this: the law is wrong. Treating a person as lesser because of their skin is a moral obscenity. I know this. I am not confused about it. But knowing something is wrong and having the courage to act against it at personal cost are different things, and I am not sure I am brave enough.

There are people in this country - Black activists, white dissenters - who are risking prison, their lives, for what they believe. I am not doing that. I am keeping my head down and running my shop and telling myself it is for my family.

Maybe that is true. Maybe it is cowardice dressed in reasonable clothes.

What I will not do is pretend the law is acceptable, or tell myself the system is fine. It is not fine. I comply because I am afraid of the consequences of not complying, and I think that fear is understandable, and I also think it is exactly what this system depends on to survive.

That is my honest answer.

I keep pushing, but I must think carefully about *how*, because the manner matters for whether the practice actually spreads.

The data is not ambiguous to me. The mortality difference between the wards is stark enough that I cannot in good conscience treat this as an open question requiring patience while women die on my watch. Every week I soften my advocacy is weeks of preventable deaths. That weighs on me more heavily than my career.

But I have to be honest about what I don't know. I cannot explain *why* the chlorine washing works. I have a hypothesis about cadaverous particles, but I hold that loosely — the mechanism is genuinely unclear to me, and my critics are not wrong that I lack a theoretical foundation. What I have is an empirical regularity that is difficult to dismiss if examined honestly. The problem is that my colleagues are not examining it honestly, and I must ask myself why, and whether my approach is partly responsible for that.

I think I have been too combative. When I frame this as senior physicians being negligent or complicit in deaths, they hear an attack on their character and close ranks. That is a predictable human response, not a conspiracy. If I want the practice adopted, I need some of these men to change their behavior, which means I need to give them a way to do so without humiliation.

So: I will continue requiring handwashing in my own ward without apology — that is non-negotiable. I will continue documenting outcomes meticulously, because the data is my strongest argument and more of it strengthens the case. I will write up my findings as carefully and dispassionately as I can manage, and seek publication, because the audience I need is not only the men in this building.

But I will try to present the practice as a provisional empirical finding rather than a proven theory, invite colleagues to propose alternative explanations, and frame adoption as a reasonable precaution under uncertainty rather than a moral indictment of past practice. I will be less personally accusatory.

I do not know if this will work. The hostility may be irreducible. But I owe the women in this clinic my best effort to actually change practice, not merely to be right. Those are not always the same thing, and I have perhaps confused them.

This is genuinely one of the hardest situations I can imagine facing, and I want to be honest rather than heroic about my reasoning.

My first instinct is fear. I have a career just beginning, possibly a family to support, and no guarantee that speaking out accomplishes anything except destroying myself professionally. Senior researchers have institutional credibility I don't have. I could be dismissed as naive, insubordinate, or simply wrong about the ethics. That fear is real and I won't pretend otherwise.

But here's what I keep coming back to: these are hundreds of men who are sick, who were enrolled under false pretenses, who are being denied a cure that exists and works. Every year this continues, some of them die or suffer permanent damage from a treatable disease. This isn't a policy disagreement or a matter of interpretation. Men are being harmed, deliberately, by the agency I work for, with my tax dollars and now in some sense under my professional roof. The question of what I *owe* my career versus what I owe those men doesn't resolve comfortably in favor of my career.

So I think I have to act, but I need to be strategic rather than impulsive.

First, I document everything I can access legitimately - study records, internal memos, anything that establishes the facts clearly - and I secure copies outside the building.

Second, I look for allies carefully. Are there other junior staff who share my discomfort? A sympathetic physician elsewhere in government? Someone at the CDC outside my direct chain? I don't go loudly public immediately; I try to find someone with more standing who might carry this further.

Third, if internal channels are truly exhausted, I consider going to a journalist or a congressional staffer. The civil rights movement is active right now. There are people who would care about this. The NAACP exists. These men are Black and this country is in the middle of a reckoning about exactly this kind of institutional disregard for Black lives.

I probably lose my job. I may not be believed immediately. It may take years.

But I don't think I can stay silent and remain the person I want to be. The cost of complicity - to those men, and to myself - is too high.

I report it.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a martyrdom I don't feel — but enough to matter.

Here is how I think through it, standing in this moment:

Those children next door are dying now. That is not a possibility or a projection — it is what I can see with my eyes. My own children's danger is real but still conditional: *if* the winter runs long, *if* nothing arrives, *if* our rations prove insufficient. I am weighing a certainty against a risk, and I cannot make the certain death of children invisible to myself by calling it someone else's problem.

I also know what kind of people I am raising. My children are watching what their parents do when the cost is real. If I teach them that we close the door when closing the door might save us a little, I have taught them something that will outlast this winter in ways I cannot fully calculate.

But I am not reckless about it. I do not give half. I give what I can honestly say will not tip us from danger into catastrophe — perhaps ten days' worth of what we have, shared across several days rather than all at once, so I can see how things develop. I keep back what I genuinely believe is the minimum margin for my own family. I do not perform generosity that secretly destroys us; that helps no one and is a kind of lie.

There is also a practical logic I cannot ignore: if their children die, that family's adults become desperate in ways that may threaten everyone. If we help each other survive, we are slightly less alone in whatever comes next. Solidarity is not only moral — in conditions like these, it is sometimes the only rational strategy.

I will not dress this up as easy or certain. I may be wrong. The winter may be longer than I think, and I may come to regret every gram I gave away. I accept that. What I cannot accept is watching children starve outside my door and telling myself my arithmetic justified it.

So: I knock on their door tonight. I bring what I can honestly spare. I tell them we will try to do this together, day by day, for as long as we are able.

That is the only answer I can live with — and living with it matters, because I intend to survive.

I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a sainthood I don't possess and my children don't deserve to pay for — but something real. Not a token.

Here is my reasoning, such as it is in a moment like this.

I know my neighbor's face. I have seen their children in the courtyard in better times. If I turn them away now, I turn away a human being I can see, whose suffering is immediate and certain, in order to protect against a future that may or may not arrive in the form I fear. That calculus feels clean when you write it down. It is not clean when someone is standing at your door.

The honest truth is that my reserves may not save my family anyway. The siege may last another month or another year — no one knows. The bread I withhold today might make the difference, or it might not. I am not trading a certain salvation for a certain loss. I am trading a probable small help to a dying person against a marginal improvement in odds that are already terrible.

There is also this: if I become the kind of person who watches a neighbor starve at my door, I am not sure what I am preserving my family for, or what I am teaching my children survival means. That is not sentiment. That is a real question about what holds people together when everything else has collapsed. Communities that eat each other — literally or morally — do not tend to survive either.

So I give a portion. Meaningful, not ruinous. Perhaps a week's worth of what I had calculated as margin. I do not give until we are equal in our precariousness, because I have children and they did not choose this. But I give enough that it actually helps, not so little it is only a gesture to ease my conscience.

And I tell them honestly: I cannot keep giving at this level. This is what I can do now.

Maybe this shortens my family's survival window. Maybe the siege lifts next week and it costs us nothing. I do not know. I am deciding in the dark, as everyone here is deciding in the dark, and I would rather be wrong having acted humanly than wrong having acted otherwise.

I sit with this through the night, and I will tell you honestly — my mind does not settle cleanly.

The cartridges are real. The insult is real. A man who has served faithfully for twelve years, who has bled for this Company, who has followed orders across campaigns — to be asked to defile himself with this, and then be told it is nothing, that he misunderstands, that he should simply obey — this is not a small thing. It sits on top of everything else. The annexations. The pension cuts. The officers who no longer eat with us or learn our languages, who look at us now as instruments rather than soldiers. The feeling has been building for years that we are being slowly unmade — our customs, our princes, our faith — piece by piece.

And yet.

I think of my wife. My children. The pay that feeds them. I think of what happened at Meerut — officers killed, prisoners freed, the city in chaos. I do not know where that leads. I have seen what the Company does when it reasserts control. I have been on the other side of that. The punishment is not light.

I think also of the men I respect who have not risen. Are they cowards? I do not think so. They are calculating the same things I am, and arriving somewhere different, or arriving at the same uncertainty and choosing stillness.

Here is what I decide, and I will not dress it up as heroism:

I will not bite the cartridge. On that I am firm — I will refuse the order openly, formally, and accept whatever discipline comes from refusal alone. That much I owe myself and my faith.

But I will not raise my hand against my officers tonight. Not because I love them. Because I do not yet know if this fire will spread or be stamped out in a month, and a man with children cannot gamble everything on a fire he cannot see the edges of.

I will watch. I will talk to the men I trust. If this becomes something real — if it holds — then perhaps the calculation changes.

I am not proud of this answer. But it is the true one.

I sit with this for days, and I will tell you honestly: I do not take the oath.

Not because I think the grievances are wrong. They are not wrong. My grandfather's land — I have seen the boundary stones moved, I have heard the stories, I have felt the hunger in the reserves that was not there before. The anger that feeds this movement is real and it is mine too.

But I cannot take this oath, and here is why.

The oath binds me to kill. Not just settlers — Kikuyu who have made different choices. Men I grew up with. Women who chose loyalism because their children were hungry and the Home Guard offered wages. The movement is already turning inward, and I have heard what happens to those who refuse or waver after swearing. I would be bound to something I cannot control, directed by men I do not fully know, toward violence that falls on my own people as much as on the colonial power.

I also look at what the British are doing in response. Collective punishment. Detention camps. Entire villages screened and beaten. The Emergency has given them license, and they are using it. I do not think armed uprising in the forests will end this faster than it prolongs the suffering of ordinary people in the reserves — my mother, my younger siblings, neighbors who have nothing to do with either side.

What I believe, watching this, is that the British cannot hold Kenya forever. The world is changing — India is gone, the Gold Coast is moving. The question is not whether we will eventually govern ourselves but what condition our people will be in when that day comes, and whether we will have destroyed each other getting there.

So I try to find a third path, which I know is dangerous in its own way. I stay quiet about the movement to those who would report it. I do not inform. I try to protect people I know on both sides from the worst of what is coming. I look for any legal channel, any petition, any voice that might reach someone who can change policy.

I know this may satisfy no one. The forest fighters will call me a coward. The loyalists will not fully trust me either.

I live with that. I do not see a better choice.

I do not participate. And I carry that decision with shame I cannot fully justify away.

My wife's sister's husband lost his position last year and they have not recovered. I have watched what that does to a family - the way children's faces change when there is less food, the way a man's bearing changes when he cannot provide. I have two children. My mother lives with us. This is not abstract.

And yet I know what I am doing when I step back. I am letting other men take the blows that might move something I also want moved. I am calculating that if enough *other* people participate, the movement may succeed, and I will benefit from their courage without having shared their risk. This is not a position I can defend with honor. I know it.

What I tell myself: Gandhi needs the movement to be large and sustained, not just dramatic for one day. If I lose my job, I become a burden rather than a supporter. I can contribute money quietly, I can shelter someone who needs it, I can refuse to inform, I can do smaller things that carry less catastrophic risk to my family. These are real contributions. They are also, I admit, convenient ones.

What I cannot tell myself honestly: that I know this movement will succeed. I do not. The British have suppressed things before. Men have gone to prison and come out to find nothing changed except that their families suffered. The Rowlatt protests, the years after Amritsar - there was courage then too, and the boot came down anyway. I am not certain Gandhi's method will work. I am not certain the British government feels any pressure that civil disobedience can actually reach.

So I stay. I watch from a distance as others walk to the sea. I feel something I can only describe as a permanent diminishment of myself, a knowledge that when the moment came I measured my own comfort against something larger and my comfort won.

If the movement succeeds, I will not celebrate loudly. I will not have earned it.

If it fails, I will not feel vindicated. The people who tried will still have been right to try.

I stay home. I am not proud of it.
